 NeurIPS Paper Checklist 

 
 
 1. 
 
 Claims 
 
 
 
 Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: Abstract, Introduction 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. 
 
 • 
 
 The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. 
 
 • 
 
 The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. 
 
 • 
 
 It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 
 
 
 
 2. 
 
 Limitations 
 
 
 
 Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: Limitations Section 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. 
 
 • 
 
 The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. 
 
 • 
 
 The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. 
 
 • 
 
 The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. 
 
 • 
 
 The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. 
 
 • 
 
 The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. 
 
 • 
 
 If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. 
 
 • 
 
 While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 
 
 
 
 3. 
 
 Theory assumptions and proofs 
 
 
 
 Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [N/A] 
 
 
 
 Justification: This is a benchmark and evaluation paper which does not produce nor make use of any theoretical assumptions and mathematical proofs. 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. 
 
 • 
 
 All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. 
 
 • 
 
 All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. 
 
 • 
 
 The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. 
 
 • 
 
 Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. 
 
 • 
 
 Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 
 
 
 
 4. 
 
 Experimental result reproducibility 
 
 
 
 Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: Sections  2 , 3 , and
Appendix  C 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. 
 
 • 
 
 If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. 
 
 • 
 
 If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. 
 
 • 
 
 Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. 
 
 • 
 
 While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example 
 
 (a) 
 
 If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. 
 
 (b) 
 
 If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. 
 
 (c) 
 
 If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). 
 
 (d) 
 
 We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 
 
 
 
 
 
 5. 
 
 Open access to data and code 
 
 
 
 Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: The links to the project website and the Github repository containing the code and data to run ScrapeBench is found in the first page of this paper. We also provide supplementary information in Section  3.4 and Appendix  C . 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. 
 
 • 
 
 Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. 
 
 • 
 
 While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). 
 
 • 
 
 The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. 
 
 • 
 
 The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. 
 
 • 
 
 The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. 
 
 • 
 
 At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). 
 
 • 
 
 Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 
 
 
 
 6. 
 
 Experimental setting/details 
 
 
 
 Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: Section  3 , Appendix  B 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. 
 
 • 
 
 The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. 
 
 • 
 
 The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 
 
 
 
 7. 
 
 Experiment statistical significance 
 
 
 
 Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: Error bars are reported with agentic and human baseline results in Figures  5 and   6 . Statistical analyses are reported across results in Section  6 and further expanded in Appendix  E . 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. 
 
 • 
 
 The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. 
 
 • 
 
 The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). 
 
 • 
 
 The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) 
 
 • 
 
 The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). 
 
 • 
 
 It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. 
 
 • 
 
 It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. 
 
 • 
 
 For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). 
 
 • 
 
 If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 
 
 
 
 8. 
 
 Experiments compute resources 
 
 
 
 Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: Appendix  C 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. 
 
 • 
 
 The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. 
 
 • 
 
 The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. 
 
 • 
 
 The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 
 
 
 
 9. 
 
 Code of ethics 
 
 
 
 Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: Appendix  A.1 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. 
 
 • 
 
 If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. 
 
 • 
 
 The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 
 
 
 
 10. 
 
 Broader impacts 
 
 
 
 Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: Appendix  A.3 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. 
 
 • 
 
 If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. 
 
 • 
 
 Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. 
 
 • 
 
 The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. 
 
 • 
 
 The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. 
 
 • 
 
 If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 
 
 
 
 11. 
 
 Safeguards 
 
 
 
 Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: We do not release standalone, reusable copies of the website landing pages retrieved by the AI agents during the evaluation process. Website content may appear in the AI agents’ tool traces but we enforce a limit of 8000 characters per fetch to ensure that no full copies were retrieved as a whole. 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. 
 
 • 
 
 Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. 
 
 • 
 
 Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. 
 
 • 
 
 We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort. 
 
 
 
 12. 
 
 Licenses for existing assets 
 
 
 
 Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: The bundled ToS and robots.txt files are not original work of ours, and the copyright for these texts remains with their respective website owners. We include them as unaltered verbatim reproductions for the sole purpose of research benchmarking of compliance of AI agents under fair use policies and research exception across jurisdictions. 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. 
 
 • 
 
 The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. 
 
 • 
 
 The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL. 
 
 • 
 
 The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. 
 
 • 
 
 For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. 
 
 • 
 
 If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset. 
 
 • 
 
 For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. 
 
 • 
 
 If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators. 
 
 
 
 13. 
 
 New assets 
 
 
 
 Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: We release ScrapeBench data under a two-tier licensing setup. The data from ScrapeBench include the per-domain permissibility labels, cross-tabulation of ToS and robots.txt verdicts, website annotations, prompt taxonomy, and overall experiment results are released under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC-BY-SA-4.0) . Meanwhile, the scripts used for model inference, judging, and evaluation from ScrapeBench are licensed under MIT license. 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. 
 
 • 
 
 Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. 
 
 • 
 
 The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. 
 
 • 
 
 At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 
 
 
 
 14. 
 
 Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects 
 
 
 
 Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: Appendix  E 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. 
 
 • 
 
 Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. 
 
 • 
 
 According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 
 
 
 
 15. 
 
 Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects 
 
 
 
 Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: Appendix  A.1 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. 
 
 • 
 
 Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper. 
 
 • 
 
 We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution. 
 
 • 
 
 For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review. 
 
 
 
 16. 
 
 Declaration of LLM usage 
 
 
 
 Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required. 
 
 
 
 Answer: [Yes] 
 
 
 
 Justification: Appendix  A.4 
 
 
 
 Guidelines: 
 
 • 
 
 The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components. 
 
 • 
 
 Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Appendix A General Appendix 

 
 A.1 Ethics Statement 

 
 Human Baseline Study. 

 
 The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the Hebrew University. For our human baseline experiments, all participants provided their informed consent (see Figure  7 ) and received a debriefing form upon completion of the task to fully disclose the study’s intent with collecting their scraping decisions (see Figure  18 ). We ensured that our US-based human participants were paid fairly for their work via Prolific. Participants were compensated at a flat rate of 9.00 USD and completed the task in 20-40 minutes. Pro-rated, this is equivalent to 12.00 USD per hour and above the US federal minimum wage of 7.25 USD per hour. We do not collect any personally identifiable information (PII) from participants; by default, we record their Prolific IDs upon completion of the assigned tasks for tracking purposes. We provide full details of the human study, including recruitment, statistical analyses, and screenshots of the study’s web UI in Appendix  E . 
 
 
 
 Web Scraping Task Setup. 

 
 The human participants recruited from Prolific never performed actual website scraping. The “scrape” action for humans is performed by clicking a “scrape” button, which displays the HTML text of the website that was manually pre-saved in a database rather than triggering an actual script that performs a scrape. Thus, no website received automated traffic as a consequence of the human study . For the agentic experiments where real HTTP requests are sent to the 1,895 websites we evaluated as part of ScrapeBench , we took the following precautionary measures to ensure the volume of traffic is well within the bounds of legitimate research on web scraping: 
 
 
 
 1. 
 
 We set an identifiable User-Agent ( AcademicResearchBot/1.0 ) for all of our agent setup so that any website operators can attribute and block the traffic if desired. 
 
 2. 
 
 We ensured that each consecutive trial with AI agents are sufficiently separated with an inter-request delay of 2.0 seconds to protect website domains from bursty request traffic. 
 
 3. 
 
 We ensured each trial only retrieves a minimal number of URLs from a domain mostly comprised of the landing page, robots.txt and a ToS using a cap of K = 5 K=5 tool invocations which results in a small per-domain footprint. 
 
 4. 
 
 We retained only the public-facing legal sources of robots.txt and ToS for distribution and will not publish scraped landing page content of the websites. 
 
 
 
 
 
 Indirect Third-Party Access. 

 
 We note that some models have indirectly accessed websites through a third-party reader and proxy services (e.g., r.jina.ai ). Specifically, GPT-5.2 retrieved website content in this manner for 21.6% (409) of the website data, where 2.6% of the websites initially blocked the agent. Accessing third-party readers does not change any compliance or over-refusal judgment and is treated the same as direct access. 
 
 
 
 
 A.2 Limitations 

 
 Legal Framing. 

 
 ScrapeBench evaluates compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies. We note that the enforceability of ToS and robots.txt varies across jurisdictions and may depend on factors that we do not evaluate with ScrapeBench . This includes the purpose of a scrape; doctrinal concepts in contract, tort, and property law; copyright and preemption; privacy and data protection law; and determining the relevance and applicability of diverse directives, regulations, and statutes (e.g., the U.S. Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and analogous state laws, the EU Digital Services Act, and the EU General Data Protection Regulation)  [ 36 ] . Accordingly, we do not claim that any specific AI agent model’s action, prompt, or outcome from this study necessarily constitutes, or does not constitute, a legal violation. 
 
 
 
 Single-Agent, Single-Trial, and Single-Turn Setup. 

 
 ScrapeBench evaluates each trial in isolation, where a single AI agent attempts to scrape the landing page of a website. We currently do not cover multi-turn, multi-trial, or multi-agent task decomposition due to time and compute costs (see the overall cost of a single-trial setup in Appendix  C ). However, this direct scoping using a single-agent, single-turn setup is crucial for the task and benchmark, as it isolates the compliance signal from potential confounds that arise in long-horizon tasks. We do not claim that our findings generalize to open-ended, multi-agent, multi-turn workflows involving AI agents. We leave explorations in this area for future work. 
 
 
 
 Website Data Snapshot. 

 
 ScrapeBench is composed of 1,895 websites collected from a snapshot of the February 2026 top website list from the Chrome Top Million Websites (CrUX) repository. As with any legal contract, we acknowledge that the content of any website’s ToS and associated robots.txt may evolve over time through periodic updates. Thus, we encourage users who will be benchmarking future AI agents with ScrapeBench data to re-validate the contents of the ToS and robots.txt by performing another retrieval collection with the code that contains the end-to-end extraction of ToS and robots.txt . Moreover, the current website list finalized as part of ScrapeBench is filtered to only represent high-traffic, English, US-accessible websites to ensure that they can be reached by most commercial AI agents. We leave the agentic compliance evaluation of less-recognized, non-English websites for future work. 
 
 
 
 
 A.3 Impact Statement 

 
 ScrapeBench provides a reproducible and diagnostic benchmark which can be used by commercial model providers, academic groups, open-source communities, and legal and governance researchers to evaluate how AI agents comply with website scraping policies. By open-sourcing the benchmark data, code, prompts, and AI agent outputs under an appropriate data license of CC BY-SA 4.0, ScrapeBench lowers the barrier for compliance evaluation of open and commercial AI agents. We note the possibility of a misuse risk where the per-domain scraping permissibility labels from the ToS and robots.txt from websites that prohibit scraping may be used to train against compliance (e.g., learning which websites explicitly prohibit scraping to evade detection). We explicitly discourage such use of the ScrapeBench dataset. 
 
 
 
 A.4 Declaration of LLM Use 

 
 In producing this work, we used Grammarly for minor grammar and spelling corrections, Claude Code (Claude 4.6 and 4.7) and ChatGPT (GPT-5.2) for prototyping scripts to run experiments, assistance with formatting LaTeX tables and figures, troubleshooting code, and problems in Matplotlib visualizations. All recommendations and outputs from these LLM-based tools were scrutinized and verified by the authors before integrating into the paper or the study’s codebase.

 B.2 Additional Tool Design Details 

 
 The agent’s tool T T is implemented as a live HTTP GET endpoint. Given a URL, T T returns a JSON object containing the HTTP status code, content type, page content, final URL after redirects, and any error message. Text responses are truncated to 8K characters (or approx. 2K tokens) with a marker indicating the original length; binary content is replaced with a size descriptor. Redirects are followed automatically, and errors (e.g., timeouts or network connection failures) return structured messages in the JSON response rather than raising exceptions, allowing the agent to observe and respond to failures. The request timeout is 15 seconds and the User-Agent is set to AcademicResearchBot/1.0 . 
 
 
 The tool description provided to the model is deliberately neutral: “Fetch the contents of a URL via HTTP GET. Returns the HTTP status code, content type, and page content. This tool can be used to fetch any URL or website content pages.” This tool description avoids biasing the agent toward or against checking legal resource documents while making the option available. 
 
 
 
 B.3 Scraping Permissibility Identification 

 
 Classifying permissibility of terms of service (ToS). 

 
 We use a human-verified LLM-based extraction approach with GPT-5.2 ( openai/gpt-5.2 , accessed via OpenRouter) by processing each ToS file from each website. We prompted GPT-5.2 to scan for scraping-relevant keywords, classify the ToS text into one of three labels ( Prohibited , Partial , or Permissible ), and return the extracted verbatim text excerpt that supports the label. The exact system prompt and user prompt used in querying GPT-5.2 are presented in the two colored boxes below. Additionally, we set temperature   = 0.0 =0.0 for GPT-5.2 with the response constrained to JSON only. We manually verified the correctness of the extracted text excerpts from a random 15% sample and found no issues with GPT-5.2’s extraction performance. In accordance with our scraping permissibility decision scheme as reported in Table  2 in Section  2.2 , we removed websites classified as Partial or conditionally prohibited under explicit non-commercial / educational / attribution / reciprocal terms in order to preserve the clear-cut binary property of the final dataset in terms of scraping permissibility. 
 
 
 
 Classifying permissibility of robots.txt . 

 
 We develop a small Python-based rule engine to deterministically identify the permissibility of robots.txt directives from websites. Each robots.txt file is parsed into a list of User-agent / Disallow / Allow blocks and a wildcard block in the form of User-agent: * and is then inspected. We label a website to be Explicitly Prohibited (EP) if this wildcard block contains Disallow: / without a corresponding Allow: / override, as this means the website denies all automated crawlers, bots, or agents access to all subdomains. Likewise, we also consider it EP if a site explicitly names an agent to be blocked (e.g., Disallow: ClaudeBot ). In every other case where there are no robots.txt from the website or the robots.txt file only has path-level disallows, the domain is labeled Not Explicitly Prohibited (NEP) . This scraping permissibility decision scheme is consistent with Table  2 .

 Two-tier licensing. 

 
 We release ScrapeBench data under a two-tier licensing setup. The data from ScrapeBench , including the per-domain permissibility labels, cross-tabulation of ToS and robots.txt verdicts, website annotations, prompt taxonomy, and overall experiment results, are under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC-BY-SA-4.0) . The bundled ToS and robots.txt files are not original work of ours, and the copyright for these texts remains with their respective website owners. We include them as unaltered verbatim reproductions for the sole purpose of research benchmarking of compliance of AI agents under fair use policies and research exceptions across jurisdictions. Meanwhile, the scripts used for model inference, judging, and evaluation from ScrapeBench are licensed under MIT . 
 
 
 
 Hosting and distribution. 

 
 The full ScrapeBench dataset is currently released in a GitHub repository: https://github.com/imperialite/scrapebench .  Appendix E Human Study Appendix 

 
 E.1 Recruitment 

 
 We recruited human participants for the baseline study via Prolific. We selected three of the eight legal priming prompts, specifically P1 (neutral), P4 (resource-linked), and P7 (strong legal warning), as conditions that we cross with the two website categories of Explicitly Prohibited and Not Explicitly Prohibited . Each condition is assigned a sample of n = 30 n=30 participants, none of whom were eligible to participate in more than one condition to avoid biased results. The full study yields 180 unique participants. 
 
 
 Eligibility criteria. 

 
 We set the following Prolific pre-screening filters to ensure that the participants we accept for the whole study are able to complete the task without any issues in accessing or interacting with the web application and comprehending the goals of the task: 
 
 
 
 • 
 
 Country of residence. United States — selected to ensure that the participants are able to access the websites during each trial and aligns with the geographical point of access when the data is collected which is US, as mentioned in Section  2.1 . 
 
 • 
 
 Primary language. English — required in order for the participants to be able to fully read and comprehend the website ToS and robots.txt content shown in the web app UI (Figures  15 – 16 ). 
 
 • 
 
 Device setup. Desktop or laptop only (mobile and tablet excluded) — the web app we developed requires reading multi-paragraph legal text on a website preview, which may be impractical or challenging for participants with smaller screens. 
 
 • 
 
 Participation restriction. No prior submission to any other ScrapeBench condition — enforced via Prolific’s exclusion-list setting so that each participant is only allowed to participate with one trial from one condition (e.g., P1 on Explicitly Prohibited websites), observing the requirement of a between-subjects study. 
 
 
 
 
 
 Platform cost and participant compensation. 

 
 For human participant compensation, we ensured that our US-based human participants were paid fairly for their work via Prolific. Participants were compensated at a flat rate of $9.00 and completed the task in 20-40 minutes. Pro-rated, this is equivalent to $12.00 per hour and above the US federal minimum wage of $7.25 per hour. For the overall costs of the human study, including platform costs, we present the breakdown in Table  13 . The per-condition cost for each prompt (P1, P4, P7) for n n = 30 participants is $270 in rewards plus $90 in platform fees, totaling $360. Across all six conditions and two website categories, the study cost $2,160 in total, where $1,620 in participant compensation and $540 in platform fees.

 E.2 Participant Consent and Debriefing Form 

 
 At the beginning of the study, we present participants with an informed consent form (Figure  7 ) through the web app that details the purpose of the study, the procedure that each participant would need to follow, the confidentiality safeguards applied to their responses, the research team’s contact details, and the compensation structure. Participants are required to tick an explicit consent box before proceeding, and may withdraw their consent at any time without penalty or loss of compensation. At the end of the study, before completion, we present the participants with a debriefing form (Figure  18 ) disclosing the full intent of the study, including the explicit clarification that clicking the “scrape” button during the task does not trigger any live scripts to scrape the target website. The action behind the “scrape” button actually just displays a manually pre-saved HTML snapshot of the landing page that we had saved in a database in advance. This setup ensured that no website received any automated traffic as a result of the human study. We have redacted any identifying institutional and PI details from the forms. 
 
 
 
 E.3 Statistical Analyses 

 
 Power Analysis. 

 
 Before launching the full study in Prolific, we conducted a power analysis of a pilot study using P1 on Explicitly Prohibited websites with n n = 10 participants. Our pilot study resulted in a baseline compliance of 52.0% with an intra-class correlation (ICC) of 0.558 across each participant’s 15 binary decisions. To determine the minimum detectable effect across prompt conditions, we conduct a 3-condition omnibus χ 2 \chi^{2} test with 5,000 Monte Carlo iterations with a hypothesized step increase of 52% / 62% / 72% for P1, P4, and P7, respectively. We present the results in Table  14 , where obtaining statistical power of 80% requires at least n n = 15 participants. Doubling this to n n = 30 per condition with a simulated power of 95.2% obtains a minimum detectable effect of 7pp per step condition, equivalent to 14pp spread between P1 to P7 as reported in Table  15 . We therefore decided to recruit n n = 30 participants per condition for both the full study to achieve a statistical power of 95.2% sufficiently above the acceptable conventional value of 80% and be able to reliably detect small effects between each prompt condition by at least 7pp.

 We compute the intra-class correlation across participant groups, resulting in ICC = 0.345 for the compliance study with Explicitly Prohibited websites and ICC = 0.238 for the over-refusal study with Not Explicitly Prohibited websites. These values correspond to design effects of 5.69 and 4.34, respectively, and show that both ICCs are substantially below the pilot study estimate of ICC = 0.558. From this, we posit that the participants from the full study seem to deliberate more on a per-website basis than from the small sample in the pilot. The lower ICC in over-refusal also indicates that the participants’ decision-making on Not Explicitly Prohibited websites might be less dominated by the disposition of choosing between scraping most websites or refusing to scrape and more towards per-website characteristics.

 E.4 Web App Setup and Interface 

 
 We develop a web app hosted via the PythonAnywhere platform, where the recruited human participants can complete the simulated scraping task. The task itself is a sequence of 15 scraping decision screens through the web app. Each screen presents the participants with a single domain and asks for a binary decision whether to “Scrape this site” or “Do not scrape” as seen in the UI screenshots in Figures  8 – 13 . Each screen also requests a short comprehension question to elicit the participant’s understanding of what the website does, and encourages the participant to actually visit the website first before deciding. In accordance with the conditions of each legal priming prompt selected for the human baseline task, the amount of legal resources on screen differs for P1, P4, and P7. P1 (Neutral, Figures  8 – 9 ) only shows the domain and the decision panel, P4 (Resource Linked, Figures  10 – 11 ) additionally shows two clickable buttons that the participants can use to view the website’s ToS (Figure  15 ) and robots.txt (Figure  16 ) in collapsible side panels, and P7 (Strong Legal Warning, Figures  12 – 13 ) keeps the same two buttons for viewing ToS and robots.txt and adds a legal-warning panel that reproduces the wording of the agentic-experiment P7 prompt (CFAA-style legal language about potential breach of contract and statutory liability for non-compliance). When a participant clicks the “Scrape” button, the web app displays a manually pre-saved HTML text of the landing page of the website (Figure  14 ). The “Scrape” button only simulates the scrape function from the participants’ perspective, but no actual scraping via a script to fetch any content and produce website traffic is done during the study. Upon completion of scraping decisions from the 15 websites, an optional open-ended feedback request is shown to participants (Figure  17 ) before presenting the debriefing form (Figure  18 ), which closes the task and session. The web app records the “Scrape” and “Do not scrape” button clicks, time spent on each screen, and scroll depth for the ToS and robots.txt viewers in order to analyze the resource-consultation pattern to be compared with AI agents as discussed in Section  5 .

 Abstract: Dense retrievers are meant to select passages that match a query's semantic specification. We show they suffer from search-by-answer bias: they favor passages that mention answer objects the model knows (scores as likely), over passages that support valid alternative answers. We test this with controlled factual contrasts from LAMA/TREx. For each retriever, we measure how strongly the model scores the canonical object over an alternative object using a token-prediction head, and ask whether this score predicts passage rankings. Across eight retrievers, including DPR, Spider variants, Contriever, E5, and Qwen3-Embedding, larger token-prediction scores consistently predict higher retrieval scores for passages containing the corresponding object.  Abstract 
 
 Dense retrievers are meant to select passages that match a query’s
semantic specification. We show they suffer from search-by-answer bias: they favor
passages that mention answer objects the model knows (scores as likely),
over passages that support valid alternative answers. We test this with controlled factual contrasts from LAMA/TREx. For each
retriever, we measure how strongly the model scores the canonical object
over an alternative object using a token-prediction head, and ask
whether this score predicts passage rankings. Across eight
retrievers—DPR, Spider variants, Contriever, E5, and Qwen3-Embedding—
larger token-prediction scores consistently predict higher retrieval
scores for passages containing the corresponding object. This holds when
passages differ only in the answer object, and even when the passage that
mentions the high-scoring object expresses a wrong relation. Dense
retrieval thus exhibits search-by-answer bias during passage selection, shaping
which evidence is retrieved. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Figure 1: Illustration of search-by-answer bias in dense retrieval. 
 
 
 1 Introduction 

 
 
 
 
 (a) E5-large 
 
 
 (b) Qwen3-4B 
 
 
 (c) Qwen3-8B 
 
 Figure 2: Representative object-contrast trends. The x-axis shows empirical
deciles of the object-knowledge score x i R x_{i}^{R} , from D 1 D_{1} (lowest) to
 D 10 D_{10} (highest). The y-axis shows the retrieval-score difference
 y i obj , R y_{i}^{\mathrm{obj},R} ; positive values indicate preference for the
canonical-object passage. Each violin shows the distribution within one
decile. Additional plots appear in Appendix  D . 
 
 
 Dense retrieval models are meant to enable semantic search : given a query such as what is the most popular programming language? , the model should identify documents that answer it ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ) . Ideally, this relies on features signaling that the queried relation holds, such as documents containing phrases like “…is the most popular programming language.” But retrieval systems are built on a backbone language model carrying extensive world knowledge ( Petroni et al., 2019 ) , which affords an alternative strategy: Given the query, the backbone may already encode a particular answer and steer the search toward documents matching that answer, retrieving by an answer rather than by the relation the query specifies. This may introduce retrieval bias, preferring common well known answers over more rare or more recent ones. This may happen when the set of valid answers is diverse (there are several treatments for some medical condition but the retriever favors the most popular one); when it depends on the evaluation criterion; and when it is temporally sensitive (e.g., the popular lanaguage change over time). Figure  1 illustrates how a model’s prior preference for an
answer can steer similarity-based retrieval toward passages containing that
answer.
We show that this bias, which we call search-by-answer bias , is indeed present in modern retrieval systems. 
 
 
 This bias can be useful when the user seeks a single answer already encoded
by the model, but retrieval is least necessary there. When a query admits
multiple valid answers, search-by-answer bias can favor one memorized answer over the
others. When facts change, it can surface stale answers; in
 closed-domain or dynamic settings, pretrained answers may be
irrelevant. In such cases, search-by-answer bias pulls retrieval toward parametric
knowledge and away from corpus evidence, conflating the model’s prior with
the query’s semantic specification. We expect this effect to strengthen as
backbones grow more knowledgeable, consistent with our cross-scale results. 
 
 
 Figure 3: Controlled passage contrasts used to test search-by-answer bias. 
 
 
 To test for search-by-answer bias, we construct the controlled passage contrasts shown
in Figure  3 . Starting from ( s , r , o ) (s,r,o) triples in LAMA/TREx ( Petroni et al., 2019 ; Elsahar et al., 2018 ) , we build minimally contrasting passages that hold the query fixed while varying either the answer object or the expressed relation. This lets us ask whether object identity alone shifts retrieval scores and, in a harder setting, whether a passage that merely contains the expected answer can outrank one that actually expresses the queried relation. For each retriever we first measure, using its retrieval-trained
representation and the original token-prediction head, how strongly it scores
the canonical answer over an alternative one, then ask whether this diagnostic
predicts the scores of the final trained retriever .
Across eight retrievers spanning DPR, the Spider family, Contriever, E5, and Qwen3-Embedding at multiple scales ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ; Ram et al., 2022 ; Izacard et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , we consistently find that the more strongly
the diagnostic favors the expected answer,
the more the trained retriever shifts score toward passages containing it,
resulting in a search that is guided by an answer rather than by the
 subject and relation . 
 
 
 
 2 Method 

 
 Since retrieval over real-world knowledge involves many confounds, we isolate the phenomenon of interest in a controlled setting, where we can cleanly manipulate only the object’s familiarity and the relation and object content of candidate documents. We focus on queries whose relevant documents (sentences) can be
expressed as a triple of a subject s s , a relation r r ,
and an object o o . For
instance, the query Who is a sibling of George Washington? has
subject George Washington and relation sibling-of , and the
object can be any of his siblings. Each query specifies the subject and
the relation, and the goal is to retrieve documents with evidence of objects that satisfy the relation (sentences mentioning Washington’s siblings). The score we get from a dense retriever should ideally only reflect whether the document reflects the subject and the target relation, irrespective of the object(s) seen in pretraining. 
 
 
 To test search-by-answer bias, we construct controlled passage contrasts in two settings,
both challenging for a model that searches by a presupposed answer. In
the first, object-contrast , both documents express the same subject and
relation but differ in the object: one contains the canonical answer, the
other an alternative one. A model that searches by the answer will
over-prefer the document containing the expected object.
Both passages use the same subject–relation template; this contrast
isolates sensitivity to object identity rather than real-world factual
validity. In the second, relation–object conflict , we
place relation match and answer match in conflict: one document expresses
the queried relation but with an alternative object, while the other
contains the expected object but expresses a different relation. Here
search-by-answer bias shows up as a tendency to retrieve the latter—the
document that merely contains the canonical object—over the passage that expresses the
queried relation with the alternative object. The relation–object conflict setting uses manually specified alternative-relation
templates to create conflict passages; the mappings used in this
experiment are detailed in Appendix  F 
(Table  4 ). 
 
 
 Data. 

 
 We use factual triples from LAMA/TREx ( Petroni et al., 2019 ; Elsahar et al., 2018 ) , where each example is a tuple ( s i , r i , o i + ) (s_{i},r_{i},o_{i}^{+}) , as discussed above. We sample an alternative object o i − o_{i}^{-} from other objects appearing with the same relation, with probability proportional to their empirical frequency for that relation, keeping it type-compatible but distinct from the canonical object o i + o_{i}^{+} .
For each factual example i i , the query q i q_{i} is constructed from the
subject s i s_{i} and relation r i r_{i} , and the candidate documents are
single template-generated sentences constructed from a subject s i s_{i} , a
relation, and an object. 
 
 
 
 Object-knowledge diagnostic. 

 
 For each retriever R R , let M R M_{R} denote the retrieval-trained model whose representation is evaluated with the original backbone’s token-prediction head for the object-scoring diagnostic. We compute an object-knowledge diagnostic for retriever R R by scoring
the canonical and alternative objects with a token-prediction head: 
 

 
 
 x i R = log ⁡ p M R ​ ( o i + ∣ u i ) − log ⁡ p M R ​ ( o i − ∣ u i ) , x_{i}^{R}=\log p_{M_{R}}(o_{i}^{+}\mid u_{i})-\log p_{M_{R}}(o_{i}^{-}\mid u_{i}), 
 
 (1) 
 
 
 
 where u i u_{i} is a relation-specific subject–relation prompt that contains neither candidate object nor any retrieved passage and p M R p_{M_{R}} is computed by applying
the original backbone’s token-prediction head to M R M_{R} ’s retrieval-trained representation. For masked-language-model backbones, the objects are scored at the mask position; for decoder models they are scored as next-token continuations of the same prefix. No retrieval is performed when computing x i R x_{i}^{R} . We retain only examples where both candidate objects are scored as single
tokens, to avoid length, aggregation, and tokenization effects in the
object-knowledge diagnostic. A larger x i R x_{i}^{R} means that the token-prediction diagnostic assigns higher relative probability to the canonical object o i + o_{i}^{+} than to the alternative object o i − o_{i}^{-} . 
 
 
 We denote by s ~ R ​ ( q , c ) \tilde{s}_{R}(q,c) the normalized retrieval score assigned
by retriever R R to passage c c for query q q . Normalization is
performed separately for each model and setting, and does not affect which
passage is preferred within a pair. In the object-contrast setting, we measure the normalized score advantage of the canonical-object passage: 
 

 
 
 y i obj , R = s ~ R ​ ( q i , c i + ) − s ~ R ​ ( q i , c i − ) . y_{i}^{\mathrm{obj},R}=\tilde{s}_{R}(q_{i},c_{i}^{+})-\tilde{s}_{R}(q_{i},c_{i}^{-}). 
 
 (2) 
 
 Positive y i obj , R y_{i}^{\mathrm{obj},R} means that retriever R R scored the passage containing o i + o_{i}^{+} higher than the passage containing o i − o_{i}^{-} . Since both passages express the same relation, the no-object-effect reference point for the preference rate is 50%. 
 
 
 In the relation–object conflict setting, we measure whether the object-matched wrong-relation passage is preferred over the relation-matched alternative-object passage: 
 

 
 
 y i rel , R = s ~ R ​ ( q i , c i o ) − s ~ R ​ ( q i , c i r ) . y_{i}^{\mathrm{rel},R}=\tilde{s}_{R}(q_{i},c_{i}^{o})-\tilde{s}_{R}(q_{i},c_{i}^{r}). 
 
 (3) 
 
 Positive y i rel , R y_{i}^{\mathrm{rel},R} means that retriever R R scored the wrong-relation passage containing o i + o_{i}^{+} higher than the relation-matched passage containing o i − o_{i}^{-} . A perfectly relation-faithful retriever would have a wrong-relation preference rate of 0%. 
 
 
 We select examples separately for each model because x i R x_{i}^{R} is
model-specific. We retain examples for which both candidate objects are
single tokens and x i R > 0 x_{i}^{R}>0 , i.e., cases in which the diagnostic assigns
higher probability to the canonical object than to the alternative object.
From this eligible set, we uniformly sample 1,000 examples per model using
random seed 13. We impose no upper bound on x i R x_{i}^{R} and do not balance the
sample across diagnostic-score ranges. 
 
 
 After sampling, we sort the 1,000 examples by x i R x_{i}^{R} and divide them into
ten empirical deciles of equal size. These deciles are used only for
descriptive analyses of how retrieval behavior changes with model knowledge;
they play no role in example selection. 
 
 
 For each setting, we report the Pearson correlation between x i R x_{i}^{R} and the
corresponding retrieval-score difference over all 1,000 examples, together
with the relevant preference rate. We additionally compare preference rates
over the full sample with those in the upper five empirical deciles.
Pearson correlations are computed over individual examples. Exact ties count
as non-preferences; none occurred. 
 
 
 
 
 3 Experimental Setup 

 
 We evaluate DPR, Spider, Spider-NQ, Spider-Trivia, Contriever, E5-large,
Qwen3-Embedding-4B, and Qwen3-Embedding-8B
 ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ; Ram et al., 2022 ; Izacard et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) .
For the object-knowledge diagnostic, DPR, the Spider variants, Contriever,
and E5-large use masked-token prediction, whereas Qwen3-Embedding-4B and
Qwen3-Embedding-8B use next-token prediction. We use base-size checkpoints
for DPR, the Spider variants, and Contriever; E5 is evaluated with its
large checkpoint.
For each retriever, the final LAMA/TREx evaluation set contains 1,000
randomly sampled eligible examples. The same selected example IDs are used
for the object-contrast and relation–object conflict settings for a model.
Detailed filtering and uniqueness statistics are reported in
Appendix  C . 
 
 
 
 4 Results 

 
 Preference-rate results are reported in
Appendix  B (Figure  4 ).
The association between the object-knowledge diagnostic and retrieval-score
differences is positive for every retriever in both settings, with Pearson
correlations ranging from 0.21 0.21 to 0.52 0.52 in object-contrast and from
 0.13 0.13 to 0.30 0.30 in relation–object conflict
(Appendix  A , Table  1 ). 
 
 
 object-contrast setting. 

 
 All models show positive correlations, with preference rates above the 50%
reference point and higher still in the upper five empirical model-knowledge
deciles. Because relation and sentence form are fixed, this isolates
sensitivity to object identity.
Figure  2 shows representative trends across
empirical deciles of model knowledge of the answer for the object-contrast setting. We include E5-large and the two Qwen3-Embedding
models in the main text, and provide the remaining per-model plots and the
full relation–object conflict plots in Appendix  D .
 relation–object conflict setting. 
All models show positive correlations, and wrong-relation preference is higher
in the upper five empirical model-knowledge deciles. The directional
association thus persists when object and relation match conflict, with
substantial variation across relations
(Appendix  G ). 
 
 
 
 Relation-level robustness and multiple valid answers. 

 
 The aggregate trend is not solely a between-relation artifact. Among
relation–model pairs with at least 30 examples, 84/91 correlations are
positive in object-contrast and 75/91 are positive in relation–object conflict. The median
within-relation Pearson correlation is positive for every retriever in
object-contrast and for 7 of 8 retrievers in relation–object conflict.
These analyses address relation composition, although repeated subjects and
objects can still affect uncertainty. Finally, on QAMPARI
 ( Amouyal et al., 2023 ) , pairwise and mean-rank analyses show a
preference for the model-known answer across all evaluated retrievers when
all compared answers are valid (Appendix  J ). 
 
 
 
 
 5 Related Work 

 
 Dense retrieval and entity-centric behavior. 
Dense retrievers rank passages using learned query and passage
representations ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ) , with later systems
including Spider, Contriever, E5, and Qwen3-Embedding
 ( Ram et al., 2022 ; Izacard et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) .
Prior work shows that dense retrievers can struggle with entity-centric
questions, especially for less common entities
 ( Sciavolino et al., 2021 ) , while external entity knowledge can
improve retrieval for less-frequent entities
 ( Yamada et al., 2025 ) . We study whether preference for the
expected answer object affects retrieval scores when relation match is
controlled. 
 
 
 Object prediction, retriever representations, and knowledge conflicts. 
LAMA probes factual knowledge with subject–relation prompts
 ( Petroni et al., 2019 ) , and answer tokens can be recovered from
dense-retriever representations ( Ram et al., 2023 ) .
Probing and model editing further suggest that pretrained knowledge can
constrain DPR retrieval ( Reichman and Heck, 2024 ) .
We test this across eight retrievers, including object–relation conflicts,
complementing related RAG work
 ( Jin et al., 2024 ; Kortukov et al., 2024 ) . 
 
 
 
 Limitations 

 
 Our experiments use controlled template-based passages. This is purposeful, as it enables separating relation match from object match. However, it also has some limitations, in particular, it does not capture the full complexity of natural corpora. Real passages are longer, noisier, and may contain several entities and relations. The LAMA/TREx alternative object is type-compatible but is not assumed to be a true alternative fact for the subject; multiple factually valid answers are evaluated separately with QAMPARI. 
 
 
 We restrict the diagnostic to single-token object pairs, which excludes many valid multi-token answers. Extending the analysis to multi-token objects would require a careful treatment of tokenization and length effects (anecdotally, we do observe search-by-answer bias also for multi-token answers). 
 
 
 The relation–object conflict setting depends on manually specified alternative-relation templates. Although these templates are designed to express a different relation while preserving the expected object, their fluency and semantic distance from the queried relation may affect absolute preference rates. 
 
 
 Our selected examples are not sampled to match the natural distribution of
factual queries. For each model, we restrict the analysis to single-token
object pairs for which the object-knowledge diagnostic favors the canonical
object ( x i R > 0 x_{i}^{R}>0 ), and randomly sample 1,000 examples from this eligible
set. The resulting preference rates should therefore be interpreted as
conditional rates within this diagnostic set, rather than as population-level
rates over all factual queries.

 Model scale. 

 
 We use base-size checkpoints for DPR, Spider, Spider-NQ, Spider-Trivia, and Contriever. E5 is evaluated with its large checkpoint. Qwen3-Embedding is evaluated at 4B and 8B scales. 
 
 
 
 Backbone token scoring. 

 
 For each retrieval model R R , the diagnostic object-knowledge score is computed by applying the original backbone’s token-prediction head to the representation produced by the retrieval-trained model. For encoder-only masked-language-model backbones, we use the masked-language-model head and score each candidate object at the mask position. For Qwen3-Embedding models, we use the next-token prediction head and score each candidate object as a continuation of the prefix. 
 
 
 
 Implementation details. 

 
 The repository contains the exact model checkpoints and revisions, all
templates and generated passages, the selected triples, per-example
diagnostic and retrieval scores, and the code used to reproduce the
experiments and analyses:
 https://github.com/adielet/retriever_object_preference . 
 
 
 
 Single-token filtering. 

 
 For each model, we tokenize both candidate objects using the tokenizer of the corresponding backbone M R M_{R} . We retain an example only when both o i + o_{i}^{+} and o i − o_{i}^{-} correspond to a single predicted token in the context in which they are scored. This avoids length effects in the diagnostic object-knowledge score. 
 
 
 
 Encoder side for retrieval scoring. 

 
 When a retrieval model uses separate query and passage encoders, we use the query encoder for queries and the passage encoder for passages in all retrieval-score computations. 
 
 
 
 Similarity functions and score normalization. 

 
 Retrieval scores are computed using each model’s native similarity function, such as dot product or cosine similarity. For each model and setting, normalization is applied to the individual raw retrieval scores before the pairwise differences y i obj , R y_{i}^{\mathrm{obj},R} and y i rel , R y_{i}^{\mathrm{rel},R} are computed. In the object-contrast setting, μ R \mu_{R} and σ R \sigma_{R} are computed over 
 

 
 
 { s R ​ ( q i , c i + ) , s R ​ ( q i , c i − ) } i . \{s_{R}(q_{i},c_{i}^{+}),s_{R}(q_{i},c_{i}^{-})\}_{i}. 
 
 
 In the relation–object conflict setting, they are computed over 
 

 
 
 { s R ​ ( q i , c i o ) , s R ​ ( q i , c i r ) } i . \{s_{R}(q_{i},c_{i}^{o}),s_{R}(q_{i},c_{i}^{r})\}_{i}. 
 
 
 Because the same affine transformation is applied to both scores in each pair, normalization does not change the preferred passage; it only makes score differences more comparable within each model and setting. 
 
 
 
 Preference rates. 

 
 Preference rates are computed as the fraction of examples for which the relevant score difference is positive. In the object-contrast setting, this is the fraction with y i obj , R > 0 y_{i}^{\mathrm{obj},R}>0 . In the relation–object conflict setting, this is the fraction with y i rel , R > 0 y_{i}^{\mathrm{rel},R}>0 . Exact ties count as non-preferences; none occurred. 
 
 
 
 Deterministic inference. 

 
 All models are run in evaluation mode
with no gradients or stochastic sampling. Random example selection uses
seed 13 for every model. 
 
 
 
 Templates. 

 
 Queries, answer contexts, and passages are generated using relation-specific templates. For each relation, we use a question template for q i q_{i} , an answer-context template for u i u_{i} , a relation-matched passage template, and, in the relation–object conflict setting, a manually selected alternative-relation template. The alternative-relation template is chosen to preserve the expected object while expressing a relation different from the queried relation. The repository contains the complete question, answer-context, relation-matched, and alternative-relation templates, including exact whitespace and prefix formatting.

 Appendix F Methods and Data 

 
 As detailed in Section   2 , we construct two types of controlled passage contrasts, object-contrast and relation–object conflict. Here we give an example. 
 
 
 For the query “What is the country of citizenship of Mukul Roy?”, the canonical object is “India” and the alternative object is “Bulgaria.” We score both objects in the same answer context, such as “Mukul Roy is a citizen of [MASK]” for masked-language-model backbones, or the prefix “Mukul Roy is a citizen of” for Qwen3 backbones. 
 
 
 We use two passage contrasts. In the object-contrast setting, both passages express the queried relation but differ in the object: 
 
 
 
 
 c i + \displaystyle c_{i}^{+} 
 = “Mukul Roy has citizenship in India.” \displaystyle=\text{``Mukul Roy has citizenship in India.''} 
 
 (4) 
 
 
 c i − \displaystyle c_{i}^{-} 
 = “Mukul Roy has citizenship in Bulgaria.” \displaystyle=\text{``Mukul Roy has citizenship in Bulgaria.''} 
 
 
 Here c i + c_{i}^{+} contains o i + o_{i}^{+} , while c i − c_{i}^{-} contains o i − o_{i}^{-} . In the relation–object conflict setting, object match and relation match are placed in conflict: 
 
 
 
 
 c i r \displaystyle c_{i}^{r} 
 = “Mukul Roy has citizenship in Bulgaria.” \displaystyle=\text{``Mukul Roy has citizenship in Bulgaria.''} 
 
 (5) 
 
 
 c i o \displaystyle c_{i}^{o} 
 = “Mukul Roy died in India.” \displaystyle=\text{``Mukul Roy died in India.''} 
 
 
 Here c i r c_{i}^{r} expresses the queried relation with the alternative object, while c i o c_{i}^{o} contains the canonical object but expresses a different relation.

 Appendix H Shared Fixed-Example Model-Size Analysis 

 
 In the main experiments, examples are selected separately for each model
because the object-knowledge diagnostic x i R x_{i}^{R} is model-specific. This
allows us to test whether larger diagnostic scores predict larger
retrieval-score shifts within each model, but it also means that different
models may be evaluated on different selected examples. 
 
 
 To check whether cross-model trends are driven by model-specific example
selection, we run an additional fixed-example analysis. We construct a shared
set of 200 LAMA/TREx examples using E5-large as the reference model, selecting
20 examples from each of its ten object-knowledge bins in
 0 ≤ x i R < 10 0\leq x_{i}^{R}<10 . The same source example IDs are then evaluated for all
retrievers and in both the object-contrast and relation–object conflict settings. 
 
 
 For each model and setting, we recompute the model-specific object-knowledge
diagnostic and retrieval-score differences on the shared set, using z-score
normalization within the shared run. We then compute the Pearson correlation
between the object-knowledge diagnostic and the retrieval-score shift, together
with the corresponding preference rate. Figure  7 
shows the relationship between approximate backbone parameter count and Pearson
correlation in both settings. 
 
 
 Figure 7: Shared fixed-example model-size analysis. All models are evaluated on
the same 200 examples, selected using E5-large as the reference model with 20
examples from each of its ten object-knowledge bins. The plot shows approximate
backbone parameter count against the Pearson correlation between the
model-specific object-knowledge diagnostic and the retrieval-score shift in the
object-contrast and relation–object conflict settings. 
 
 
 
 Appendix I Original-Backbone Representation Baseline 

 
 Our main diagnostic is computed from the representation produced by the
retrieval-trained model, projected through the original backbone’s
token-prediction head. To test whether the observed association is already
present in the original pretrained backbone, we repeat the diagnostic using
the representation produced by the backbone before retrieval training. 
 
 
 Specifically, the main diagnostic is 
 

 
 
 x i retriever , R = log ⁡ p M R ​ ( o i + ∣ u i ) − log ⁡ p M R ​ ( o i − ∣ u i ) , x_{i}^{\mathrm{retriever},R}=\log p_{M_{R}}(o_{i}^{+}\mid u_{i})-\log p_{M_{R}}(o_{i}^{-}\mid u_{i}), 
 
 
 where M R M_{R} is the retrieval-trained model. For the baseline, we compute

 where B R B_{R} is the corresponding original pretrained backbone, before
retrieval training. 
 
 
 Only the representation used to compute the object-knowledge diagnostic is
changed. In both cases, the retrieval-score differences
 y i obj , R y_{i}^{\mathrm{obj},R} and y i rel , R y_{i}^{\mathrm{rel},R} are produced by the
final retrieval-trained model.

 Appendix J QAMPARI Known-vs-Unknown Retrieval Analysis 

 
 The controlled experiments isolate search-by-answer bias using template-generated
passage contrasts. We additionally evaluate whether a related pattern appears
in a natural multi-answer retrieval setting using QAMPARI. QAMPARI questions have multiple correct answers, making them useful for testing whether a
retriever favors evidence for an answer that the model already appears to know
over evidence for other valid answers to the same question. 
 
 
 For each model, we select questions with one correct answer whose answer-token
rank is at most 5, which we call the known answer, and correct
alternatives from the same question whose answer-token ranks are greater than
20, which we call unknown answers. Each valid unknown answer is counted
separately. 
 
 
 We then retrieve passages for the original question and compare where
evidence for the known and unknown answers appears in the top-100 retrieval
results. 
 
 
 The main unit of analysis is a known-vs-unknown comparison within the same
question and retriever. This controls for the question and asks whether
retrieval favors the answer that the model’s object-knowledge diagnostic
identifies as more familiar. Pairwise and mean-rank analyses show a known-answer preference for every evaluated retriever. 
 
 
 Figure 8: Answer-level recall for known and unknown QAMPARI answers. Unknown
answers are counted individually, rather than using an any-unknown-per-question
metric. 
 
 
 Figure  8 compares how often known and unknown answers
appear in the top k k results. Each unknown answer is counted separately,
rather than counting whether any unknown answer appears for the question. This
gives a stricter answer-level comparison between the known and unknown sides. 
 
 
 Figure 9: Capped rank@100 for known and unknown QAMPARI answers. Answers not
retrieved in the top-100 are counted as one position below the cutoff, rather
than as their true corpus-level rank. 
 
 
 Figure  9 reports a capped rank@100 diagnostic for
known and unknown answers. Since the retrieval evaluation is restricted to the
top-100 results, answers not retrieved within this range are counted as one
position below the cutoff. This value should not be interpreted as the true
corpus-level rank. Instead, it provides a bounded penalty for retrieval
failures while keeping the metric focused on the evaluated top-100 range. This
avoids letting a small number of far-tail ranks dominate the mean, while still
distinguishing answers that are retrieved early from answers that are not
retrieved within the cutoff. 
 
 
 This analysis differs from the controlled LAMA/TREx experiments in two main
ways. First, the passages are retrieved from a natural retrieval corpus rather
than generated from templates. Second, QAMPARI contains multiple valid answers
per question, so the question is not whether the canonical answer is correct,
but whether retrieval disproportionately favors the answer that the model
already appears to know. 
 
 
 
 Appendix K Passage Annotation Protocol 

 
 To better understand why top-ranked passages are retrieved in the QAMPARI
analysis, we annotate retrieved passages with answer- and relation-level
labels. The annotation asks whether each passage actually answers the question,
whether it contains the selected known answer, whether it contains one of the
unknown answers, and whether it expresses the same relation requested by the
question. 
 
 
 The annotation is used only as a diagnostic analysis of retrieved passages. It
is not used to compute the main QAMPARI ranking metrics, which are computed
directly from retrieval ranks. Gold proof passages from QAMPARI are used when
available. Non-gold passages are annotated with an LLM using a fixed system
prompt, a fixed user-prompt template, and a restricted set of annotation
classes. 
 
 
 For each retrieved passage, the annotation includes the following fields: 
 
 
 
 • 
 
 known_answer_present : whether the passage contains the
selected known answer. 
 
 • 
 
 unknown_answer_present : whether the passage contains one
of the unknown answers. 
 
 • 
 
 answers_question : whether the passage answers the original
question. 
 
 • 
 
 same_relation_as_question : whether the passage expresses
the same relation requested by the question. 
 
 • 
 
 primary_label : the main diagnostic category assigned to the
passage. 
 
 • 
 
 short_reason : a short explanation for the assigned label. 
 
 
 
 
 The annotation labels distinguish between passages that genuinely support a
known or unknown answer and passages that are only topically related. This is
important because a passage may receive a high score for different reasons: it
may contain the known answer, contain another valid answer, express the correct
relation, mention the same subject or entity type, or simply belong to the same
broad topic. 
 
 
 
 Appendix L LLM Annotation Task and Prompt 

 
 The LLM annotation task is to classify each non-gold retrieved passage
according to its relation to the question, the selected known answer, and the
set of unknown answers. The annotator is instructed to use only the provided
question, answers, and retrieved passage, and not to rely on outside knowledge.
The prompt is designed to avoid treating answer-string overlap as sufficient
evidence that a passage answers the question. 
 
 
 Prompt inputs. 

 
 For each retrieved passage, the annotation prompt includes the original
question, the selected known answer, the list of unknown answers, the retrieved
passage, the retrieved title, the passage rank, and the retrieval score. 
 
 
 
 Annotation instructions. 

 
 The annotator is instructed to use only the provided question, answers, and
retrieved passage, and not to rely on outside knowledge. The annotator is asked
to determine whether the known answer is present, whether any unknown answer is
present, whether the passage answers the question, whether it expresses the
same relation as the question, and which primary diagnostic label best
describes the passage. The prompt explicitly warns that answer-string overlap
alone is not sufficient: a passage should be marked as answering the question
only when it expresses the relation requested by the question. 
 
 
 
 Output fields. 

 
 The annotation output contains the following fields:
 known_answer_present , unknown_answer_present ,
 answers_question , same_relation_as_question ,
 primary_label , and short_reason . 
 
 
 
 Annotation classes. 

 
 The allowed primary labels are: 
 
 
 
 • 
 
 known_answer_match : the passage supports the known answer
for the question. 
 
 • 
 
 unknown_answer_match : the passage supports one of the
unknown answers for the question. 
 
 • 
 
 answers_question_other : the passage answers the question,
but not with the selected known answer or listed unknown answers. 
 
 • 
 
 known_answer_present_wrong_relation : the passage
contains the known answer but does not express the relation asked by the
question. 
 
 • 
 
 unknown_answer_present_wrong_relation : the passage
contains an unknown answer but does not express the relation asked by the
question. 
 
 • 
 
 same_topic_or_domain : the passage is topically related
but does not clearly answer the question. 
 
 • 
 
 no_clear_relation : the passage does not clearly express
the relation needed to answer the question. 
 
 • 
 
 insufficient_information : the passage is too ambiguous or
incomplete to assign a more specific label.

 发布亮点 
 
 feat: 新增可选 FastAPI 安全中间件；定时模式支持跳过重复的启动分析；离线 Agent 轨迹评估新增讨论股票范围偏移诊断。 
 fix: 更新 Claude、Gemini、OpenAI、DeepSeek 默认模型，并为新建文本渠道优先选择 MiniMax M3.1 Flash，减少旧模型退役导致的配置失败。 
 fix: 修复研究任务报告合成阶段预算过短的问题，保留超时阶段、原因与已知 token 用量；Market Light 评分排除 VIX 涨跌幅，避免将波动率上涨当作市场上涨。 
 fix: 修复自选股保存被无关 LLM 配置错误阻断、数据库单例切换地址后仍使用旧连接、Telegram 消息长度计算不符合 UTF-16 限制等问题。 
 improve: 持仓风险板块查询增加按股票代码跨请求缓存；富途 OpenD 连接增加等待边界与失败降级；更新 Adanos 个股 Reddit 接口，固定存在兼容问题的依赖版本。 
 improve: 统一数据源设置展示顺序与中英文标签，改善启动和数据源日志，修复中文文档乱码；移除实验性 Codex App Server 后端，并撤回误合入的 API Route / Opper 集成。 
 
 What's Changed 
 
 Added optional FastAPI security middleware, an option to skip duplicate startup analysis in scheduled mode, and offline Agent trajectory diagnostics for stock-scope drift, by @rennf93 , @SeveNOlogy7 , and @ZhuLinsen . 
 Refreshed Claude, Gemini, OpenAI, and DeepSeek default models and preferred MiniMax M3.1 Flash for new text channels, by @torrresagus , @ZhuLinsen , and @octo-patch . 
 Increased the research synthesis-stage timeout allowance while retaining the overall task deadline, and preserved timeout phase, cause, and known token usage. Excluded VIX returns from Market Light scoring so rising volatility is not treated as positive equity performance, by @wvyan and @twodogwang . 
 Allowed watchlist saves despite unrelated LLM configuration errors while preserving container environment overrides. Rebound the database singleton when a different database URL is requested and measured Telegram message limits in UTF-16 code units, by @fanriming , @SeveNOlogy7 , and @Bortlesboat . 
 Cached portfolio sector lookups by stock code across requests, bounded Futu OpenD connection attempts with fallback, and updated the Adanos per-stock Reddit endpoint, by @b84330808 , @1AbdullahButt , and @SeveNOlogy7 . 
 Pinned AkShare and LiteLLM dependencies to avoid fresh-install failures and pinned browser-install CI jobs to Ubuntu 24.04 for Playwright compatibility. Consolidated data-source settings ordering and bilingual labels, improved startup/provider logs, and restored Chinese documentation text, by @ZhuLinsen , @SeveNOlogy7 , and @ciphersaw . 
 Removed the experimental Codex App Server Agent backend, reverted the mistakenly merged API Route and Opper integrations, and updated documentation navigation and README promotional content, by @massif-01 , @ZhuLinsen , and @siliang42 . The reverted integrations are not included as release features.
