Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters France Iran was behind cyber-attack on French supermarket freezers, Paris says French foreign minister vows European sanctions against Tehran over ‘unprecedented’ hacks last month Kim Willsher in Paris Mon 9 Nov 2026 12.54 EST First published on Mon 9 Nov 2026 11.53 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google France has said Iran was responsible for a massive cyber-attack on supermarket freezers and chiller cabinets that was described by its foreign minister as being an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression”. Jean-Noël Barrot said “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible, adding that the attacks – which took control of digital thermostats to push temperatures up to above 50C – constituted “a major violation of the nation’s interests”. At a press briefing during the G7 summit in Paris, he said: “Thanks to the remarkable efforts of government agencies, I am able to confirm that the Islamic Republic of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards are responsible for this attack.” He said the Iranian ambassador had been summoned “to protest in the strongest possible terms against this extremely serious act.” Swathes of French supermarkets were hit in the cyber-attacks on 11 and 12 October. Some were forced to throw away entire inventories of perishable food. Similar incidents have been reported since, including on supermarket fridges in other European countries last week and on a French blood bank. The Paris public prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, said on Monday that specialist investigators and government agencies had identified “a modus operandi” characteristic of the Iranian group Shahid Kaveh, a cyber warfare unit linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC). This included “the use of Farsi and IP addresses traced back to devices located in Iran”, she said. Beccuau said her office had opened an investigation against the head of Shahid Kaveh, his deputies and “others who will be identified” on charges of “fraudulent attacks on an automated data processing system committed as part of an organised crime ring and of causing damage dangerous to persons”. She said the offences were “aggravated by the fact they were committed to serve a foreign power – in this case Iran”. Gérôme Billois, a partner at the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said Shahid Kaveh had been active since 2020 and was known to have carried out cyber-attacks mostly on water distribution systems in the US. “Two countries are known for this kind of attack: Iran and Russia. Given that recent cyber-attacks on supermarkets and the blood bank in France concerned freezers it is reasonable to think Iran is directly linked to both,” he said, “For the moment they are attacking easy equipment but as a state group that has the means, the determination and the time, we should be prepared to see attacks on other systems like water or electricity.” During the attack last month, hackers remotely overrode the temperature setting on thousands of freezers , fridges and chiller cabinets in as many as 700 supermarkets and shops across France, pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F) in some cases. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion Thousands of tons of food had to be dumped and in some stores the extreme temperature rise sparked fires, triggering sprinklers and water damage. Hackers last week accessed control systems at cold stores stocking blood products. The French blood service (EFS) said temperature and defrosting thresholds and been raised to “very high level” but that technicians had been alerted by alarm systems allowing them to disconnect the cold stores before the products were destroyed. It is not clear whether the two attacks are linked. The following day retailers in 11 European countries including the UK, Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with refrigeration systems. A regional branch of France’s Crédit Mutuel bank also reported losing more than €100m in a cyber-attack on Friday. The bank said it had recuperated some of the money. The European Commission did not immediately comment on the French foreign minister’s statement. Kaja Kallas, the head of foreign affairs for the EU said: “We have the foreign affairs council next Monday, so we will have the opportunity to discuss this. These cyber incidents occurring in Europe, if attributed [to Iran], also call for a strong response on our part.” In a significant decision this year, the EU designated the IRGC a terrorist organisation , ending years of division over the issue. The designation became possible after France dropped its long-held opposition, having previously feared it would damage diplomatic channels and the interests of French nationals in Iran.  For more than two decades , Google has worked with machine learning and AI to make our products more helpful. AI has helped our users in everyday ways from Smart Compose in Gmail to finding faster routes home in Maps. AI is also allowing us to contribute to major issues facing everyone, whether that means advancing medicine or finding more effective ways to combat climate change . As we continue to incorporate AI, and more recently, generative AI, into more Google experiences, we know it’s imperative to be bold and responsible together . Building protections into our products from the outset An important part of introducing this technology responsibly is anticipating and testing for a wide range of safety and security risks, including those presented by images generated by AI. We’re taking steps to embed protections into our generative AI features by default, guided by our AI Principles : Protecting against unfair bias: We’ve developed tools and datasets to help identify and mitigate unfair bias in our machine learning models. This is an active area of research for our teams and over the past few years, we’ve published several key papers on the topic. We also regularly seek third-party input to help account for societal context and to assess training datasets for potential sources of unfair bias. Red-teaming: We enlist in-house and external experts to participate in red-teaming programs that test for a wide spectrum of vulnerabilities and potential areas of abuse, including cybersecurity vulnerabilities as well as more complex societal risks such as fairness. These dedicated adversarial testing efforts, including our participation at the DEF CON AI Village Red Team event this past August, help identify current and emergent risks, behaviors and policy violations, enabling our teams to proactively mitigate them. Implementing policies: Leveraging our deep experience in policy development and technical enforcement, we’ve created generative AI prohibited use policies outlining the harmful, inappropriate, misleading or illegal content we do not allow. Our extensive system of classifiers is then used to detect, prevent and remove content that violates these policies. For example, if we identify a violative prompt or output, our products won’t provide a response and may also direct the user to additional resources for help on sensitive topics such as those related to dangerous acts or self harm. And we are continuously fine-tuning our models to provide safer responses. Safeguarding teens: As we slowly expand access to generative AI experiences like SGE to teens, we’ve developed additional safeguards around areas that can pose risk for younger users based on their developmental needs. This includes limiting outputs related to topics like bullying and age-gated or illegal substances. Indemnifying customers for copyright : We’ve put strong indemnification protections on both training data used for generative AI models and the generated output for users of key Google Workspace and Google Cloud services. Put simply: if customers are challenged on copyright grounds, we will assume responsibility for the potential legal risks involved. Providing additional context for generative AI outputs Building on our long track record to provide context about the information people find online, we're adding new tools to help people evaluate information produced by our models. For example, we've added About this result to generative AI in Search to help people evaluate the information they find in the experience. We also introduced new ways to help people double check the responses they see in Bard. Context is especially important with images, and we’re committed to finding ways to make sure every image generated through our products has metadata labeling and embedded watermarking with SynthID . Similarly, we recently updated our election advertising policies to require advertisers to disclose when their election ads include material that’s been digitally altered or generated. This will help provide additional context to people seeing election advertising on our platforms. We launched Bard and SGE as experiments because we recognize that as emerging tech, large language model (LLM)-based experiences can get things wrong, especially regarding breaking news. We're always working to make sure our products update as more information becomes available, and our teams continue to quickly implement improvements as needed. How we protect your information New technologies naturally raise questions around user privacy and personal data. We’re building AI products and experiences that are private by design. Many of the privacy protections we’ve had in place for years apply to our generative AI tools too and just like with other types of activity data in your Google Account, we make it easy to pause, save or delete it at any time including for Bard and Search . We never sell your personal information to anyone, including for ads purposes — this is a longstanding Google policy. Additionally, we’ve implemented privacy safeguards tailored to our generative AI products. For example, If you choose to use the Workspace extensions in Bard, your content from Gmail, Docs and Drive is not seen by human reviewers, used by Bard to show you ads, or used to train the Bard model. (Update, October 16, 2026: You can view the latest about how some new features work here . As we’ve continued to make Google products more personalized and helpful, we’ve added features that enable users to choose to connect Workspace apps to other Google services. If users choose to enable these new features, data from Workspace Apps will be processed to personalize other Google experiences, and depending on a user’s settings, that same subset of data can be used to train generative AI models. It can also be subject to human review in limited circumstances.) Collaborating with stakeholders to shape the future AI raises complex questions that neither Google, nor any other single company, can answer alone. To get AI right, we need collaboration across companies, academic researchers, civil society, governments, and other stakeholders. We are already in conversation with groups like Partnership on AI and ML Commons , and launched the Frontier Model Forum with other leading AI labs to promote the responsible development of frontier AI models. And we’ve also published dozens of research papers to help share our expertise with the researchers and the industry. We are also transparent about our progress on the commitments we’ve made, including those we voluntarily made alongside other tech companies at a White House summit earlier this year. We will continue to work across the industry and with governments, researchers and others to embrace the opportunities and address the risks AI presents.

 The first half of my second career (third maybe) in software was spent in satellite ground processing. My first true culminating project, so to speak, was when the portion of the US Maritime Domain Awareness meant for use by the Navy went to initial operational capability. I checked out your site briefly. It's mildly amusing to note differences between that and a real system in use by military units. It'd be nice to be able to use a selector of some sort rather than typing in a location. The globe itself is most obvious, but a flat map works. If you're going to suggest arbitrary locations underneath the text entry box, you should probably suggest places you actually have imagery for. I don't care what looked at the hotel I'm in this morning and don't know coordinates for places off the top of my head, but I can find them on a map. The real version of a system like this doesn't try to draw orbits and estimate what was overhead when. The imagery archives already have geolocation information you should be able to query directly instead of trying to project backwards like that. There are at least three downsides to the way you've done it. One, users typically don't care whether an image was collected from orbit. They just want to know what happened in location X at time Y. If you have aerial imagery or even ground imagery you can correlate with, augment, or entirely replace orbital imagery if it doesn't exist, that's just as useful. Two, satellites don't need to be overhead to collect on a location. The exact angles they can collect from are classified (and of course depend on atmospheric conditions and potentially other obstructions), but they don't have to be overhead. Three, not all satellites have fixed orbits. You can't always solve Kepler's equations to figure out where they've been from their current velocity. Some make changes to their own orbits. Seeing things like this puts me in weird headspace. I think a lot of you get dazzled by how easy it's become to put together software. I want to reiterate the "not the bottleneck" phrase you probably keep hearing. Being able to do something like this relies on decades of past effort to put the sensor platforms in orbit in the place, create imagery from the data they collect, and archiving that imagery in a way that users can query. MDA itself was first announced by George Bush in his 2004 budget request. We went live with our first users in 2016. The effort involved was massive, but we had to invent new sensors, put them in orbit, test them in controlled, uncontested waters, figure out how to simulate data feeds that didn't yet exist in order to create software processing capabilities without being to run against real sensor feeds during the development, figure out how to chip, compress, and redact the massive files we produce so they can be disseminated over radio to tablets on ships in the middle of nowhere to field commanders that don't have top secret clearances with compartments for the collection method, or to partner nations that don't have US clearances at all. The web frontend was such a small part of this that we never even retrained or hired JavaScript developers. The original non-browser frontend was a Java Swing desktop UI, so they just ported it to use the Google Web Toolkit, which transpiles Java to JavaScript, and that code was touched at a rate of maybe a few hundred lines a year, in contrast to every other part of the system involved in orchestrating the batch workload scheduling, order queueing, dissemination logic, everything that made it possible to process more data per hour than any other computing system on the planet, or at least they told us that in 2009. I'm sure that is no longer true thanks to LLM training. But man, we basically wrote our own Borg before Kubernetes existed (they of course migrated to Kubernetes eventually, which is why I'm in a hotel at KubeCon NA). We wrote our own filesystem because we couldn't get the IO throughput we needed from what the proprietary Unixes of the 90s offered. We wrote our own network protocols. We scrounged for replacement parts on eBay to service end of life SGI Altix boxes while the government squabbled over how to fund and who to award a contract to build a classified cloud, meanwhile canceling hardware refresh funding to already running operational systems. There are so many battle stories I really hope I can tell someday before I die when they're declassified. I'm sure the commercial providers you're querying have similar stories. This is a nice effort, by the way. I don't want to come across like I'm downplaying it. I just want the next generation as they get awed at what they can do in days or even hours from a browser to understand you can only do that because of the supporting infrastructure and data that is out there. Bringing that data into existence took a lot of work. It was done by people. Without it, you're drawing ellipses on a screen. We had pocket computers that could do that with a few keystrokes 30 years ago. reply wnissen 16 hours ago | prev | next [–]

Components · CUI, native UI components for C 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 CUI 
 
 
 Overview 
 Guide 
 Components 
 Showcase 
 Apps 
 Changelog 
 
 
 
 
 Search… Ctrl K 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Components Every component of CUI, each with a live example, its options and what it does with the keyboard. Basics Text : Headings, body text, labels, links and inline code, with wrapping that avoids a lone last word. Icons : The Lucide icon set embedded as a font, used by name through CUI_ICON_* constants. Badge, avatar and keycap : Small labels: a badge for a status or a count, an avatar for a person, and a keycap for a keyboard key. Card and metric : A card is a surface that groups content. A metric shows one number with its change and an optional sparkline. Image : Shows a picture loaded from a file or made from your own pixels. Actions Button : Starts an action when clicked. It comes in six variants and three sizes, with an optional icon and a loading state. Icon button : A round button with only an icon, ghost by default. Button group, copy and hold to confirm : Three small helpers for actions: buttons joined into one group, a button that copies text to the clipboard, and a button that must be held to fire. Split button : A main action with a menu of related actions behind a chevron. Toggle group : A row of joined toggle buttons, each on or off, or exactly one on at a time. Confirm button : A button for destructive actions that asks for a second click before it fires. Status button : A button that shows the progress of the work it started: a spinner while busy, then a check or an error. Reactions : Reaction buttons with a count each, as under a message or a post. Speed dial : A round floating button that fans out a few related actions. Theme switcher and toggle : Controls that switch the app between light, dark and the system theme. User menu : An avatar, a name and a detail line that open an account menu with a header. Swipe actions : A row that slides sideways to reveal actions such as archive or delete. Inputs Text field : A single-line field that edits text in a buffer you own, with a label, an icon, a hint and an error. The search field is a variant. Text area : A multi-line text field that wraps and scrolls. Number field : A field for a number in a range, typed or stepped with its buttons and the arrow keys. Tag input : A field that turns typed words into removable chips, kept as a comma separated list. One time code : A row of boxes for a verification code, filled by typing or pasting. Password strength : A meter under a password field that scores the password from too short to strong. Inline edit : Text that turns into a field when clicked, for renaming things in place. Scrub field : A number you change by dragging sideways on it, as in design and 3D tools. Money field : A field for an amount of money, with a currency symbol and grouped digits. Prefix and suffix : Fixed text before or after a field's value, such as https:// or a unit. Shortcut recorder : A field that records a key combination, for settings where people choose their own shortcuts. Dropzone : An area that takes files dropped from the desktop, and can open the system file dialog on a click. Avatar upload : A profile picture you replace by dropping an image on it. Signature pad : A box to sign in with the pointer or a finger, with strokes you can read back. Selection Segmented control : A compact set of two to five choices where one is always selected, for switching between views of the same content. Checkbox, switch and radio : The three basic choices: a checkbox for an option, a switch for a setting that applies at once, and radio buttons for one of several. Slider : Picks a number, or a range with two thumbs, by dragging along a track. Chips and rating : A chip is a small toggle for filters and tags. A rating picks a number of stars. Radio cards : One choice out of a few, shown as cards with a title and a line of explanation each. Pickers Select and combobox : Picks one item from a list that opens under the field. With search it becomes a combobox. Date picker and calendar : Picks a date from a month grid, as a field that opens a calendar or as a calendar shown inline. Color picker : A swatch that opens a saturation and brightness square, a hue bar and preset swatches. Multi-select : Picks several items from a list and shows them as chips in the field. Date range picker : Picks a start and an end date, with presets such as the last 7 days. Time picker : Picks a time of day from scrolling columns of hours and minutes. Wheel picker and time dial : Touch-style pickers: drums of options you spin, and a clock face for setting a time. Ruler and histogram sliders : Two sliders that show context: a ruler that slides under a fixed marker, and a range slider drawn over the distribution of the data. Knob, fader and level meter : A rotary knob, a vertical fader and a level meter: the controls of audio, synth and mixer panels. Emoji picker : A searchable grid of every emoji in nine groups, with the recently used ones first. Navigation Tabs : Switches between views with a row of labels and an underline that slides to the active one. Sidebar navigation : The items and section titles of an app's sidebar, with one highlight that follows the selection. Breadcrumb, pagination and stepper : Three ways to show position: the path to a page, the page of a list, and the step of a process. Table of contents : A list of a page's sections that follows the reader and scrolls to a section when clicked. Menu bar : The File, Edit, View row of a desktop app, with a menu under each title. Toolbar : A row of small buttons, toggles and separators for an editor's most used commands. Document tabs : Closable tabs for open documents that can be dragged into a new order, as in an editor. Status bar : The thin bar at the bottom of a window for state, counts and background progress. Docking : Panels the user arranges by dragging: split, tabbed and resized, with a layout you can save and load. Overlays Dropdown and context menu : A menu of commands that opens from a button, or at the pointer on a right click. Popover : A small floating panel anchored to a control, for content that does not need a dialog. Tooltip : A short label that appears when the pointer rests on a control. Dialog : A modal window for a decision or a short form, which blocks the rest of the app until it is closed. Sheet : A panel that slides in from an edge. Command palette : A search box over the app's commands, opened with a shortcut. Hover card : A preview card that opens when the pointer rests on a link, a button or another component that reacts to the pointer. Confirm popover : A small question anchored to the button that opened it. Expandable text and card : Long text clamped to a few lines with a Show more link, and a card that opens to show its details. Guided tour : A spotlight on one control at a time, with a card beside it saying what the control does, for onboarding and "what's new". Feedback Toast : A short message that appears in a corner and goes away by itself, with an optional action. Alert : An inline message in a tone of information, success, warning or danger, which can be dismissed. Progress, meter, spinner and skeleton : Ways to show waiting and amounts: a progress bar, a meter against a limit, a spinner, a gauge and placeholder shapes for content that is loading. Empty state : What to show where there is nothing yet: an icon, a title, a line of help and an action. Banner and countdown : A full-width announcement that can be dismissed, and a countdown to a moment in time. Onboarding checklist : A card with a progress ring and steps; the first unfinished step opens to show its description and action button. Undo toast : A toast with an Undo action and a visible timer, for actions that can be taken back. Data display Table : Rows and columns of your data, with sortable headers, selectable rows and any component in a cell. List and tree : List rows with an avatar or an icon, a title and a detail line, and a tree of items that fold. Accordion : Sections that fold open and closed under their headers. Timeline and progress ring : A vertical list of events in order, and a ring that fills with a percentage. Reorderable list : A list whose rows the user drags into a new order. Data grid and filter bar : A grid for very large data with sticky headers, resizable and sortable columns and editable cells, and a bar of filters to go with it. Tree table and path bar : A tree with columns, as in a file explorer or a debugger's variables, and a path bar for moving up through folders. File browser and picker : A folder view with sorting and navigation, and the open and save dialogs built from it. Code block : Read-only source code with syntax highlighting, optional line numbers and a copy button. JSON viewer : JSON shown as a tree that folds, with a color for each type of value. Markdown view : Renders markdown text as native content: headings, lists, tables, code, task lists and links. Code editor : An editable code field with syntax highlighting, for shader editors, script consoles and config files. Diff viewer : Compares two versions of a text line by line. Property inspector : A panel of named properties in folding groups, each edited with the control that fits its type. Log console : A log view for many thousands of lines, with level filters, search, follow and copy. Terminal : Output over an input line, for build logs, a game console or a REPL. Hex viewer : The bytes of a file or of memory in hex and ASCII, for binary tools, emulators and debuggers. Flame graph : A profiler timeline: time runs left to right and call depth top to bottom, so each span sits in the row of its depth, under its parent. Curve editor : Keyframes on a plot, for easing, animation timing and response curves. Gradient editor : A color ramp with its stops underneath, over a checkerboard so transparent stops read as transparent. Timeline editor : A dope sheet for animation, video and audio tools: tracks, a time ruler and keys you can move. Charts Charts : Line, bar and donut charts and sparklines, with axes, a crosshair and a tooltip on hover. Heatmap : A grid of cells colored by value, for one category against another. Calendar heatmap : A year of days as small squares colored by activity. Treemap and radar : A treemap shows the parts of a whole as rectangles sized by value. A radar chart compares items across several axes. Funnel, split bar and waffle : Three charts for shares: a funnel for the steps of a conversion, a single bar split into parts, and a waffle of 100 squares. Sankey : Flows between stages, drawn as ribbons whose width follows the amount. Bar list and activity rings : A ranked list with a bar behind each row, and concentric rings that fill toward a goal. Scatter and bubble : Points on two axes, with an optional third value as the size of each bubble. Radial gauge : One value on a dial, for dashboards: speed, load, temperature, a score against a goal. Candlestick chart : Open, high, low and close per period, for prices. Planning Kanban board : Columns of cards the user drags between stages. Week calendar : A week of timed events on a day grid, which can be moved and resized by dragging. Month calendar : A month grid with the events of each day, for schedules and planners. Gantt chart : A task list on the left and a timeline that scrolls sideways, with months, day numbers and shaded weekends. Node editor : A canvas of nodes joined by curved links, for shader graphs, audio patching or visual scripting. Conversation and media Chat : Message bubbles for a conversation, with grouping, dividers and a typing indicator. Comments : A comment with its author, time, replies indented under it and a like button. Presence, counter and ticker : Small live pieces: who is here now, a number that rolls when it changes, and a line of text that scrolls past. Carousel : A strip of slides the user drags or steps through, one at a time. Image compare and card stack : A divider that reveals one picture over another, and a stack of cards the user swipes through. Image viewer and cropper : A picture you can zoom and pan, and a crop tool with a frame you drag. Motion Text effects : Animated text: a shimmer, a typewriter, words that rotate in place and text that reveals itself. Rolling numbers : A number whose changed digits roll into place. Gradient text and spotlight cards : Text filled with a gradient, and a card with a glow that follows the pointer. Loaders : Animated indicators for work in progress, in five styles. Dock : A row of icons that grow under the pointer, as in a desktop dock. Control tiles : Large toggle tiles for quick settings such as Wi-Fi or Do not disturb. Now playing, waveform and tab bar : A media player card, an audio waveform to scrub through, and a bottom tab bar for phone layouts. AI interfaces Reasoning and tool calls : A folding block for a model's reasoning, and a row for each tool it calls with its status. Agent plan and status : The steps an agent is working through, and a pill that says what it is doing now. Sources and citations : Citations inside an answer and the list of sources they point to. Composer and model picker : The message box of a chat, with attachments, send and stop, and a menu for choosing the model. Suggestions, response actions and the context meter : Prompt suggestions to start from, the actions under a response, and a ring that shows how full the context is. Voice orb : An animated orb for voice modes that shows listening, thinking and speaking. Developer tools Key-value editor : Rows of key and value fields for HTTP headers, query parameters or environment variables. Problems panel : Compiler and linter output grouped by file, with each file's count. Pipeline : A CI or CD run: each stage is a column of its jobs with their status and duration, and connectors run between the stages. Query builder : A filter built from conditions joined by all or any, in groups that nest. Schedule picker : A cron schedule edited through plain choices instead of the expression, with the next runs listed. Keymap : A keyboard with the shortcuts on it. Commit graph : Version history with its branch lanes. Dependency graph : Nodes and directed edges laid out in layers, for build targets, packages, services or call graphs. Network waterfall : HTTP requests as a table with a timing bar each. Trace viewer : A tracing timeline in the manner of a performance panel. Regex tester : A pattern, its flags and a test text, with every match and group highlighted. Test explorer : Test results as a tree of suites and tests, each with its status and time. Stack trace : An exception with its call stack. HTTP request bar : The method, the URL and Send, as in an API client. Uptime bars : A status page: each service's current state and a bar for each day of its history. Time histogram : Event counts over time, stacked by series, as above a log search, with a legend that shows each series' total. Coverage : Test coverage as a tree built from the files' paths. Blame : Source with who last changed each line. Feature flags : Flags against environments, edited in place. API explorer : The endpoints of an API grouped by tag, each opening to show its parameters. Instruments Dot-matrix chart : A chart that draws values as a grid of dots, lit up to each column's value and dim above it, with a readout under the pointer. Chart annotations : Lines, thresholds and points drawn over a chart, each with a two-line label that moves out of the way of the others. Event track : A time axis with moments on it as dots, which people drag, add with a click and remove with a double-click. Readout : One figure as an instrument shows it: a small label, the value in the monospaced font with its unit, and a line of context. Dot-matrix display : Text drawn with a 5 by 7 dot font, for clocks, counters and status lines.

 Search Ctrl K Cancel All posts November 9, 2026 5 min read Amazon saves millions by replacing Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider Two Amazon engineers swapped Claude Sonnet 4.6 for a decision model in one of the world's biggest internal ticketing systems. Carr Onstott , Mehul Jaiswal , Strands Agents Team For a while, Amazon and AWS teams relied on Claude Sonnet 4.6 to label tickets in an internal system
without breaking the bank. 
 Sonnet 4.6 fit the goldilocks choice of balancing intelligence with cost. Considering it dealt with one
of the world’s largest internal ticketing systems, the nine month old model did well. However, two
Amazon engineers recently swapped out Sonnet 4.6 for
 Strands Decider , a decision model we launched a month ago, that
performed just as well at 98% less cost . This change will save millions of dollars of token costs in
a year. 
 Carr and Mehul, who work on the internal ticketing system, walk through how this happened below. 
 Replacing an LLM’s job with a decision model 
 We had Sonnet 4.6 labeling tickets at enormous scale. The tickets could be customer escalations, capacity
requests, automated alarms, security findings, or anything else across the company that needed to fit
within 20 category types. The agent ran with a long system prompt on every ticket, generating JSON and
reasoning against a fixed set of labels. 
 A decision model can’t generate text. It’s first given some state and a question with a set of
options, then the decision model returns a probability for each option plus a confidence score. We saw
this method fit perfectly with ticket labeling: the state is the ticket, the options are the label
catalog. 
 We started with the original Strands Decider 2B . On a test set of
tickets, the E4B Gemma 4 build got clearly better results, so
we switched to it. Afterwards, we tuned how confident the model needed to be before applying a label.
The results showed E4B beating production Sonnet on a separate set of our tickets. 
 We ran E4B on SageMaker ml.g5.xlarge instances (one A10G, 24 GB each). The model used about 19 GiB,
and one request took about 640 ms on one instance. The endpoint autoscales with traffic, but its network
was isolated, preventing outbound access to the container. SageMaker copies the model weights in from
S3 before start-up. 
 Customers can do this too! Apart from our ticketing APIs, everything in the path is a standard AWS
service. Ticket events land in an SQS queue that then triggers a Lambda function. It reads the ticket
data and calls the model, a SageMaker AI Endpoint with Strands Decider. AppConfig holds the switch
(described below), and CloudWatch carries the logs, metrics and alarms. The stack is defined in CDK with
deployment stages for Beta, Gamma, and Prod. 
 Running Sonnet 4.6 and Strands Decider on the same tickets 
 We didn’t want to flip a switch and hope. The labeling Lambda reads a three-way setting from AWS
AppConfig on every message: 
 
 BEDROCK : Sonnet labels every ticket, but Strands Decider isn’t called. 
 DUAL : Both the Sonnet and Strands Decider models are called in parallel. The results from the
Sonnet model are applied to the ticket and compared with Strands Decider results. 
 DECIDER : Strands Decider labels every ticket and Bedrock isn’t called. 
 
 What we measured 



































 Claude Sonnet 4.6 Strands Decider E4B % Improvement Average time per call 4,215 ms 897 ms 78% Input tokens per ticket 6,554 2,009 Output tokens per ticket 170 1 Total tokens, per ticket 6,724 2,010 70% 
 The token drop had two sources. Strands Decider produced one output, the choice, instead of a JSON
answer. Its prompt was also much shorter than Sonnet 4.6’s. Production’s label descriptions alone are
longer than Strands Decider’s 4,096-token window, so we rewrote each of the 20 labels as a one- or
two-sentence criterion and sent them as the options of a single choice question, plus a “none” option.
The ticket data is the same as what Sonnet gets, except that on long tickets Strands Decider drops the
oldest comments to fit. 
 Below is a graph of our Lambda durations on the day we turned off the Sonnet usage, showing the average
Lambda execution duration dropping 74%. 
 
 What it costs 
 At published us-east-1 on-demand prices: 

























 Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Bedrock, global endpoint) Strands Decider E4B (SageMaker, ml.g5.xlarge ) Price $3.00 per 1M input, $15.00 per 1M output tokens $1.408 per instance-hour Per ticket $0.0222 about $0.0005 Per million tickets about $22,200 about $500 
 Sonnet’s cost per ticket comes straight from the token counts above. Strands Decider’s depends on how
busy each instance is. At about 640 ms per request, one instance can handle about 5,600 tickets an hour,
which would be $250 per million tickets at full use. We keep headroom for bursts, and in practice it
comes to about $500 per million. That is about 44 times cheaper than Sonnet, a 98% reduction. 
 These are published list prices. They leave out the Lambda, which also runs for less time per ticket
now. 
 One thing that surprised us was that JSON key order changed the answer. Sending the same content with
keys in a different order moved the output probabilities by up to 0.19. We now send every request with
sorted keys, so if you serve a decision model behind an API, check this before you compare runs. 
 Our lessons 
 This worked because the task is a closed choice from a known catalog, the volume is high, and the
latency of the old path mattered. If your labels need explanation text, if the catalog changes weekly,
or if you can’t fit the useful context into a few thousand tokens, a decision model probably can’t
replace the LLM’s job. 
 The part we’d copy regardless of model is the three-way switch. Running both on real traffic, then judging every disagreement, told us more than any offline eval would have. It also meant
going back was a 45-second config change. 
 The world of agents gets a lot more exciting (and less costly) with decision models. If you’re running
a classification agent, try the Strands Decider repo 
and its

Amazon saves millions by replacing Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Amazon saves millions by replacing Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider ( strandsagents.com ) 383 points by aloukissas 6 hours ago | hide | past | favorite | 132 comments help 
 
 armcat 5 hours ago | next [–] 
 About six years ago we built a ticket classification/routing model and pipeline [1]. The initial version was trained using SVMs, it took a couple of minutes to train, and the ticket classification was just a few milliseconds. It's so fascinating to watch how the field moved over to LLMs, and then back to faster/cheaper classifiers again. [1] "Linnaeus: A highly reusable and adaptable ML based log classification pipeline", https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.06927 NOTE: the work was actually accepted at the International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE) in 2021. reply jval43 5 hours ago | parent | next [–] 
 SVMs in big data were already well liked back in 2010 as they could be scaled via map-reduce. An issue in industry was that companies would not allow training on their data across customers. Understandably so, as SVM dimensions are readily interpretable given some thought. General purpose datasets were ill-suited too depending on the task. So you'd start from scratch every time, annotate features like crazy, and often didn't have enough training data overall. LLMs "solved" that by just ignoring the previous rules and training on everything, which lets the necessary world knowledge seep back in. I'm sure we'll see many combinations of LLMs and regular machine intelligence in the near future. reply miki123211 2 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 LLMs, and other transformer models before them like BERT for example, have the benefit of "transfer learning." If you want to make a ticket classification model, you don't need to train across many customers doing ticket classification, who might not want you to train on their data and whose data is impossible to obtain unless you already are a large company. Instead, you can train on a completely different task which forces the model to learn the syntactic and semantic structure of the English language — say predicting missing words in Wikipedia articles, which you can't do successfully without a good understanding of English — and then fine-tune that model on your specific task with much less data. Because the initial task is so general, you can have one company do the expensive pretraining, share the base model, and then have everybody else just do the finetuning on their (small) proprietary dataset. LLMs and models like Jev go one step further, letting you use them as classifiers with no training at all, with nothing but rules in the prompt. And with a few tricks, you can indeed use them to get pretty high-quality labels, which you can then distill into a fine-tuning dataset for a much smaller model. reply thesz 1 hour ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 > say predicting missing words in Wikipedia articles, which you can't do successfully without a good understanding of English
 
This is word2vec model, one of - predict a word from context. The other one is to predict surrounding words (context) from a word. It did a good job when I used it, words' classes were impeccable for most practical purposes. Word2vec is a two layer perceptron. reply mrbungie 1 hour ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] 
 ¿Por qué no los dos? Big skill issue, you can even route known problems to a trained in-house simple classifier and low-confidence problems to Jev-like "zero shot classifiers" or LLMs. I feel like people in the field forgot everything. reply abhgh 2 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] 
 Agree to all of this but I would make a minor correction: the interpretability is true under certain conditions, e.g., you use something like n-grams and train an SVM with a linear kernel. You could change the representation back then too, e.g., LDA (topic models), Latent Semantic Indexing, and of course, you could change the SVMs kernel as well, e.g., use a sequence kernel [1]. Some of these were much less interpretable. But the common pipeline back then was indeed n-grams + Linear SVM. Today it is easy to modernize the pipeline by just changing the representation step to use an embedder like ModernBERT. I have a "one page" classifier if you want to try it out - [2]. [1] I went down the rabbit hole of using sequence kernels quite a bit back then, see https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.13800 , but the timing was terrible. RNNs and variants like LSTMs were beginning to become popular, and everyone (including me) switched. [2] https://pocket-text-lab.abhishek-ghose-82.workers.dev/ reply exe34 4 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] 
 And you can now get that world knowledge out of llms and generate synthetic data to train your svm and fine tune on your own dataset! reply flatline 3 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 I’ve hand-labeled so many freaking datasets over the years for supervised learning tasks, if only to build out a PoC. Would 100% hand this off to an LLM and just fine tune the results. I definitely do not want an LLM in the loop at inference time for anything I could build a simple classifier for. reply IanCal 2 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 Llm labelling is so incredibly useful, as is transforming labelled data to other valid but different forms (like where you might train on sentences but also randomly replace days of the week with others). You can also do stuff like setup active learning but have the labeller be an llm as well to make things more efficient. Definitely worth it for PoC level things if not full ones. Edit - also reviewing, so it can run training, test, review failure cases and investigate itself. You can leave them to plough through a few iterations where the early part is the classic time you’d have a few obviously bad sets of results. reply armcat 50 minutes ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 I've seen a few people comment along the lines of "yes but LLMs dont need lot of data nor competence". So with our classifier "Linnaeus", the data came from JIRA tickets plus additional signals. To get up and running we didn't use a lot of data (a few dozen tickets across approximately 20 classes to begin with - eventually expanded to 120+ classes). There was very little to no manual data labelling - mostly it was devs selecting "gold standard" JIRA tickets for us to ingest. The model was retrained daily, and we had extra signals like thumbs up/down with comments that would be used for re-training. reply benrutter 5 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 Yeah, its pretty wild! I think one of the benefits, but also potential risks, with LLMs, is you can just point them at anything without a lot of expertise. Building an SVM isn't a tricky job, but you probably need a data scientist involved, and to think carefully about a labeled dataset. I think we're seeing the modelling equivalent of something like electron apps. Where they waste a tonne of resources, but make an easier developement experience. Will be interesting to see how much or little this changes with LLM costs. reply Foobar8568 3 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 I have seen Phd in stats validating models with data the models have been trained on. And I don’t live in a country with dubious universities. So between llm and pseudo experts, at this stage, I prefer to go with a LLM. reply IshKebab 3 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] 
 > Building an SVM isn't a tricky job, but you probably need a data scientist involved, and to think carefully about a labeled dataset. Well not anymore... You can just get AI to build it. reply benrutter 3 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 True I guess. I think most companies would at least want sign off from someone who's heard of SVMs that it isn't doing something mad. Just like, LLMs can build web back ends, but I'd want a security professional to give it some kind of thumbs up. Especially if a lot of money rides on it. reply solidasparagus 4 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 What has changed is that expensive models can be deployed instantly and generate training data until you swap over to training your own cheap models. Your model only took minutes to train if you don't count the data collection and labelling work reply autuni 4 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 I think this kind of change will pop up more often. In software engineering, we learned a long time ago that giant monoliths are not the answer. You want smaller, but specialized units that work together. They perform better at their specific task, are more maintainable, you can just upgrade one part of the system without having to impact the others, .... I don't know where the focus on building a single model that can do everything comes from. reply Geezus_42 4 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 I was thinking about this recently as well. Smaller, specialized models that can run on device just make so much more sense to me than these huge generalized models that need huge infrastructure run. reply ivell 4 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] 
 I am not sure a best practice in one area translates nicely to another. LLM's power comes with it being a monolith. reply autuni 4 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 Does it though? Let's say you use an LLM to write code, do you think it benefits from the fact that the same model is capable of translating corporate messaging into internet slang for marketing? I would assume a smaller model trained specifically to produce code based on natural language input would perform at least just as well, which would already be better given the smaller size / probably lower training resource requirements.
This is of course, as already said, an assumption. But generalizing typically comes at a cost, there is no reason why this wouldn't apply to LLMs, it even applies to humans. reply duskdozer 1 hour ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 They need some of that fluff to keep up the illusion of intelligence and sycophancy that gets people to rely on them. Additionally, they need to make sure they don't prune so much that the model size seems manageable on consumer or standard business hardware, otherwise more people may become tempted to self-host a distilled or other semi-open model. The model size is also a marketing point. reply IanCal 2 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] 
 Or would it be worse as it wouldn’t have the broader knowledge to understand the reason you’re coding what you are anyway, understand the logs and iterate? Coding an exercise app will benefit from a model that can code and understands what exercise is. A car showroom website will benefit from a model that understands what relevant filters would be. reply autuni 1 hour ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 Of course there are synergies between different fields. I'm not saying cutting everything off as close as possible to it's purpose must be the best way. But that's a long way from a single generalized model. reply ianjbutler 30 minutes ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 > not saying cutting everything off as close as possible to it's purpose must be the best way Nah, let’s stand firm here and not give in so easily. Parent suggests a coding model needs exercise info in case you want to code an exercise model? Absurd, that leads to the know everything monolith to do anything. Language, reasoning, tool use, and domain knowledge.. in this case the domain is coding. Someone wants an exercise app? Great, so we look that shit up, we don’t bake it in. We don’t want to bake anything we don’t need in. We don’t even need to explain this completely reasonable and totally normal engineering preference that small is beautiful. it’s the other side that needs to justify wtf exercise has to do with coding or why everything from twitter posts to a working knowledge of 15th century French poetry just might be helpful for disconnected domains, like say serious work in contemporary astrophysics. Back to basics, No one asked for that, No one should accept as given that this is the way anything needs to work reply heggy 3 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] 
 Isn't this just the Bitter Lesson over and over again? Specialised approaches get outperformed by more compute and a simpler general approach pretty much every time. reply try-working 2 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 Bitter lesson is wrong. Large general models are outperformed by small specialized models. reply 9rx 1 hour ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 The Bitter Lesson makes no distinction between large general models and small specialized models, assuming they are both trained from data. The Bitter Lesson is that human-written rule models will always lose out to trained models in the end. reply 9rx 3 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] 
 > LLM's power comes with it being a monolith. Does it? All of the latest frontier models that have made technical details publicly available are using MoE; smaller specialized units that work together. reply nixon_why69 1 hour ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 Yeah but they're all trained together along with their gate tensor. Evaluating a moderate length prompt pulls in most/all of them. reply darylteo 1 hour ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] 
 > single model that can do everything "AGI" reply matthorse 3 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 It's pretty interesting how a very broad field of machine learning got reduced to only LLMs for most consumers. Probably it's due to marketing (and of course how powerful these models are), but their lack of capability in many tasks already forces people, even amateurs, to use LLMs to write deterministic code instead. I wonder if the sudden appearance of viral classifiers predicts more common use of smaller ML models as the next step? reply miki123211 2 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 non-LLM models just aren't visible to consumers. Saying that the field got reduced to only LLMs is like saying that the field of combustion engines got reduced to cars. The trucks, combine harvesters and peaker plants are still here, they're just in the background, invisible to people who are not part of the industry. Banks still use random forests and SVMs, medicine and image processing still use CNNs (and people who take photos with their phone don't even realize how much image processing is being done), TTS, ASR and predictive typing models are in wide use, and there's probably still plenty of BERT in spam classification and such. reply pletnes 4 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 Interesting! I had the idea to compute embeddings of log lines to look for “black swans” in my logs. A small model running locally would do. Then PCA, SVM - any old school method should work, I guess. Haven’t seen it done but it must be tried by someone somewhere. reply elvircrn 3 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 Svaka cast :) reply chaostheory 5 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] 
 The tech industry is not that far off from the fashion industry reply floro 5 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–]

For the latest on the Fireworks AI incident, see their official security updates here . Following an investigation by the Notion security team, we have determined that <1% of Notion workspaces may have been affected by the Fireworks security incident. Some unattributable chat sessions with Notion AI may have been exposed in this incident. “Unattributable” means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results. Beyond what’s in the chat transcript itself, there’s no information tying the chat back to a workspace, user, or company. No other data from within the workspace is affected. What is Fireworks AI and how we used them Fireworks is one of the most-used global AI infrastructure platforms powering tens of thousands of customers, and used by hundreds of thousands of developers. We used Fireworks for classification jobs to help customers understand their own AI usage through a feature in Notion called Insights , and we used them as a general inference provider to serve open-weight models inside our product. The Insights feature has been disabled as we investigate this incident, and we are no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks. What happened and how we addressed it We learned from Fireworks about potential incidents earlier this month, and we shut down all connections to their systems out of an abundance of caution. On November 6, Fireworks notified us that malicious actors may have accessed potential customer data. Our team immediately began another internal investigation. On November 8, Fireworks confirmed this new dataset for us. Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included unattributable Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature. Chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain any tool call results. Beyond the words in the chat transcripts themselves, the data contained no information that could specifically identify the workspace, user, or company. No other Notion data from your workspace is affected, and we continue to monitor this incident. Who was affected by the Fireworks AI incident If neither you nor your workspace owner has heard from us, that means your workspace is not affected, and no action is needed right now. For the workspaces impacted by the Fireworks AI incident (<1% of the Notion workspaces), we have contacted the workspace owners. Affected customers will be able to retrieve and review the affected data securely inside their workspace. What affected workspace owners should do For the workspaces affected by the Fireworks AI incident, workspace owners can view the affected data by going to their workspace sidebar → ? → Security incident review . To view this data, use the desktop app or a web browser and make sure you’re on the latest version of Notion. This data is not accessible on mobile. Workspace owners on Enterprise plans can access: A CSV of your workspace’s data affected by the incident. Only workspace owners can see this data. An annotated CSV of the same affected workspace data with additional metadata, such as the user associated with each chat transcript, to help you understand and run your own analysis of the impact. These added annotations and metadata were not exposed as part of the incident. Additional annotated fields are marked with __metadata or __analysis respectively. Only workspace owners can see this data. Note: These resources are only available if you have managed members for your workspace. Reach out to your account team if you have questions. Workspace owners on all other plan types can access: A page that includes a link they can share with affected members to review their own data. For other workspace roles: Workspace owners can provide a link to members so members can see their own affected data. Once shared, the link will provide members with a CSV of only the member's own data affected by the incident. We recommend that you treat this data as if it were exposed. If you or anyone on your team pasted sensitive information like passwords, API keys, or other credentials into Notion AI during this timeframe, we recommend rotating them right away. FAQs What is Fireworks and how did Notion use them? Fireworks AI is one of the most used global AI infrastructure platforms powering tens of thousands of customers and used by hundreds of thousands of developers. As of November 3rd, we have disconnected our systems from Fireworks, deleted all data in the Fireworks system, and stopped sending all data and traffic to Fireworks. We have also halted all training runs. We previously used Fireworks for classification jobs to help customers understand their own AI usage through a feature in Notion called Insights and as a general inference provider to serve open-weight models inside our product. What does “unattributable” mean? Could the conversations still contain sensitive information? Following an investigation by the Notion security team, we have determined that <1% of Notion workspaces may have been affected by the Fireworks security incident. Some unattributable chat sessions with Notion AI may have been exposed. "Unattributable" means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from. The transcripts also did not contain tool call results (e.g., Notion page content, or external data pulled in by Notion AI.) Beyond what’s in the chat transcript itself, there’s no information tying the chat back to specific workspaces, users, or companies. No other data from within your workspace is affected. As a precaution, we recommend that you treat this unattributable data as if it were exposed. If anyone on your team pasted sensitive information like passwords, API keys, or other credentials into Notion AI during this timeframe, we recommend rotating them right away. How did Notion use Fireworks with the Learning and Early Access Program (LEAP)? Customers in the Learning and Early Access Program (LEAP) volunteer their data to help Notion test new AI technology. In the past, we used this volunteered data to experiment with training task-specific models on Fireworks. Where can I learn more about Notion’s security practices? Visit our Security page for an overview of Notion’s security and privacy practices. For more information on security policies, security audit reports, penetration test results, and additional resources, visit the Notion Trust Center . Try Nexus Products Models Research Customers Resources Docs Log in Nexus Platform Get started Nexus For work and co-work Platform For systems and apps All security bulletins Security bulletin Update on October 2026 security incident Last updated November 9, 2026 Active monitoring On this page The update Further activity Data involved What we have done Contact The update This is an update to our previous security bulletin published on October 9, 2026. In response to the incident, we notified law enforcement and obtained assistance from a leading cybersecurity firm, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, to help conduct forensic analysis. At the time of publishing the bulletin, only Fireworks stored secrets (e.g. used in evaluation jobs) were known to have been accessed. Since then, we discovered impacts to account and billing information. For a limited set of accounts, we also discovered impact to secrets, datasets, and incomplete models. The evidence indicates links to a cybercriminal threat actor group, which is financially motivated and aimed at selling tokens from unauthorized access to Large Language Models (LLMs) to illicit routing gateways, known as "LLMJacking". On November 2, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant published a blog post about the rise of LLMJacking, their motives, techniques used, and mitigation. Further activity A third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks R&D machines experienced a security incident on October 23. On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact. We detected this activity on the same day, and followed our incident response processes to take immediate remediation measures and close known critical vulnerabilities. As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use. Data involved The affected internal application provided access to the following categories of information: Resource metadata , such as Fireworks resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, creation time, etc. Billing information , such as billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment history, account balance, and credit usage. Payment card numbers are not stored by Fireworks and were not impacted. Model weights and datasets , for certain customers, a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets were accessed. We are notifying customers whose data was impacted, and providing details about the impact and recommended response actions. We have not detected any impact to Inference , Training SDK and Nexus , which are all zero data retention (ZDR) by default. These findings are based on our investigation to date. Our investigation is ongoing and may reveal additional information. What we have done Working with Unit 42, Fireworks identified and implemented security hardening procedures, including: Access and credential lockdown . Fireworks revoked and replaced credentials and service accounts, removed unnecessary elevated privileges, and tightened controls designed to prevent new unauthorized credentials from being created. Network isolation . Fireworks restricted unauthorized network pathways and isolated affected systems designed to prevent further unauthorized activity and movement between systems. Data protection . Fireworks reviewed and tightened access to data storage and analytics systems and enforced controls designed to prevent public or unauthorized access to stored data. Forensic and audit integrity . Fireworks secured and enhanced our logging and monitoring systems. As part of our response, we’ve disabled self-serve dataset uploads and downloads used by Batch Inference and dataset-based training while we investigate this incident. Training SDK remains available with ZDR, i.e. no training data stored at rest, and Fireworks Lab-based training operates in an isolated environment with additional network and storage protection. We continue to work with Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 on our investigation and security hardening. We will continue to monitor our systems 24/7 and will provide further updates on our investigation as appropriate.  Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude 
 9th November 2026 



 Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven’t unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn’t want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. 
 Here’s what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: 
 
 You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners—I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. 
 The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn’t work particularly well, so I added a “Rough mode” where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. 
 Once that’s set up, the devices all listen for the beep! 
 I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room—displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. 
 Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the “Sounds located” log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click “This is the mystery beep” to mark them as such. 
 Once you’ve confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. 
 The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced. 
 How it works 
 When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here’s that paper’s abstract: 
 
 We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting. 
 
 That sounded exactly like what we needed to build! 
 Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js ), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server. 
 When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep. 
 How I built it 
 I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here’s that shared starter session , which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository: 
 
 Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve 
 There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it 
 I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from 
 There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app 
 Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though? 
 
 That got me this problem.md file . As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file. 
 The research looked good, so I told it: 
 
 Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else 
 
 That got me to this point —most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet. 
 I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released , and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces. 
 I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran. 
 This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients. 
 On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn. 
 From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran: 
 
 I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate 
 
 This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map. 
 
 what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...] 
 Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps 
 
 That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps. 
 
 each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp 
 
 That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound. 
 
 The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays 
 
 Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for. 
 
 There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for 
 Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is 
 
 At this point I was getting close—I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn’t it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location? 
 
 I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app. 
 
 And since I had one spare device, I then said: 
 
 add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far 
 
 Giving Claude Code ears 
 I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it’s possible to give Claude Code ears . 
 Claude doesn’t have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone. 
 I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket. 
 Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem. 
 I’m reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not. 
 Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

 Around '05 or so, the house we were staying in started beeping. Smoke alarm sounds, as usual. For almost a day we couldn't find the source. Contacted the owners -- they didn't know it either. They bought the house few years prior, so not much of a help. Standing in the hallways listening at different angles, as the article says, didn't help. No Fable in '05 either. So I had to improvise. Got a ~1 meter stick and two headphones (every headphone is a microphone, even if it sucks as a microphone). Plugged them into the stereo mic port, and started recording in Audacity. The phase shift between L and R pointed directly to the source. Took about 4 or 5 beeps to get the sucker. Turns out, it was hiding above the ceiling tiles in the garage. My wife still tells this story to all her friends as one of my biggest life achievements. Everything I shipped, the companies I founded -- pales in comparison to finding a dead smoke alarm reply rkagerer 10 minutes ago | parent | next [–]

 it didn't have to be sensitive or even high quality. The beep was loud enough to register on these improvised "mics" and the phase shift of up to 3ms (~50 samples at 16 kHz) was clearly visible reply brookst 42 minutes ago | parent | prev | next [–]

It was maddening, I was contemplating of buying 1000 batteries, print a manual and shoving it in peoples mailboxes, although somehow I think it wouldnt have made a difference. I moved out eventually (not because of the beeps) reply db48x 4 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 It’s because it doesn’t have enough overtones, or a notable attack. You might have noticed that some trucks these days make a weird noise when they back up instead of a beep. They’re using white noise because it’s easier to locate; it has many overtones that allow your brain to pick the sound out of the background more easily, and thus more easily correlate the signals from both ears. You get a much more accurate location just from hearing that sound than you ever could with a pure tone. reply HPsquared 2 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] 
 Consider a pure sine wave, it's harder (in theory anyway) to match the signals from the left and right ears, and identify the time delay between the two signals: each cycle of the wave is just like the others, so there's no distinct signature to match and say "the sound reached the left ear 0.5 ms before it reached the right ear". This is especially the case for higher frequencies where there can be something like aliasing. Animal species sometimes use this in different sounds they make. An alarm call has that kind of "smooth tone" characteristic, so a predator can't locate the source of the sound but it still works to raise the alarm. Meanwhile more social sounds are more "chirpy" and sharp, so they can locate each other. reply thenthenthen 4 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–]
