Smart home devices should work without the internet — Do Code That Matters Do Code That Matters Blog About Do Code That Matters Blog About Smart home devices should work without the internet Oct 2026 · 4112 words · 21 min read · Spencer Kittleson Your browser does not support the audio element. Download audio Scissors cutting an ethernet cable under the words No Internet, No Problem. 
 AI;DR: I wrote the first draft, AI helped me edit and rewrite it, and I made the final pass. The rules, setups, and talks are my own. 
 
 TLDR; Nothing core in my house depends on a vendor’s server. If the internet goes down, the house keeps running. That’s been rule one for about ten years, and my other rules came out of it. This post has the rules, then both talks I’ve given on home automation, slide by slide. 
 Why local 
 My Nest integration worked until Google broke the API. That’s the failure I plan around now. The talks have a few more: a Samsung fridge showing a TLS certificate error on its own screen, and a Camp Chef grill controller that needs Wi-Fi to show you the temperature. 
 Everything that matters runs on hardware I own. That’s Tasmota on ESP boards, an MQTT broker, and Node-RED on a Raspberry Pi. I do use some cloud services, mostly Alexa and a few AWS ones. Alexa is just another way to flip a switch. If it’s down, the wall switches and the wall dashboard still work. 
 The rules 
 From the first talk, restated in the second: 
 
 No internet, no problem. Core stuff has to work with the internet unplugged. Alexa can be a way in, but never the only way. 
 Don’t remove the old way while adding the new one. If someone tapes a wall switch on so a smart bulb keeps power, I skipped this rule. 
 Be agile. Rooms get used differently and people move in and out, so it all has to be cheap to change. 
 Check your automations. I once had four scheduled triggers hitting the same garden pump. 
 Exceptions must be exceptional. I can break a rule, but only for a reason I’d still agree with six months later. 
 
 Added after year five, once more people lived in the house: 
 
 A cloud device needs an API with logs or it doesn’t get installed. I don’t want a black box in the house. 
 Config lives in one place instead of five vendor apps. 
 More than one way in: an app, Alexa, a QR code, or an NFC tag. 
 If I keep doing the same steps, they become a routine. 
 Devices talk pub/sub over MQTT instead of point to point. 
 No batteries unless they last a year or more between changes. Nobody wants to swap a door sensor battery at 2am. 
 
 The build I get asked about most is the Tasmota sprinkler controller . It’s in both talks, and so is the garage door setup, which has been running about as long. 
 Talk One: Home Automation 
 
 Nobody needs any of this. I like building things that just work in the background, and each automation is a small puzzle. 
 
 Everything talks to a cloud now: phones, laptops, thermostats, locks. Those clouds may or may not be up when you need them, so know what you’re signing up for before you plug something in. 
 
 Most people start here: a thermostat, a plug, a lock. Each has its own app and account. 
 
 Every device lands somewhere on this triangle. A cloud camera is cheap and easy, and it costs you privacy. A switch I flash myself takes longer to set up, but I can hook it into anything. I figure out where a device lands before I buy it. 
 
 Someone (often me) automates a light, then has to tape the wall switch on so the smart bulb keeps power. If a switch in a room ever did nothing, this is why. 
 
 The better fix is an in-wall Wi-Fi switch. The switch still works like a normal switch and I can still automate it. It’s more work to install than a smart plug, but nobody has to change their habits. 
 
 Rule one: if the internet goes down, my lights still turn on. 
 
 It’s never done. Rooms get used differently, people move in and out, new devices show up. Whatever you build has to be cheap to change. 
 
 The garage cooling flow starts from a manual trigger and checks if the door is closed. Then it opens the door, waits, and turns on the fan. If cooling is already running, it just sends a notification. Small flow, but it has kept the garage from baking more than once. 
 
 The door sensor and reed switch both report into a transform step that sets a global garage-closed flag and logs to Grafana. Below that is the chart from a few real days: 21 opens, with spikes showing when each one happened. It’s easy to skip reporting/alerting. This can alert me if the garage was left open, which is useful when I accidentally leave it open. 
 
 Four scheduled triggers all hit the same pump. It’s easy to end up with automations fighting over one device, so every so often I check whether they still make sense together. 
 
 I’ve broken all of these plenty of times, so they’re more like guidelines. 
 
 Three ways to do “event in, action out.” Node-RED is my main tool. Alexa routines and IFTTT-style applets cover the stuff I don’t want to build myself. 
 
 MQTT keeps things decoupled. The temperature sensor publishes and doesn’t care who’s listening, so a phone and a backend can both subscribe without the sensor doing anything extra. The sprinkler controller in the Tasmota post works the same way. 
 
 A Sonoff Mini fits inside the fireplace wiring, and the dashboard or Alexa can flip it. A fake fire you can turn on by voice is a good party trick. 
 
 The whole sprinkler build: the relay and ESP module in the enclosure, the 3D board render, the Tasmota UI with BME280 sensor readings, the Node-RED schedule feeding the pump, and the finished PCB layout. The sprinkler post has the full writeup, including why I picked Tasmota over custom firmware. It’s a bit hacky but I love it :D 
 
 The whole talk in five lines. The one I break most is the first, don’t introduce a new way while removing the old one, and I regret it every time. The last one stops me from breaking the others for no good reason. “I was in a hurry” doesn’t count. 
 
 
 That was talk one. Most of the “memorable automations” later broke in some new way or got replaced, so there’s a sequel. 
 Talk Two: Home Automation, The Sequel 
 
 Enough time passed between the talks that I had a new list of problems. 
 
 More devices means more decisions made without me. It’s a little unsettling but mostly harmless. 
 
 
 Same slide as before, with more icons. 
 
 Everyone else is dealing with this too: a fridge showing a TLS certificate error, a grill controller that needs Wi-Fi to show the temperature, and a note taped to a pole about an internet-connected printer someone forgot to log out of. 
 
 The same rules from talk one, worded a bit tighter, since part of the audience hadn’t seen the first talk. 
 
 The rules stayed the same, but what they had to survive got harder. 
 
 My setup assumed one person lived in the house. When that changed, I had to patch a single-user system into a multi-user one. The next few slides are how that went. 
 
 More people meant more foot traffic and more keys, and longer trips away meant things could fail with nobody around to notice. A water flooding scare finally got me to take leak and presence detection seriously. 
 
 Same joke, new rules. The first set came after year one, these after year five. 
 
 These are rules 6 to 11 at the top of the post, written after the house went from one person to several. 
 
 Now the builds, my favorite part. 
 
 A motor and PVC pipe rig for outdoor lighting, a UV grow light clipped to a houseplant, and a UV strip under the cabinets for sanitizing. 
 
 Same sprinkler slide as talk one. It’s one of the few builds that never needed a rewrite. 
 
 A sensor that sits on a credenza, a robot vacuum that runs on its own, and an AirGradient kit I put together from a CO2 sensor, a particulate sensor and a microcontroller, with its own dashboard. The air quality kit gives me the most peace of mind of anything here. 
 
 This dashboard replaced more apps than anything else: garage door, side door unlock, front lock, all lights on or off, brightness, a coffee bar color picker, and warm-to-cool for the living room. It’s one cheap tablet next to the thermostat, so nobody digs through five apps. 
 
 The lights behind the TV run through the same system instead of their own remote. 
 
 The smart locks came out of the more-people-more-keys problem. The newer one takes a password, the app, a keycard or a regular key, so everyone uses what they’re comfortable with. 
 
 The parts bin, for anyone who wants to build this. 
 
 The ESP32 D1 mini handles anything custom. The smart plug is the off-the-shelf shortcut when I don’t need custom. The Pi 4 runs Node-RED and Grafana. 
 
 LED strips for ambient lighting, power transistors for higher-current loads, and small relay modules so a microcontroller can switch mains voltage safely. 
 
 The rest of the bin: a resistor assortment, color-coded wire so I can trace a circuit later, and a capacitor kit for smoothing and timing. 
 
 Node-RED for the logic, Grafana to see what’s happening, Tasmota on anything I flash, Telegram for notifications, and Python or JavaScript for glue code that doesn’t fit in a flow. 
 
 The garage flow today. The door sensor and reed switch feed Grafana and a global closed state. Toggle nodes publish straight to Tasmota command topics. Notifications go to Telegram and an audio chime, and a light-on counter resets at midnight. The tabs across the top (Lights, Sensors, Garage, Sprinkler, NFC Tags, Door Lock Security) show how much it has grown since the single garage cooling flow in talk one. 
 
 This is the “is everything okay” dashboard: humidity, temperature, dew point, pressure and gas on one side, and energy use, door opens and on-status history on the other. I built it because I got tired of guessing. 
 
 Dashboards and Grafana panels work for me. Everyone else in the house just wants the light on. 
 
 The “more than one way in” rule in hardware: the wall tablet for whoever is standing there, NFC tags and a QR code to tap, and an Echo Dot for anyone who would rather talk to the house. 
 
 The tools I build and debug all of this with. 
 
 A soldering iron for permanent connections, a 3D printer for enclosures and brackets you can’t buy, a multimeter for when something isn’t working, and a precision screwdriver kit for devices the manufacturer didn’t want opened. 
 
 That’s both talks, five years apart. The rules barely changed between them, but the list of problems kept growing. 
 A third talk is coming, built around agentic use cases. The same rules should hold when an AI agent is the one flipping the switches, and I expect to add a few. 
 What readers told me 
 I shared the “no internet, no problem” rule on LinkedIn and asked for the most pointless internet dependency people had found in a device. Dozens of people answered. A Hacker News thread added more. Here’s what came back. 
 Everyone has one 
 Most examples were basic functions locked behind an app, an account, or a server: 
 
 A fridge whose temperature can’t be changed because of a bug in the manufacturer’s phone app. 
 A TV that can’t even switch inputs when the internet is down, and another that has to be signed in before it works as a plain HDMI monitor. One reader’s older smart TV has dead apps but still works as a regular TV, which is how a device should fail. 
 A heating system whose app doesn’t work from the local network. 
 A kitchen vent and a dishwasher that need the internet even when you control them from Home Assistant. 
 A smart plug that can’t be set up on an isolated network. 
 Noise-cancelling headphones that search for a Bluetooth device forever, so you can’t just turn on the noise cancelling. 
 Synthesizers and MIDI keyboards that need a cloud login for first use or firmware updates. 
 A meat thermometer that only worked through its app and stopped working when the company went out of business. 
 
 The meat thermometer bothers me most. The hardware outlived the company, and it stopped working anyway. 
 Rules readers added 
 
 Offline first, with the internet for extras. A device should do its main job on its own. 
 Treat every third-party dependency as a risk. APIs change, so plan a local fallback or a clear degraded mode. One mobile developer works the same way: the core action works offline or from cache, and only the extras wait for a connection. 
 Decide what must work offline. My answer is turning things on and off, temperature and safety controls, and anything a guest has to use without learning an app. As one reader said, if a visitor can’t turn something on or adjust the temperature without an app account, the design has failed. 
 A stricter version of my first two rules: everything core works with the Wi-Fi or the automation server shut down, and smart features never take away the dumb ones. The wall switch should control the light directly and let automation flip it. A switch that only sends a request to the automation fails. That reader says my sprinkler controller fails this bar too. The only sprinkler controller they’d found with a local API and full control on the device itself was RainMachine, which is gone. 
 Clean up when you throw things away. Remove a connected printer from your account first. An abandoned connected device can be an easy way in for an attacker. 
 
 Practical tips 
 
 Use local protocols. One reader recommends Zigbee and Z-Wave over Wi-Fi, because a switch that doesn’t need the cloud tends to behave the same year after year. Another uses Zigbee for the smart plugs that can’t be set up without internet. 
 Let an LLM find the firmware. One reader buys the cheapest hardware that does the job, ignores reviews that complain about the app, and asks an LLM for local-first custom firmware once it arrives. That has worked for their switches, a thermostat, an air quality monitor, a thermometer, and a window fan. They’d have paid about 2.5x for hardware that was local out of the box. 
 Old Nest thermostats have a way out. No Longer Evil is open source firmware for Nest Gen 1 and Gen 2 thermostats. 
 Smart TVs can be tamed. Reset the TV and never connect it to the network, and the input problem goes away. 
 Remote access is the cost of staying local. I use Tailscale on the router and keep the individual devices off the tailnet. One reader ran OpenVPN on OpenWrt, which worked but felt clunky, and is now trying Tailscale. 
 There’s a gap to fill. One reader would happily pay for a pre-built, open “works with everything” Raspberry Pi image with MQTT. DietPi and OpenWrt come close and have a small footprint, but you need some understanding to get going. Another wanted a hub that ships with the house, like a water heater or a router. Home Assistant sells hub hardware that’s close to that. 
 Right to repair is the bigger fight. Readers pointed to the right-to-repair movement and groups like the FULU Foundation , which work to keep companies from locking you out of what you bought. 
 
 Counterpoints 
 Connectivity has real uses. A connected meat thermometer lets you watch the game while the steak cooks. The same reader also had an oven decide to update its software in the middle of cooking. One reader pointed out the business model behind all of this: companies would rather sell you a service than a product. Another expects the shift away from internet-connected devices to come from resilience worries rather than consumer complaints, since enough connected homes make a target. And one skips connected appliances entirely, keeping only computers and phones online.

 Bought our home almost 20 years ago, and the former owner (apparently) owned a now-defunct home automation business. The upside was 100% X10/Insteon power and light controls, top alarm panel, environmental controls and so on running off of a wall-mounted "SmartLinc" touch panel. I expanded the system with Axis cameras and a Mac Server running Indigo and SecuritySpy (non-subscription), which enabled remote monitoring and control, but it all operates locally. In a moment of weakness, I bought a D-Link wireless (wifi) water detector for the sump pit (it was on clearance for $30); it relied on a D-Link Home cloud service (free) that was closed down a few years ago. Not wanting to toss it, I repurposed a spare Chromebook 14 that I was going to recycle and turned it into a Alpine monitor for the water detector, which I'm powering from the Chromebook's USB port (if power is lost in a rainstorm, I need to know about it before the sump pit fills up). An immediate issue was that the D-Link firmware tried to "phone home" every 24 hours and would drop from the local network, since the server was kaput, and I had no clue what response it was expecting from the server to keep it alive. Solution; "reboot" the unit by interrupting USB power (with a Pico and MOSFET) every 23 hours. There's no question that home automation should work without the internet. reply knodi123 9 hours ago | parent | next [–]

 I think this interpretation is a bit too negative. Undoubtedly the companies want to spy on you, and with Thread 1.3 they were already perfectly capable of doing so - via your Thread border router, which connects to the normal LAN and can talk to the Internet (if you let it). Allocating Thread devices from global IPv6 blocks (GUAs) doesn't change that, it just removes the NAT between Thread devices and the border router. Before Thread 1.4 the IPv6 addresses used by the Thread network were all ULAs - i.e. the devices were only routable locally and didn't have a global IPv6 address, so if you did happen to want to talk to your Thread devices over the internet, it was possible but the Thread border router had to do NAT for you. With Thread 1.4 the border router can assign device IPs straight from the global IPv6 block assigned by your ISP, which means you can directly access your Thread device over the internet without the NAT provided by the Thread border router. If you don't want to locally host your smart home automations (you and I do, but the average consumer doesn't) this can be very useful. It's also really helpful if you want to access your own devices remotely over the Internet and not need to bother with port forwarding. IMO this fits perfectly with the philosophy of IPv6 - every device can have a globally routable IP address without needing NAT. If you don't want your devices reaching out to the Internet (like I don't), the solution is to put all that stuff on its own VLAN with no Internet access (which I do). reply ketzu 8 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–]

 Good Things Come in 5.3s 

 Gaussian splats, DLSS denoising, light dispersion, EEVEE fisheye, Outliner sorting, ripple video editing, and so much more. 
 
 
 
 
 Download Blender 5.3 
 
 
 Watch Recap Video 
 
 
 
 
 

 
	
	
 
	
 




 
 
 
 
 
 
 Watch the Recap Video 



 
 
 New features overview by Jonathan Lampel and Wayne Dixon from CGCookie . 
 
 



 
 
 
 Make a Splat 



 Welcome native 3D Gaussian Splats support to Blender 5.3! 



 Import them as point clouds, experiment with Geometry Nodes, preview them in Workbench, and render them natively with EEVEE or Cycles. 
 
 



 
 
 
 Gaussian Magic 



 3D Gaussian Splats are commonly used to reconstruct 3D scenes from photos or videos. They consist of many small, soft, transparent blobs that combine to represent complex geometry and shading. 



 Blender can now import Gaussian Splats from PLY , SPZ , and glTF files, store them as point clouds, process them with Geometry Nodes, and render them in EEVEE, Cycles, and Workbench (solid mode). 
 



 
 PLY file imported as gaussian splats, featuring DOGWALK by Blender Studio. 
 
 



 
 
 
 
 
 



 
 Point of View 



 Gaussian splats are represented as point clouds, using a new type to tell them apart and with special attributes: 



 
 scale : A vector represneting the size of the splat. 



 rotation : A quaternion to control the rotation of the splat. 



 radiance:base : 4D Vector as base (DC) radiance of the splats, followed by opacity. 



 radiance:sh_{index} : Coefficients of the spherical harmonics bands >= 1. The order is <L=1 M=-1> , <L=1 M=0> , <L=1 M=1> , <L=2 M=-2> … where L is the band index and M is the basis function. 
 



 
 Read Manual 
 
 
 



 
 
 Radiant Future 



 By default, a 3D Gaussian Splat is rendered using an emissive shader. The radiance attribute provides access to the resolved radiance of the splat at the current shading point. 



 There is rudimentary support for making the splat relightable by replacing the Emission node with a hard surface BSDF such as Diffuse BSDF. 



 Performance is still being optimized. Rendering may produce inaccuracies due to differences between the sRGB space used by most Gaussian Splat authoring tools and Blender’s linear color space, particularly in areas with low opacity and high radiance. 
 



 
 
 
 Simple example of relit Gaussian Splat. 
 
 
 



 
 More About Shading 


 

 
 
 
 Added support for seven Geometry Nodes 
 
 
 
 Improved color management interoperability 
 
 
 
 See all rendering changes 
 
 
	
 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 
 CYCLES 



 Divide and Shine 



 
 The Principled BSDF now supports Dispersion ! 



 Turn ordinary glass and diamonds into beautiful little rainbows by splitting white light into its colorful components. 



 Cycles Dispersion overview on YouTube by Chris Tyler 
 
 
 



 
 
 
 Butterflies specter shader by Cartesian Caramel 
 



 
 CYCLES 



 A diamond in the Rough 



 With Dispersion in the Transmission panel, the Principled BSDF can now reproduce the characteristic rainbow effect seen in glass and gemstones. This corresponds to OpenPBR v1.1.1. 



 Roughness anisotropy is also now supported by the Glass BSDF and the transmission component of the Principled BSDF. It behaves just like anisotropy for specular reflections. 



 
 Read Manual 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 
 
 CYCLES 



 Gone with Denoise 



 Blender 5.3 integrates DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction as a new denoiser, delivering cleaner images faster by upscaling and reusing samples from previous frames. 



 Think Cycles looks with EEVEE responsiveness. 
 



 
 
 



 
 
 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 NVIDIA DLSS brings near-final render quality to the viewport, making lighting and look development faster and more responsive while virtually eliminating flickering between frames during animation playback. 



 Find it in the Denoise panel under Render properties, Sampling. 



 DLSS denoising requires NVIDIA driver version 620 or newer. 



 
 Learn More 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 



 
 Ready to Spark 



 
 Blender 5.3 brings native support for NVIDIA RTX Spark devices running Windows 11, including memory optimizations. 



 
 Learn More 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 
 EEVEE 



 Lights Meet Material Nodes 
 



 
 Material Lighting nodes allow authoring how the Material reacts to Lights. 



 This can, for example, be used for toon and stylized shading, but also for complex physical effects like iridescence. 
 
 



 
 
 
 
 
 
 All the nodes you need to adjust lighting to your liking. 
 



 
 Lighting to Your Liking 



 Per-light data, evaluation, and shadow information are now available in the Shader Editor, giving you more control over how materials respond to individual scene lights. 



 Four new nodes and two that received a “Light” mode/space: 



 
 Light Accumulation : Evaluates its inputs for each light in the scene and accumulates the results. 



 Light Info : Exposes light data properties (Color, Power, and Position). 



 Light Evaluation : Evaluates position-dependent light properties (Diffuse/Specular Term, Attenuation Mask, Direction, and Distance). 



 Shadow Raycast : Outputs a shadow mask value for the light being shaded. 



 Attribute (Light Mode) : Queries custom properties from the Light Object or Light Data being evaluated. 



 Vector Transform (Light Space) : Transforms coordinates to and from the local space of the light being evaluated. 
 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 A Wider Perspective 



 EEVEE can now render panoramic cameras, supporting all types of projections, from equirectangular and cubemap formats to various fisheye models and mirror ball. 
 



 EEVEE fisheye matching Cycles 1:1 



 
 The current implementation has a few limitations: depth of field, raytracing, and volumetric temporal reprojection in the viewport are not yet supported. 
 



 
 Learn More 
 
 



 
 More in EEVEE & Viewport 


 

 
 
 
 Sky Texture now shows Sun Disc 
 
 
 
 Vulkan is now default 
 
 
 
 Raytraced Shadows in Workbench 
 
 
 
 See all EEVEE & Viewport changes 
 
 
	
 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 Give back to Blender. 

 
 



 Releases are possible thanks to donations by the community. 



 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 
 COMPOSITOR 



 Side Effects 



 You can now stack Effects on your scene just like you would modifiers or constraints. 



 Applying compositing effects has never been easier. 



 Scene Effects stack featuring Storm by Blender Studio 
 



 
 
 
 
 New Compositor & Effects tab in the Properties editor. 
 



 
 
 One-click, Bloom ! 



 Choose from built-in effects such as Bloom , Chromatic Aberration , Film Grain , and Vignette , as well as effects from online asset libraries or your own custom compositor node groups. 



 Internally, each effect is its own node group, with its output passed on to the next effect. 



 You can further customize effects at any time in the Compositor editor. 



 
 Read Manual 
 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 COMPOSITOR 



 Bundle Up 



 
 17 Geometry Nodes are now supported in the Compositor, bringing a range of new capabilities across bundles , math and logic, and utility operations. 



 This includes bundle support with Get Bundle Item , Store Bundle Item , Combine Bundle , Typed Bundle , and Separate Bundle . 



 Math and logic nodes such as Boolean Math , Compare , Float to Integer , Integer Math , Matrix SVD , Combine Transform , and Separate Transform . Plus utility nodes including Hash Value , Random Value , Is Viewport , Import Text , and Bone Info . 



 
 See All Compositing Nodes 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 
 
 Play Fast 



 Playback is now up to 2x faster on GPU, particularly when playing back EXR sequences. 



 The interactive compositor now supports playback caching . It can be enabled from the sidebar, Options panel. 



 Anisotropic Kuwahara is now up to 10x faster on Apple GPUs, 2x faster on NVIDIA GPUs, and 25-30% on CPU.

 Blender splash artwork source files are available for you to play with!

 More Splash Blend Files 
 
 



 
 
 
 OVERGROWN, by Blender Studio 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 
 
 
 The new File → Project menu, to create, open and access projects. 
 



 
 CORE 



 Blender, meet projects . 



 Until now, Blender’s preferences (such as asset libraries) were shared across all projects, and it was up to users to keep related files and resources organized. 



 Blender now supports projects, giving you a way to group related files, share resources, and manage settings across an entire project, whether you’re working alone or as part of a team. 
 
 



 
 
 
 Everything Everywhere All In a Project 



 Projects support custom variables that can be used throughout a project, such as a character’s name or a frequently used file path. 



 Per-project asset libraries and color management configurations are also supported. You can even set up a custom splash screen for your project, providing quick access to its files and other recent projects. 



 Add-ons and other extensions per-project will follow in future Blender versions. 



 Projects are entirely optional, most of the time you’ll probably work without one.

 Project-specific splash and color management configuration. 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 
 
 
 
 ASSETS 



 Asset Libraries ♥ Extensions 
 



 
 Asset libraries can now be shared as extensions! Just like add-ons or themes. 



 Browse hundreds of public domain assets available on the Extensions platform via the Get Extensions tab and install them directly from within Blender. 



 Create and share your own asset library extension. Optionally, access can be controlled via authentication tokens . 



 
 Browse Asset Libraries 



 Read Manual 
 
 
 



 
 
 
 A selection of public domain assets by the popular library Poly Haven is now available from within Blender. No add-ons required. 
 
 
 



 
 See All Changes to Assets 
 
 
 



 
 
 
 
 



 
 GREASE PENCIL 



 Drawn to Select 



 Draw Mode now has its own selection tools: Tweak , Lasso , Box , and Circle . Select strokes and adjust them right where you draw. 



 Move, rotate, scale, duplicate, copy, paste, and delete strokes using the usual shortcuts, or access all these actions from the new Stroke menu. 



 
 Read Manual 
 
 
 



 
 
 Carve Diem 



 Meet the new Carver tool in Draw Mode. 



 It cuts shapes using proper Boolean subtraction, creating clean cuts in strokes and fills based on a lasso selection. Holes are created automatically when needed. 



 When a shape has both a stroke and a fill, carving a hole into it also creates a stroke around the hole. Fills that are split apart become separate shapes, making them easy to sculpt further. 



 
 Read Manual 
 
 



 
 The new Carver tool uses booleans to cut through strokes and fills. 
 
 



 
 
 Fill with color multiple regions at once using the new Fill tool in Blender 5.3. 
 



 
 One Tool to Fill Them All 



 The Fill tool can now fill multiple regions at once. 



 Simply draw a path across multiple regions to fill them all as a single shape, with no gaps or borders in between. 



 
 Read Manual 
 
 
 



 
 
 Ramp It Up 



 Gradient fills now use a ColorRamp input instead of being limited to just two colors. 



 
 Read Manual 
 
 



 
 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 Assign Flip View a shortcut or add it to Quick Favorites for easy access. 
 



 
 Flip Out 



 Mirror the camera view horizontally with the new Flip View operator to evaluate the composition from a different perspective and spot asymmetry or visual imbalances. 



 This only affects the viewport display. It does not change the camera object’s transform or the final render, which remains unchanged. Use the operator again to restore the original orientation. 



 Flip View has no shortcut assigned by default, but you can assign your own through the right-click menu or add it to Quick Favorites (Q) for easy access. 



 
 Read Manual 
 
 
 



 
 
 See all Grease Pencil changes 
 
 
 



 
 
 
 
 I/O 



 USD Collection Importer 



 
 Collections can now be associated to importers . 



 Similar to the Collection Exporters introduced in Blender 4.2 LTS, Collection Importers make it easy to re-import data with a single click, without having to navigate menus or adjust settings repeatedly. 



 Configure them through the Importers panel under Collection Properties. Settings are stored in .blend files, making them easy to share and preserving them across Blender sessions. 



 Only the USD importer is supported in Blender 5.3. 
 



 
 Read Manual 



 Learn More 
 



 See all USD , Alembic , glTF , OpenEXR , and other I/O changes. 
 



 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 



 
 
 VIDEO SEQUENCER 



 Cut to the chase 



 The Video Sequencer gets a full ripple editing framework, a rewritten blade tool, and a long list of editing, interface, and performance improvements, including initial OpenTimelineIO support. 
 



 
 
 
 Ripple, Shuffle, Overwrite 



 Welcome Ripple editing to Blender 5.3! 



 This new overlap mode automatically moves strips forward or backward as edits are made, maintaining timeline continuity without the need to manually close gaps. 



 Ripple , Shuffle , and Overwrite modes are now consistently used across editing operations. Switch between them while moving strips using R , S , and V . 
 



 
 
 
 
 
 



 
 



 
 
 
 
 
 
 



 
 Making Waves 



 Complete the ripple workflow with these handy operators: 



 Ripple Add : Hold Shift while dragging and dropping strips to insert them using ripple behavior, automatically making room in the timeline. 



 Ripple Trim : Trim selected strips at the playhead and automatically close the resulting gaps. Use Shift+Q or Shift+W to trim from either side. 



 Ripple Delete : Delete selected strips and move subsequent content back to close the gaps. Use Shift+X . 
 
 
 



 
 Cutting Edge: Blade 2.0 



 Splits are now visualized as a line when using Blade and as a region when using Box Blade . Tooltips display frame values at the split location, while a real-time preview shows the frame beneath the cursor. 



 



 Press and hold C in the timeline to temporarily activate the Blade tool. Release it to switch back to the previously active tool. 



 
 Read Manual 
 
 



 
 But wait, there’s more: Hardware decoding , thumbnail support for Scene and other strips, OpenTimelineIO import and export, and much more. 



 
 See all Video Sequencer changes

 Search. Sort. Scribble. 



 
 Blender 5.3 gets more than a layer of polish. Long-awaited quality of life features and improvements that make this release take a leap in usability.

 Arrange your objects freely with custom sorting in the Outliner. Finally. 



 Switch back to alphabetical order from the header popover. 



 Plus improvements to filtering, drag-and-drop behavior, and hierarchy management.

 Place objects anywhere you want in the Outliner. 
 
 



 
 
 
 
 Press Ctrl/Cmd + F to find anything in the sidebar.

 Sidebars in all editors now support search , making it possible to find any property or operator, even inside tabs created by add-ons.

 To clear the search, press Alt/Option + F .

 The Blender UI now supports rendering basic Markdown formatting. 



 In node editors, write markdown directly in the new Comment node, or in regular layouts for scripts/add-ons through the label_markdown widget. Another handy widget for long strings is label_multiline , it behaves just like labels but allows text to wrap.

 I've been using Claude to drive Blender with the official Blender MCP server. Mixed results; but some of them very good. Claude Opus is very good at creating geometry nodes for specific applications. You have to know what to ask for. It's not a magic genie. For example, I asked it to make a node setup to create the geometry for a table. It did a mediocre job of it. Then I told it to do research on the nomenclature for tables and create a parametric control interface to generate tables with the UI using the table nomenclature. It did a very good job of that. It set it up so that I could put the units in using Imperial or metric. I also asked it to come up with reasonable default values for the parameters and it did. With just a little tweaking I have a very useful table generator for greyboxing scenes. I then did a similar round with it for book cases and straightback chairs with useful results. I asked it to make material nodes for wood: oak, maple, etc. And it did a pretty good job of that. Nothing amazing, but a useful place to start. It won't be replacing people that know what they are doing, but its useful for giving that person better specifications for what you want. I had Claude keep notes on the project and it made a skill that has been useful for later projects. Think of it as a very bright intern that works very fast but has very little practical experience. The problem, of course, is that if AI replaces interns, then there may not be a future generation of experts. By then, though, the AIs may be good enough to replace the experts. Next year? Next week? At a high-level, the problem is they don't 'learn on the job' like a human and writing their memory & learning in .md files works for some things but fails for others. While the 'rising tide' of baseline LLM knowledge continues to grow, they are still FTIs (Factory Trained Intelligences), meaning they mostly learn from data which can be assembled/tagged or synthesized in mass bulk - plus specific abilities in certain domains which the factory has prioritized for more costly special training. For some broad categories of important work, I suspect there's a significant unfilled gap in our LLM instances being able to effectively crystallize knowledge acquired on-task. Sci-fi stuff aside, it's not just a matter of the AI's telling the supporting tech what to do. We are already at the point where we can't predict what the AI will do to the supporting tech. I think nothing of having Claude whip up a special physics based particle system or compositing stack these days.  Pre-Authentication Authorization Bypass and Command Injection Vulnerabilities in Certain Barracuda Products — Updates Available 
 Overview 
 Barracuda has identified two vulnerabilities affecting certain Barracuda products: a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability and a command injection vulnerability. The vulnerabilities have been assigned CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 , respectively. 
 Successful exploitation requires an attacker to have access to the administrative interface of an affected product. If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device. 
 Barracuda immediately initiated a comprehensive remediation process and released security patches for affected products. We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations. 
 Customers should review the affected products and remediation guidance below, ensure their systems are running the latest firmware version, and have all security patches applied.

 Organizations whose administrative interfaces are not publicly accessible from the internet are less exposed to this attack path. Barracuda recommends restricting access to administrative interfaces to trusted internal networks and using appropriate network access controls to limit exposure. 
 Firmware 
 Customers using these products should verify that their systems are running the latest firmware versions and have received all security patches. The device will show the latest firmware version available. 
 If firmware on a device is multiple versions out of date, customers may need to perform more than one update. Contact Barracuda Support for assistance. 
 Patches 
 If a patch has not been automatically applied, customers should manually apply the appropriate patch as soon as possible. If customers have turned off automatic patching, Barracuda recommends setting devices to automatically receive patches.

 Dev Blogs .NET Blog Announcing .NET 11 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 November 10th, 2026 
 
 
 13 reactions 
 
 Announcing .NET 11 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 .NET Team 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Show more 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Today, we’re excited to announce the release of .NET 11! This year’s release makes building modern applications faster, more productive, and has improvements across C# 15, ASP.NET Core, .NET MAUI, and Windows development. With hundreds of runtime optimizations, more responsive SDK tooling, and less overhead in everyday commands, you can spend less time waiting and more time creating. Build richer web and cross-platform applications, take advantage of new C# language features, and explore AI-powered development with improved tools and agentic capabilities. 
 Download .NET 11 
 .NET 11 support 
.NET 11 is a Standard Term Support (STS) release with two years of support under the .NET support policy . STS and Long Term Support (LTS) releases have the same quality and servicing policies; the difference is the length of support. .NET 10 remains a supported LTS option. Stay current with servicing updates whichever release you choose.
 
 Join us at .NET Conf, November 10-13 
 Explore .NET 11 with the product teams and community at .NET Conf 2026 . The conference includes product team sessions on November 10 and 11, followed by two days of community sessions. 
 Watch the Day 1 livestream, including the keynote , or browse the conference session playlist . 
 Announcing .NET 11 
 Watch .NET Conf 
 What’s new in .NET 11 
 Some of the changes we’re most excited for you to try: 
 
 C# 15 union types and closed hierarchies help you express the possible states of your application and handle them with compiler-checked patterns. 
 A Native AOT CLI host and a warm MSBuild server reduce overhead in everyday developer workflows. 
 ASP.NET Core brings asynchronous validation, OpenAPI 3.2, and new capabilities for Blazor and SignalR applications. Experimental Blazor AI components integrate with the Agent User Interaction Protocol (AG-UI) for advanced agentic web experiences. 
 Build AI-powered, agentic applications with Microsoft.Extensions.AI (MEAI) for model access, MCP for tool integration, and Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) for agents and workflows. 
 Put agentic development tools to work with .NET Skills for .NET-specific guidance, .NET MAUI DevFlow for inspecting and testing running apps, and the .NET Upgrade canvas for reviewing modernization progress. 
 .NET MAUI adopts CoreCLR as its default runtime and improves XAML iteration and native controls. 
 The libraries add built-in Zstandard compression, simpler process execution, richer JSON support, and new ways to work with in-memory data without copying it first. 
 
 The what’s new in .NET 11 overview links to the full details. Here are the changes behind those headlines and how to start using them. 
 Languages 
 C# 15 
 C# 15 is the default language version for projects targeting .NET 11. Union types are one of its biggest additions: a value can be one of a declared set of case types, with conversions from those types and exhaustiveness checking in switch expressions. 
 Consider a product lookup that either finds a product or reports that it wasn’t found: 
 ProductLookup result = new Product(42, "Mechanical keyboard");

string message = result switch
{
 Product product => $"Found {product.Name}",
 ProductNotFound missing => $"No product with ID {missing.Id}",
};

Console.WriteLine(message);

public sealed record Product(int Id, string Name);
public sealed record ProductNotFound(int Id);
public union ProductLookup(Product, ProductNotFound); 
 The result type tells a caller which outcomes it needs to handle. There’s no need to use object or an unrelated base class just to put those outcomes behind one return type. 
 C# 15 also adds closed hierarchies . A closed class limits direct derivation to its declaring assembly, giving the compiler the information it needs to check patterns over the hierarchy. Unions are useful when you want to combine existing types; closed hierarchies fit models where you own the inheritance relationship. 
 Smaller language features help with everyday code, too. Collection expression arguments let you pass constructor or factory arguments without giving up collection expression syntax: 
 HashSet<string> names =
 [with(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), "Alice", "ALICE", "Bob"];

Console.WriteLine(names.Count); 
 This prints 2 : the comparer controls equality, so "Alice" and "ALICE" are one entry. 
 Other additions include extension indexers and labeled break and continue . These features don’t require the preview language version. The separate memory safety work remains in preview ; see the C# 15 feature documentation for its opt-in requirements. 
 F# 11 
 F# 11 improves compiler memory use and reduces allocations in FSharp.Core collection operations. It also adds ways to bound concurrent asynchronous work, useful when a collection operation would otherwise start more work than a service or machine can handle comfortably. 
 The F# release notes distinguish the default-language updates from preview capabilities, including Runtime Async support for custom computation-expression builders. 
 Platform 
 SDK 
 The SDK now enables a Native AOT CLI host by default. Commands such as help and version queries can run without starting the managed CLI, and tool launches can avoid that startup path too. Commands that need managed execution still use it. 
 The MSBuild server also stays warm between CLI invocations by default, reducing repeated startup work. SDK installers on Linux and macOS are smaller through assembly deduplication. 
 File-based apps can grow across source files with #:include , and solution filters can be created and edited from the CLI. dotnet watch adds Aspire app-host integration, crash recovery, and device selection for mobile projects. 
 For teams using Microsoft.Testing.Platform, dotnet test gains run-level timeouts, failure limits, clearer progress reporting, and per-module results directories. The test runner matters: these switches aren’t interchangeable with the VSTest command-line options. 
 Container publishing adds reproducible image digests through SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH and avoids redundant layer uploads when the target manifest already exists. NuGet source configuration gains a minimum package publication age setting, which lets teams wait before newly published package versions become eligible for selection. This is an additional policy control, not a replacement for vulnerability checks or reviewing dependencies. 
 See what’s new in the SDK and tooling for command examples and configuration. 
 Runtime and performance 
 Performance work in .NET 11 reaches both the code you deploy and the tools you use to develop it. Stephen Toub’s Performance Improvements in .NET 11 takes a detailed tour through hundreds of runtime and library optimizations, with benchmarks and code examples. 
 The just-in-time (JIT) compiler improvements remove more redundant bounds checks and branches, improve devirtualization, and fold more operations into constants. For example, the JIT can optimize additional SequenceEqual calls when it knows the inputs at compile time. These changes improve generated code without requiring you to rewrite the corresponding application logic. 
 Native AOT interface dispatch uses a shared helper that reduces the code needed at interface call sites and improves throughput for interface-heavy workloads. Hardware support also expands, including FP16 instructions for Half operations on supported x64 and Arm64 hardware and new vector construction and composition APIs. 
 There’s useful work on diagnostics, too. In-process crash report logging can capture a managed stack trace, module information, and runtime state before a process exits. Previously available on mobile platforms, this reporting path now also supports Linux and macOS. 
 As always, measure the effect on your own application. Throughput, startup time, memory use, and deployment size depend on the workload and publishing options you choose. 
 Runtime Async has been a recurring theme throughout the .NET 11 previews. It moves asynchronous suspension and resumption into the runtime instead of relying on compiler-generated state machines. 
 One especially useful result is a clearer live call stack. Profilers and debuggers can show the asynchronous methods themselves instead of the infrastructure used to execute them. This is a distinction from exception stack traces, which already hide much of that infrastructure. 
 Runtime Async remains a preview feature. To try it in a project targeting net11.0 , add: 
 <PropertyGroup>
 <Features>runtime-async=on</Features>
</PropertyGroup> 
 You don’t need to enable EnablePreviewFeatures for this scenario. The .NET runtime libraries themselves are built with Runtime Async, but opting your application’s code into the new compilation model is a separate choice. See the Runtime Async documentation for its behavior and current guidance, and test your application’s dependencies and diagnostics before adopting it. 
 AI libraries and tools 
 The .NET 11 SDK includes an MCP server template . MCP gives AI applications a common way to discover and call tools and services. The template uses the official MCP C# SDK and includes a working sample tool, so you can start exposing your own functionality without first installing a separate template package: 
 dotnet new mcpserver -o MyMcpServer 
 For applications that consume AI services, Microsoft.Extensions.AI (MEAI) provides abstractions such as IChatClient and IEmbeddingGenerator . These libraries let you compose model access with dependency injection, caching, and OpenTelemetry using familiar .NET patterns. They’re available as NuGet packages, rather than features that require you to move all of your application code to a new framework version. 
 Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) builds on these abstractions with agents that call tools and maintain conversation state, plus workflows that coordinate agents and application code. Connect agents to MCP tools to give them access to your application’s capabilities, and expose an agent through an ASP.NET Core AG-UI endpoint to build an interactive Blazor experience. The AG-UI hosting integration is currently prerelease. 
 For hands-on examples, start with .NET AI Essentials: The Core Building Blocks Explained and continue with our Microsoft Agent Framework walkthrough . 
 Libraries 
 The .NET libraries add capabilities that previously required extra setup, intermediate buffers, or custom helpers. 
 The Process API expansion includes one-shot methods to run a process and capture its output and exit status. More advanced APIs give you control over inherited handles, suspended starts, and process signaling. Build tools and developer utilities can spend less code on process plumbing while still inspecting how a child process finished. See Process API Improvements in .NET 11 for examples. 
 Zstandard compression joins the existing compression formats in System.IO.Compression . New span-based compression APIs support callers that manage their own buffers, and ZIP improvements include CRC32 validation when reading entries. 
 Four new in-memory stream adapters bridge existing data to APIs that accept a Stream : ReadOnlyMemoryStream , WritableMemoryStream , ReadOnlySequenceStream , and StringStream . For example, a pipeline’s segmented ReadOnlySequence<byte> can be read as a stream without first flattening it into a new contiguous buffer. 
 System.Text.Json adds support for C# unions, F# discriminated unions, and JSON Lines output from asynchronous sequences. F# union support uses reflection and doesn’t support source generation, trimming, or Native AOT, so check the documented limits before choosing it for a trimmed application. 
 LINQ adds FullJoin , which preserves unmatched elements from both inputs. This is useful for reconciliation work, such as comparing two inventories where you need to see missing items on either side. 
 The libraries also expand numeric types, DNS resolution, cryptography, and tracing configuration. The library overview covers the complete set of changes and marks APIs that remain experimental. 
 Entity Framework Core 11 
 Entity Framework Core 11 improves how your model becomes a query and how that query becomes SQL. 
 EF Core removes unnecessary joins in more reference-navigation and split-query scenarios, improves GroupBy translation, and translates the new LINQ FullJoin operator on relational providers that support it. These changes can simplify generated SQL while letting more queries stay in LINQ. 
 Complex types and JSON columns can now be used on entities mapped with table-per-type or table-per-concrete-type inheritance. Other improvements include migrations tooling and additional provider-specific JSON capabilities. 
 For SQL Server applications, EF Core adds support for vector indexes and approximate vector search. The SQL Server features and corresponding EF APIs are experimental. See the vector search documentation and limitations before evaluating them. 
 EF Core 11 requires .NET 11. When upgrading, check your database provider’s compatibility and the EF Core 11 breaking changes as well as the runtime changes. 
 Developer tools 
 The new dotnetup toolchain manager lets you install and update .NET SDKs and runtimes in your user account. It’s currently in public preview and helps you manage side-by-side versions and keep up with servicing updates. 
 .NET Skills gives coding agents task-specific guidance from the .NET team. Our .NET Skills introduction explains how to add these skills to your coding agent. 
 The experimental .NET MAUI DevFlow toolkit exposes a running app’s visual tree, screenshots, and interaction tools, so an agent can inspect and test the UI rather than work only from source code. 
 For modernization, the .NET Upgrade canvas gives you a visual view of a GitHub Copilot upgrade session. Review assessment findings and dependency compatibility, follow implementation tasks, and monitor failures and progress as the upgrade agent works. Our modernization walkthrough in the GitHub Copilot app covers the workflow from assessment through execution. 
 Workloads 
 Web: ASP.NET Core and Blazor 
 Application types are most useful when the rest of the stack understands them. ASP.NET Core supports C# unions wherever it uses System.Text.Json , including JSON request and response bodies in Minimal APIs and MVC. Generated OpenAPI documents describe the union’s alternatives with an anyOf schema. 
 This support applies to JSON bodies, not to route, query, header, or form binding. When multiple union cases have the same JSON shape, configure a classifier so deserialization can distinguish them. The ASP.NET Core union documentation explains those boundaries. 
 Validation also becomes more practical for rules that need to do I/O. Asynchronous validation works with the new asynchronous DataAnnotations APIs, so a validator can await a database lookup or a remote call instead of blocking a thread. Minimal APIs and Blazor forms can use this support. 
 OpenAPI 3.2 is now the default for generated documents. Among other improvements, it lets the document describe the per-event payload of a server-sent event stream. If a client generator or another part of your toolchain doesn’t yet support 3.2, you can explicitly select an earlier document version. 
 For long-lived connections, SignalR authentication refresh lets a connection refresh authentication without reconnecting. Blazor Interactive Server components can receive the updated identity and react when claims change. 
 Blazor adds capabilities for both statically rendered pages and interactive applications. 
 The new CacheView component caches the rendered output of a component subtree during static server-side rendering. On a cache hit, Blazor replays the markup without creating those child components or running their lifecycle methods. That gives you a smaller unit of caching for expensive, mostly static sections of a page. 
 Interactive Server apps can opt into automatic circuit pause when a browser tab becomes inactive . After a configurable delay, pausing frees the server memory and SignalR connection held by an inactive user. The feature requires an additional package and explicit configuration; upgrading doesn’t silently change your application’s circuit behavior. 
 Forms gain client-side validation for static server rendering and asynchronous validation support. QuickGrid and Virtualize add ways to move to a particular item, useful when returning a user to their place in a large collection. 
 Blazor also adds components for agentic user interfaces. The new Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.AI package includes components for streaming chat, tool rendering, approval flows, and shared UI state. Basic chat works with any IChatClient . For advanced experiences with a remote agent, the AG-UI .NET integration carries streamed responses, tool events, approval requests, and shared-state updates between an ASP.NET Core agent endpoint and the Blazor UI. 
 The Blazor AI components package is experimental and remains prerelease throughout .NET 11. It’s an opportunity to try the direction and give feedback, not a stable part of the ASP.NET Core shared framework. See the Blazor AI components documentation . 
 The AG-UI .NET SDK introduction covers the protocol’s client and server APIs. Build Agentic UI with the new Blazor AI components puts them together in a working app. 
 See what’s new in ASP.NET Core for the Blazor features, configuration examples, and compatibility details. 
 Client: .NET MAUI 
 .NET MAUI in .NET 11 makes CoreCLR the default runtime across its platforms. The move to CoreCLR brings mobile and desktop apps onto the same runtime foundation as other .NET workloads. On Apple platforms that don’t allow JIT compilation, the runtime uses precompiled code and the interpreter rather than generating native code at runtime. 
 Native AOT is an opt-in publishing alternative; its Android support remains experimental. Review the platform-specific runtime guidance and test your app’s libraries when choosing a deployment model. 
 The UI development loop gets attention, too: 
 
 XAML Incremental Hot Reload is a preview feature in .NET 11. It updates live instances of pages and controls, including supported structural edits, without requiring you to navigate away and back. It’s enabled by default in Debug builds. 
 Implicit XAML namespace declarations remove the need to repeat the standard namespace declarations at the root of every file. 
 Windows uses the new CollectionView2 handler by default, while Android Shell adopts a handler-based architecture. 
 New mobile test templates and dotnet test device selection bring testing into the CLI workflow. 
 
 These are meaningful runtime and handler changes, so exercise navigation, custom handlers, and trimmed publishing as part of your upgrade. The optional Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships; apps that still reference it need to migrate off it. 
 .NET MAUI follows its own support policy , separate from the .NET runtime’s STS and LTS lifecycle. 
 Windows: WinUI, Windows Forms, and WPF 
 For new Windows desktop apps, WinUI 3 is the recommended native UI framework, pairing C# and XAML with modern controls and the Fluent Design System. It’s delivered through the Windows App SDK , which also makes modern Windows APIs available to existing WPF and Windows Forms apps. 
 To add UI tests, see UWP and WinUI 3 apps: UI testing with MSTest . 
 Windows Forms in .NET 11 adds an opt-in modern visual styles mode that you can select at the application or control level. It also adds ways to react to system visual and accessibility settings, defer revealing a form until it’s ready, and suspend painting during bulk updates. 
 These controls let you introduce refreshed rendering where it makes sense for your application instead of treating a framework upgrade as an automatic visual redesign. 
 WPF updates focus on reliability, including fixes for Fluent window backdrops, window manager failures, and weak-event cleanup. Self-contained Windows publishing also includes a native dependency needed by apps that load mixed-mode WPF assemblies. 
 Get started and plan your upgrade 
 Install the .NET 11 SDK . Use a compatible, up-to-date Visual Studio 2026 installation, or Visual Studio Code with C# Dev Kit . 
 To create and run a console app: 
 dotnet new console -n HelloDotnet11 -f net11.0
dotnet run --project HelloDotnet11 
 You can replace the generated program with either of the C# examples above to try the new language features. 
 For an existing application, plan the upgrade across your development and deployment environments: 
 
 Update the SDK selection in global.json if your repository pins it, and install the matching SDK on development machines and build agents. 
 Update target frameworks to .NET 11, preserving platform-specific target framework suffixes where applicable. Update packages and workloads to compatible versions. 
 Review the .NET 11 breaking changes , including the updated minimum CPU requirements . Installing a new SDK alone doesn’t retarget your app. 
 Run your tests and measure the application under a representative workload. Validate your actual publishing mode, container base images, native dependencies, and deployment hosts. 
 
 Upgrading from .NET 8 or .NET 9 
.NET 8 and .NET 9 reach end of support on November 10, 2026. Move to a supported release to continue receiving fixes. Choose .NET 11 for the latest capabilities, or .NET 10 if its LTS lifecycle fits your requirements better. See the .NET support policy for dates and servicing requirements.
 
 If you’re upgrading from a .NET 11 release candidate, update to the final SDK, runtime, and compatible package and workload versions rather than staying on a prerelease build.

 In my experience, C# and .NET are both "underappreciated" in a large part based on the legacy. Some folks out there still think .NET is Windows only. Some folks out there haven't looked at C# since the .NET Framework days. Some folks out there are still salty about some of Microsoft's decision around OSS (debugger, hot reload fiasco, etc.) But day to day working with C# and .NET for backends? It's really fantastic. AI seems to like it a lot and a lot of tools for agents to go HAM. Roslyn analyzer, source generators, workable hot reload (for a compiled language), tons of really good docs from Microsoft, generally low variance and high consistency from codebase to codebase (e.g. encountering Drizzle vs Prisma vs TypeORM vs Kysely vs ... in Node land). My previous team switched from TS to C# and F#[0][1] and it was a blessing; a lot of the platform ops have been simplified. It's just one very solid tool chain and packages are generally stable (a lot less effort on maintaining platform config/tooling and more focus on just building). First party packages get consistent security updates and C# doesn't have nearly the same level of exposure to transitive packages that one encounters with JS/TS ecosystem. C# feels like a really solid choice in the age of AI coding because of it's general stability, strong static analyzer, insistence on types, and really good tooling. Not right for all use cases (e.g. CLI, serverless functions), but fantastic for backend APIs. If you're looking to do AI with/on C#, I wrote about some of my experience with making codebases successful for AI[2]. [0] https://engineering.usemotion.com/moving-off-of-typescript-e...  I have more detail written up here: https://chrlschn.dev/blog/2026/08/the-unexpected-ai-stack-cs... But the gist of it is that I wire it up through Aspire (don't need to, but makes it nice) to set the environment variable on my main app host. Then the agent can run `csharprepl` commands directly via CLI and read/mutate the running application state directly via the service provider (DI container) I have a small set of utility functions to access the DI container with common patterns like creating a scope for scoped services: https://github.com/zeeq-ai/zeeq-app/blob/main/src/backend/Ze... (optional, but useful) And a skill: https://github.com/zeeq-ai/zeeq-app/blob/main/.agents/skills... (also optional, but cuts down on agents relearning the #wrap and #replace behavior) I recommend you "train" the skill like I do in my the blog post. Basically ask the agent to get an instance of an object from DI like a repository class or your DbContext and have it perform some operations. Have it wrap a function and add logging. Have it replace a function. Then once it learns how to do this, have it write the skill bespoke to your project. I strongly recommend that you try it "by hand" one time via blog of CSharpRepl author: https://fuqua.io/blog/2026/06/injecting-a-csharp-repl-into-a... If you try it manually one time, it clicks what the agent is doing and why it is so powerful (because the agent accesses and modifies the running application state without a compile). reply smoe 8 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–]

 It’s also awesome for SREs / SysOps / Whatever We Call Ourselves Today: Opinionated in a good way, which means almost all C# apps have the same parameterisation with environment variables, command line, and config files.  One of my favorite things about F# is what some would consider a deficiency: that within a project, files must be ordered and you may only refer to a symbol defined earlier, with the sole exception of types which are explicitly declared together in a single statement (`type X = ... and Y = ...`). This in contrast to C# where, within one .csproj, there is no "order" and all classes and methods are able to mutually reference one another.  > go is much more efficient in syntax and memory I'm going to talk about the second part first. .NET is often deployed with a JIT compiler runtime like Java. That means that hello-world scripts use a lot more memory than Go, but that difference becomes a lot smaller on real-world programs and .NET can use less memory than Go depending on what you're doing. C#'s concurrency can also be more efficient than Go's since it's coroutine based async/await is a lightweight state machine rather than green threads. That's not to say Go is especially heavy or anything, but it is more overhead. In terms of "efficient in syntax", Go has a lot fewer features. That's one of Go's biggest strengths and weaknesses. Here's an example. With Go, you just have struct tags: strings of anything that can be attached to a field in a struct. Let's say you have a User struct and you want to make it so the JSON won't have the user's email in it. You do: Email string `json:"-"`. But what if you mess up and write "jsom" or `json:-` without the quotes? It's basically a meaningless string to the compiler. With C#/.NET, you have annotatons/attributes that are a part of the language and checked as types. You'd do: [JsonIgnore] public string Email. JsonIgnore is an attribute class so your IDE can help you. There's a lot in Go where the answer kinda becomes "f-it, we'll just use strings instead of having something meaningful." Go talks about how important error handling is, but then you get an error from a function and it's basically just a string. If you're doing good error handling, you want to handle different errors differently, but that's not easy in Go. Frankly, it's not easy in most languages, but this is definitely an area where it felt like Go gave up on creating something good in order to get something out the door quickly enough that Google didn't cancel the project. In a language like Zig, errors are enums and you get exhaustiveness checking. With Go, someone could add another error state to something you're using and you'd never know - or they could change the phrasing of an existing error and you'd silently stop matching on it. Go's lambda syntax is clunky. func(x MyType) string { x.ToString(); } vs (x) => x.ToString() There's lots of stuff like that. I'm not arguing that Go is bad, but it has a ton less stuff and that's both a blessing and a curse. reply pjc50 13 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–]

Val Town is winding down | Val Town Blog val.town blog.val.town Elsewhere Elsewhere RSS Email Twitter Bluesky Discord YouTube GitHub LinkedIn OSS Pledge Code and prose written on val.town Val Town is winding down Steve Krouse Nov 10, 2026 Dear Val Town community, 
 We’ve made the difficult decision to wind down Val Town. 
 You took a big leap of faith to build on us. We thank you for your trust, and we’re sorry we can’t continue to serve you. 
 The bad news about our business – that we couldn’t compete in the cloud computing space – is good news for you migrating off: there are many wonderful hosting providers you can migrate to, and today’s LLMs are great at these types of migrations. We have guides for migrating to Cloudflare, Vercel, Netlify, and Render. Please reach out if you need help at support@val.town or on Discord. 
 We are pausing billing today, and will continue servicing existing subscriptions for free. If you pre-paid for our annual plan, we will issue you a partial refund. 
 Here’s the timeline on our wind-down: 

























 Service End of life date New signups and plan upgrades Nov 10, 2026 (today) Read-only mode (not including sqlite and blob storage) Dec 10, 2026 All other services Jan 10, 2027 Open-sourcing Val Town Feb 1, 2027 
 Thank you, the members of the Val Town team, for giving it your all over the past four years. Thank you Tom, Jackson, Charlie, Pete, Potluck, Charmaine, Max, Andre, Sophie, Wolf, Justin, Rodrigo and JP. It was an honor. 
 Thank you, Dan Levine, for being the best investor I could’ve asked for. Thank you, my other investors, for your trust, support, and capital. 
 Thank you, our customers and users, for building on us with passion and creativity. 
 Steve Krouse Edit on val.town Share on Twitter Share on Bluesky Share on Hacker News © 2022- 2026 Val Town

 I remember Steve from my days working on Eve, he was part of that community and always a big proponent of end-user programming. I was happy to see him working on this project but am not surprised it's shutting down. Nothing to to do with the quality of Val Town, but making a business in this space is really, really hard. You can't start the business without raising millions (Eve raised $2M, Darklang raised $3.5M, Val Town raised $7M), but it's hard to scale out a proof of concept in the time investors want to start seeing an ROI. It seems to me about 2-3 years is all you get for seed runway, when realistically projects like this should take at minimum 5 years incubating. Darklang extended their runway to ~7-8 years by firing all the devs and keeping just the founder on life support. Ultimately even that wasn't enough. But maybe with AI this could work, I dunno. What's required to make it all work is a fundamental leap in programming interface design, but the business side doesn't look any different from a typical SaaS. So unless you hit the ball out of the park you're entering the market with an experimental product, then you have to deal with product-market fit even if you have the right product, so you really only have one shot. It's very hard to go back to investors and ask for another round of funding when there's no discernable market and the product isn't gaining the traction investors would like to see. Anyway, kudos to Steve for fighting the good fight! What would really be great is to read an in-depth post mortem on the project.
