 > There was a brief period of affordable threadripper, but then product segmentation made that not great for amd... The thing they're doing which is completely insane is using different sockets for Threadripper and Epyc. The primary difference between them isn't the price -- they're both expensive -- it's that Epyc uses the power budget to reach higher core counts and Threadripper uses it to hit higher clock speeds. So for example, Zen5 Threadripper 9975WX has 32 cores with a 4 GHz base clock and 5.4 GHz boost clock. There is no equivalent Zen5 Epyc, the most similar is 9375F which is 3.8GHz/4.8GHz. Conversely, Epyc 9755 has 128 Zen5 cores and Epyc 9965 has 192 Zen5c cores and there is no Threadripper with that many cores. The reason this matters is that the system boards themselves are pricey, not just the CPUs, but as the platform starts to age you start to get a lot of old servers on the used market that originally had a bottom-end Epyc in them. Which you'd then like to pull and replace with a Threadripper -- i.e. pay them more money to buy a new Threadripper -- except that they inexplicably decided to screw you and themselves by using a different socket. And the same thing the other way around. It also means you can't find an older workstation with the bottom-end Threadripper and pay them money for a high core count Epyc with better performance per watt to use it as a server.  What’s new in Ableton Live 13?
 

 
 
 
 Ableton Live 13 adds new audio and MIDI workflows, sound design tools and mixing effects. Highlights include: 
 
 
 A built-in Step Sequencer, ARA 2 support for compatible audio-editing plug-ins, Capture Automation, and Contextual Browsing for adding devices and swapping presets directly from the device chain. 
 
 
 Drum Synth, new Multiband and Mid-Side Racks, expanded Rack controls, and Envelope Clips for automating and modulating effects on return tracks. 
 
 
 Device Slots in the mixer, and new Core Library Drum Racks, instrument presets, Audio Effect Racks, samples, and MIDI clips. 
 
 
 Arrangement Sync for Ableton Link, support for exporting tempo automation and time signature changes, and more precise event timing in exported MIDI files. 
 
 
 Mixer improvements including Send sliders, a persistent Mixer Configuration menu for choosing which sections are visible, smoother mixer resizing, and an Unsolo button on the Main track, plus an updated Phaser-Flanger interface. 
 
 
 Live 13 Suite also includes Melodyne essential, Looplet, Clipper, Transient Shaper and the Classic Dynamics & EQ Pack by Softube. 
 See the full Release Notes for every change. 
 
 
 


 
 What’s new for Push?
 

 
 
 
 Push 3 gains Custom Layouts, a new Step Sequencer layout, a new Performance Mixer, and Device Mode upgrades. Custom Layouts combine Session View, note areas, XYZ and mixer controls on a single page. The Step Sequencer brings the step editing experience from Live to the hardware. Device Mode adds jog wheel navigation and up to 32 Rack Macros. 
 Push 2 supports the new Step Sequencer and most Device Mode improvements (except jog wheel navigation), but not Custom Layouts, Performance Mixer or Expressive Step Editing. 
 See the full Release Notes for every change. 
 
 
 


 
 What’s the difference between Ableton Live 12 and Live 13?
 

 
 
 
 Live 13 is the next major version of Ableton Live, following Live 12. It adds audio and MIDI workflows including ARA 2 support, Step Sequencer and Capture Automation, plus instruments and effects, expanded Rack controls, updated Core Library content, and more. Everything you can do in Live 12 you can still do in Live 13. 
 
 
 


 
 What’s the difference between Live 13 Intro, Standard and Suite? 
 

 
 
 
 Ableton Live 13 comes in three editions: Intro, Standard and Suite. 
 They share the same core workflow but differ in their features and included instruments, effects and sounds. Live Intro is limited to 16 tracks and Scenes. Standard allows unlimited tracks and Scenes, and adds many more built-in instruments, effects and sounds. 
 Suite includes everything in Standard plus Max for Live, the complete instrument and effect collection, and Live’s full Core Library. 
 Suite also comes with Melodyne essential for ARA 2 editing, plus the Classic Dynamics & EQ Pack by Softube and Looplet as free downloads at release. Compare editions in detail . 
 
 
 


 
 When is Ableton Live 13 released?
 

 
 
 
 Ableton Live 13 will be released in early 2027. Subscribe to our Newsletter to be notified at release 
 
 
 


 
 Can I pre-order Live 13?
 

 
 
 
 Yes, in two ways: 
 
 
 If you already own Live 12 – pre-order Live 13 at 20% off. 
 
 
 If you don’t own Live 12 yet – buy or upgrade to Live 12 at 20% off during the announcement offer and get the corresponding Live 13 edition free when it’s released. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 How do I upgrade to Live 13?
 

 
 
 
 Log in to your User Account and visit the Ableton shop to see the upgrade options for your license. From now until the release of Live 13, you can buy or upgrade to Live 12 and get the corresponding Live 13 edition for free on release day. 
 
 
 


 
 What happens to my Live 12 Rent-to-own license when I upgrade?
 

 
 
 
 You can extend your existing plan to cover the cost of upgrading to Live 13 Suite and start using it as soon as it’s released. Visit the Ableton shop to see your upgrade options. 
 
 
 


 
 How do I get access to the Live 13 beta?
 

 
 
 
 Limited places for the Live 13 public beta are available to Live Standard and Suite owners. Learn more about the Ableton Live beta program . 
 
 
 


 
 Which ARA plug-ins work with Live 13?
 

 
 
 
 Most ARA 2 plug-ins work with Live 13, including Melodyne. Live 13 Suite comes with Melodyne essential. A small number have known compatibility issues. See the full Release Notes for more information. 
 One ARA plug-in can be used at a time, across multiple clips and tracks.

 People here might be interested to know that you can run Scheme (lisp) code directly in Ableton through my Scheme for Max project in Max for Live. S4M is an open source extension to Max that allows you to run the s7 Scheme interpreter in a Max object, similar to the JS object in Max. Advantages over JS are that in can run in the high priority scheduler thread, enabling accurate timing, it has direct access to the file system from Scheme code, and allows you to make Scheme s-expressions directly in Max messages. It is also a very nice way to control the Live API, as the live API works on lists of symbols. https://github.com/iainctduncan/scheme-for-max

 Modulators [0], for example, they are available as a side-panel on any device which you can click the rectangle with a "+" button and select any type of modulator: LFOs (many different kinds), curves, envelopes, segments, etc. Instead of creating a LFO as part of the chain of devices it's clearly a thing embedded to the device itself, including on VSTs (so any VST can have more complex modulation than they offer natively). You can multi-target the modulator to affect any parameter on any of the devices across the whole track, so a LFO modulating something on the 1st device in the chain can also apply the same modulation to a parameter on the 9th device so they can be "coupled" to that movement, this mapping is also attenuated per application so even though the movement is the same it can have different magnitudes when assigned. It completely removes the need of LFO Tool for complex curves/ramps, etc., or the LFO as a device with the "map" button to assign to parameters, if I want 10 LFOs I can just have them all together as a side-pane of a device or the track itself. It makes much more sense that a modulator is attached to something instead of being its own thing on a long list of devices. Another improvement: macros can live on a control panel for a device, whole track, or even the whole project, so you can create a macro knob at the project-level and map it to affect any parameter of any track, and just map the project-level macro knob to a MIDI controller to modulate whatever parameter in the whole project. These are just a couple of intuitive features from the top of my head I use in almost every single project. [0] https://www.bitwig.com/userguide/latest/the_unified_modulati... Quick edit: another feature I remembered after writing this comment that I find more intuitive is the creation of control pages for a device, it's accessible right below the "modulators" button and opens a side-pane to create up to 8 control knobs mapped directly to a device's/VST's parameter or even mapped to a "macro" modulator which itself can be mapped to many parameters of a device/VST, it's really intuitive to create pages of these controls and only use the controls themselves to change parameters, I barely open the VST window after experimenting a bit with which parameters I want to play with and mapping those to controls. reply semtud 15 hours ago | prev | next [–]

 It solves for the same thing a "train of thought" (internal vocalization) solves for in the human brain: there's a lot of stuff you "know" as episodic memories of words you've heard/read, but haven't yet internalized via practice into reflex reactions. It's a lot faster and cheaper to acquire a memory of some words, than it is to acquire an entire new skill, so you end up picking up far more memories-of-words than concrete skills from a given training corpus. Reasoning (i.e. bubbling those remembered words up into your mental context, and then using a special "trigger effectively arbitrary synaptic activations dependent on the content of the attention-masked context and an ongoing state" bridging reflex on them, a.k.a. "system-2 thinking") is how you leverage memories-of-words into useful behavior. Rather than executing native skills embedded into your synaptic weights, you're running a single very fancy native skill that acts as an interpreter for word-memory data, slowly and strenuously turning words you're holding in mind into more words (synthesis), or into associations to other memories (word-memories or otherwise), or into actions/outputs, etc. (An especially useful "trick" of this system is planning , i.e. chaining the interpreter through "mere words" that conjure more "mere words" to mind until you end up at words that form a declaration of what you're about to do. # Artifact: Large-Scale Measurement and Real-World Mitigation of Web Browser Fingerprinting in the Wild

Supporting artifact for the CCS '26 paper
([10.1145/3830454.3846585](https://doi.org/10.1145/3830454.3846585)).

The paper measures browser fingerprintability across ~25 million Firefox
Release clients over a 23-day window, models three commercial
fingerprinting services against that population, and evaluates the
anti-fingerprinting protections shipped in Firefox 143.

## Contents

### `rfp_fingerprinters_tracking/`

Reverse engineering of the three modeled fingerprinting services:
obfuscated and deobfuscated scripts, captured payloads, Firefox Profiler
traces, per-vendor Web API inventories, and some analyses of each vendor's
collected signals against Firefox's protections.

- `akamai/` — Akamai Bot Manager
- `fingerprintpro/` — FingerprintJS Pro v3.12.6 (~164 signals)
- `signifyd/` — Signifyd: `lite.js` (a CreepJS fork, ~385 fields) and
  `check.js` (a bundled ThreatMetrix profiler)
- `profiler_scripts/` — extracts and categorizes Web API calls from
  Profiler traces

See `rfp_fingerprinters_tracking/README.md` for the per-vendor directory
layout.

Some script-source URLs in this copy are generalized to
"researcher-controlled test host", and exploratory working notes are
trimmed relative to the internal repository. The scripts, payloads, traces
and analyses themselves are unmodified.

### `rfp_paper_code/`

The Python analysis toolkit: reads Firefox telemetry, computes per-vendor
fingerprints, measures uniqueness and cohort structure (Simpson Index),
and simulates the effect of each candidate protection.

See `rfp_paper_code/README.md` for setup and a walkthrough.

## Data availability

The raw telemetry behind the paper's numbers is **not public**: it is
per-client Firefox measurement data that cannot be released.

### Aggregate data

The aggregate data derived from that telemetry *is* public, at
<https://storage.googleapis.com/fingerprinting-aggregate-data/> — roughly
6.2 GiB across 5,037 objects, served as a public GCS bucket (browse it via
the XML listing, or fetch individual keys directly). It comes in two forms.

**Whole-population fingerprint archives** at the bucket root, one per
protection state:

- `fingerprint_archive_anonymized_shuffled_Baseline.csv.zst`
- `fingerprint_archive_anonymized_shuffled_Phase_0.csv.zst`
- `fingerprint_archive_anonymized_shuffled_Phase_3.csv.zst`

Each is a zstd-compressed CSV of about 1.5–1.6 GB (4.6 GiB in total) with
one row per client: operating system, locale, and the fingerprint hash that
each of the three modeled services would have computed for that client
under that protection state, e.g. `os, intl_intl_locale,
Phase 3-FPJSv2_Realistic, Phase 3-AkamaiV2_Realistic,
Phase 3-Signifyd_Realistic`. 

**Per-metric value distributions**, under `Windows/`, `Mac/`, `Linux/` and
`Android/`, as sharded gzipped CSV (BigQuery export shards):

- `UserCharacteristics_<OS>_x_tbl/` — marginal distributions, one row per
  metric value: `metric1, value1, occurrences, total_occurrences,
  percentage`
- `UserCharacteristics_<OS>_x_by_y_tbl/` — pairwise joint distributions
  (the bulk of the shards, ~1.6 GiB): `metric1, value1, metric2, value2,
  occurrences, total_occurrences_for_value1, percentage`. These are the
  input to the correlation and conditional-entropy analyses.

Values too rare to release are collapsed to the literal string
`ANONYMIZED`, so counts remain correct while the underlying value is
withheld.

### Canvas Data Explorer

<https://storage.googleapis.com/canvas-comparison/index.html> is an
interactive companion page for the canvas results. It covers the 26 canvas
recipes Firefox measures (at 250×250, 240×128 and 128×128), drawn from
telemetry between 2026-03-12 and 2026-06-06 across Windows, macOS, Linux
and Android — some 684 million canvas submissions in aggregate.

For each recipe it reports submissions, distinct hashes, and how much of
the population the most common hashes cover, and it decodes the stored
pixel data so you can see the rendered images behind those hashes rather
than just their digests. Because 13 of the recipes were also captured with
software rendering forced on, the *Hardware*, *Software* and *HW vs SW*
views let you compare the two side by side — this is the entropy reduction
behind the Software Canvas protection evaluated in the paper. A *Yours*
control re-runs the same recipes in your own browser, so you can locate
your own output within the measured distribution.

### Test Data

In this repository is data that allows you to reproduce similar analyses
performed in the paper:

- `simulated-cache/` — a ~900-user sample dataset with the same schema and
  metrics as production, so the full pipeline can be run end to end. It was
  built from telemetry submissions by 6 volunteer Firefox Nightly users
  (Windows, macOS, Linux, Android); each submission was duplicated 100
  times with unique client identifiers and independently perturbed
  (WebGL strings, CSS system colors and fonts, `Accept-Language`, storage
  quota, CPU core count, canvas). The procedure is implemented in
  `generate_simulated_data.py` and can be re-run from
  `simulated-cache/source-pings/`.
- `real-output-data/` — the aggregate outputs computed from the real
  dataset, which is what the paper's figures and tables are drawn from.

Numbers produced from the sample dataset will not match the paper; it
exists to validate the methodology, not to reproduce the results.

page:https://fingerprinting.study/.text:
Large-Scale Measurement and Real-World Mitigation of Web Browser
Fingerprinting in the Wild 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Fingerprinting in the Wild 
 
 Overview 
 Paper 
 Full data 
 Download the data 
 Follow-ups 
 Test your browser 
 
 
 

 

 
 Large-Scale Measurement and Real-World Mitigation of Web Browser
 Fingerprinting in the Wild
 

 
 Tom Ritter 1 , Fatih Kilic 2 , Frederik
 Braun 1 , Elisa Luo 3 , Geoffrey M.
 Voelker 3 , Stefan Savage 3 , Christoph
 Kerschbaumer 1 
 
 
 1 Mozilla Corporation · 2 University
 of Toronto · 3 UC San Diego
 

 
 This is the companion site to a study Mozilla ran on browser
 fingerprinting. With the help of almost 25 million Firefox release
 users, we measured how identifiable browsers really are, found which
 characteristics make them unique, and used that to design the
 fingerprinting protections that shipped in Firefox 143. Here you can
 read the paper and its key findings, browse the full appendix data
 the PDF had no room for, download the privacy-preserving aggregate
 data and analysis code, learn how the data was collected, and run an
 interactive test that compares your own browser against the measured
 population. If you have a question the data could answer, there is
 also a discussion board for proposing follow-up research.
 

 
 Browser fingerprinting is a known tracking mechanism on the modern
 web, but its real-world effectiveness toward users has been hard
 to measure. To build robust protections, we measured uniqueness
 across a large, unbiased population, to determined what individual
 metrics cause users to be unique.
 These measurements used multiple privacy preserving technologies,
 like OHTTP , to ensure that
 no individual users can be identified or tracked across the web.
 The protections we built into Firefox avoid web compatibility
 problems while dropping the percentage of uniquely identifiable
 users from 75% to 46%.
 

 
 Test your own browser
 → 
 Read the paper 
 Full appendix data 
 Download the data 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Shows the percentage of users seen as unique by three commercial
 fingerprinters. Each step adds one protection on top of all the ones
 before it, weighted across the four operating systems.
 
 

 Paper abstract 
 
 
 Web browser fingerprinting has become a key tracking mechanism on
 the modern web, yet its real-world effectiveness and which of the
 existing mitigations offer value at scale remain insufficiently
 understood.
 
 
 In this paper, we present a large-scale study of browser
 fingerprinting based on real-world telemetry from almost 25 million
 Firefox release users. This dataset enables us to quantify user
 uniqueness at population scale and identify which characteristics
 contribute most to this uniqueness.
 
 
 Our analysis shows fingerprintability is largely driven by a small
 set of high-impact characteristics and their combinations, rather
 than the accumulation of many independent measurements. Building on
 these insights, we propose and evaluate fingerprinting protections
 based on their impact on uniqueness and cohort structure, and design
 data-driven mitigations.
 
 
 These protections, shipped in Firefox 143, reduce the fraction of
 uniquely identifiable users from 75% to 46% while maintaining web
 compatibility, demonstrating that practical reductions in
 fingerprintability are achievable in a mainstream browser.
 
 

 Our key findings 
 
 
 Here's what we want to present to you with this paper and the
 broader scope of our work.
 

 
 
 Uniqueness is caused by a small number of metrics - not one or
 thirty
 
 
 
 Fingerprinting test sites have a seemingly endless list of
 measurements they can pull from your browser. If a user has a
 unique fingerprint, it is typically not because of a single
 measurement, but it is also not because of 20 or 30
 measurements. It is a small number of metrics that make
 users unique .
 

 
 In fact, it's very close to the
 80/20
 rule . Specifically, of all the users seen as unique by
 Fingerprint Pro (the most discerning fingerprinter we model) -
 80% of them are unique after only 8 metrics - while the
 fingerprinter collects a total of over 50 metrics. Signifyd
 collects more metrics, but identifies fewer users as unique:
 80% of the users it sees as unique will be identified after 9
 metrics despite collecting over 80.
 
 

 The numbers only mean anything per operating system 
 
 
 Whenever someone cites a single percentage when describing "How
 many users are unique" - you should be suspicious. Because
 this collapses multiple different populations that
 behave very differently .
 

 
 Firstly, as a baseline, your operating system is always going
 to be exposed to a fingerprinter. We are always working within
 the constraint of web compatibility, and lying about the
 user's operating system breaks shortcut keys and gives
 you the wrong downloads among other problems. So if
 we know the website is going to learn your real OS
 anyway, we can use it to segment the population and analyze it
 separately.
 

 
 And when you do you see that each operating system behaves
 differently because they have different important metrics.
 Admittedly, it's very difficult to give a concise summary of
 work and also provide four sets of numbers - so even we fall
 prey to the trap of providing a single number, as we did in
 the prior paragraph. But every time we have a single
 percentage, somewhere we have that number broken down by
 operating system, and in doing so, you will see that each
 behaves differently.
 
 

 Entropy is not the measurement you want 
 
 
 It's so, so easy to take all the results for a metric and just
 calculate Shannon entropy - it's a standard yardstick in this
 literature. But as we show - a high Shannon entropy does not
 reliably predict fingerprinting impact .
 
 

 Cohort size, not just uniqueness 
 
 
 Previous analyses calculated how many people were unique, but
 they did not analyze the other people - the ones who
 weren't. All those other people might be 1 million users who
 share one fingerprint or 500,000 distinct fingerprints shared by
 2 people each - that's quite the difference. 
 
 
 We use the
 Simpson
 Index (aka the
 Herfindahl–Hirschman
 Index ) to quantify that difference and compare different
 sets of cohorts (shared fingerprints). This lets us compare
 how effective different fingerprinting defenses are based not
 just on how much uniqueness they eliminate but how much they
 collapse groups of users into each other.
 
 
 For example, two different protections can each lower the share
 of unique users by about 2.1 percentage points. But one improves
 the cohort score by 56%, while another raises it by only 13%. 
 Judged on uniqueness alone, two defenses can look equally
 effective; while the cohort improvement varies significantly. 
 
 

 The same protection performs very differently per platform 
 
 
 Protections are not uniformly impactful, and the variation is
 not small. As an example, clamping the available screen
 resolution takes 25.3 percentage points off cumulative macOS
 uniqueness but between 0 and 3 points off the other three
 platforms. Averaged across all users, that 25-point drop 
 shrinks to 3.5 - a protection that matters enormously to one
 platform can look marginal in the aggregate .
 

 
 This is yet another reason why it's so important to segment and
 analyze data on a per-operating-system basis.
 
 

 Standardization and randomization go hand-in-hand 
 
 
 Making users report the same values makes them look more alike,
 but it never makes everyone look the same. Some users will still
 stand out, and that gets worse on websites with small visitor
 populations. Standardization improves the situation, but it
 should still be paired with randomization. Randomization is very
 strong when it works, but can always be detected and bypassed.
 Neither can carry the burden of providing privacy on its
 own. 
 
 

 The data shows why values differ, not just that they do 
 
 
 Correlating fingerprinting values with users' hardware and other
 characteristics let us identify why certain measurements differed
 between users. Knowing the root cause lets us build
 protections that reach much further, and protect small groups of
 users who would otherwise stand out as a minority. 
 
 
 Addressing these differences has already produced more consistent
 outputs for
 image
 rendering ,
 Web
 Audio , and
 mathematical
 operations on Android, with more root causes being investigated.
 
 

 Users don't connect website breakage to the setting 
 
 
 Breakage from a strict mode is delayed, and the delay hides the cause. 
 Turning on a stricter mode is a one-time act - but the broken website
 arrives later and nothing connects the two. From the user's
 perspective, this website doesn't work in Firefox and they have
 no idea why and are frustrated. Report after report we see
 people posting for help, confused - despite having taken
 specific action to enable a hidden setting opting them into
 strict fingerprinting protections.
 
 

 Protections that ship have to keep the web working 
 
 
 Users don't realize that a setting they changed caused the breakage,
 and don't know how to fix it - so a protection that breaks the web
 breaks the browser along with it.
 We selected and tuned mitigations on both measured impact
 and compatibility. For a default, compatibility
 isn't a trade-off against privacy - it's a precondition for it. 
 
 

 The hard part is finding what breaks 
 
 
 The web is vast, and even the most innocuous change is likely to break
 something somewhere. Some breakage can be anticipated, which helps
 design, testing, and detection. The other breakage gets fixed only if a
 chain of luck holds: someone has to recognize the breakage, report it,
 reproduce it on the right hardware, and get it to the right
 person. 
 
 

 We are deliberately not publishing everything we could 
 
 
 Commercial fingerprinters evolve continuously, and they borrow
 openly from the community that studies them. Sites built to
 teach people about fingerprinting - CreepJS among them - get
 picked up and used outright by fingerprinting products.
 
 
 So we have been deliberately conservative. There are analyses
 this dataset would support that we have not run, data we could
 have released that we have not, and offensive angles on this
 work that we have not pursued. That is a choice rather than an
 oversight: we would rather leave a question open than make it
 easier to build a better fingerprinter .
 
 
 
 

 Test your own browser 
 
 
 This interactive test re-implements individual measurements as close
 as possible to how Firefox's own collection code performed them,
 runs in your browser, and compares each result against the published
 aggregate data. For every characteristic you can see your value and how many
 of the ~25 million measured browsers share it - overall and within
 your operating system.
 
 
 Run the browser test
 → 
 
 
 
 The test runs entirely in your browser. All comparisons happen
 locally, against our static reference files.
 No data is stored or submitted to us.
 
 
 
 If the test, or anything else on this site, looks wrong, please
 report it as an issue on GitHub .
 For a problem with the test, include the diagnostics from its
 Copy diagnostics button, or, if you would rather
 not post your measured values publicly, email them to
 tom@ritter.vg .
 
 

 Paper 
 
 
 
 The extended version of the paper is available as a PDF.
 
 
 Read the extended version
 (PDF) → 
 
 

 Full appendix data 
 
 
 The paper's appendices contain a wealth of data locked behind a
 reasonable page limit and PDF formatting. This full data page
 carries all of it - every rank for every operating system and
 all three modeled services, the complete protection chains,
 and the paper's figures regenerated at print resolution.
 
 
 Open the full data
 → 
 
 

 Data collection 
 
 
 Our measurements come from Firefox telemetry, specifically the 
 user-characteristics ping, a dedicated telemetry ping.
 Unlike normal telemetry pings that are sent regularly, this ping
 must be explicitly enabled (which has happened twice, once in 2025
 and once in 2026), and sends one data report before becoming dormant
 again.
 
 
 This ping carries no client ID, only a UUID unique to the ping used
 to de-duplicate users. It cannot be keyed to any other telemetry
 submissions. It is submitted over Oblivious HTTP 
 (OHTTP): a relay operated independently of Mozilla forwards the
 encrypted submission, so the relay can see the sender's IP address but
 not the contents, and Mozilla receives the contents but not the IP
 address. Access to the collected data was restricted to four authorized
 Mozilla employees. The data was retained for 90 days and has since been deleted.
 
 
 Read about the data collection
 → 
 
 

 Aggregate data & analysis code 
 
 
 We release four types of data: 
 
 
 A list of fingerprints generated for different phases of protections, per modeled fingerprinter, with the user's OS and locale unmasked. 
 Aggregate tables of the frequency of value per metric, split by OS 
 Aggregate tables of the frequency of value per metric, correlated by other metrics' values, again split by OS 
 A detailed analysis of rendered canvas images that allows comparison 
 

 
 In the fingerprint lists, the fingerprints cannot be recreated from
 a website measuring user characteristics, due to the way the telemetry
 was collected. After being generated, the files were shuffled to a new ordering,
 and any locale occurring fewer than 100 times was anonymized.
 
 
 In the aggregate tables, any value observed fewer
 than 100 times within a single per-OS population is withheld - so
 the published data describes cohorts, never individuals.
 
 
 In the canvas comparison, raw canvas renderings are provided, but they
 are devoid of any connection to other user data. Any unique canvas rendering
 is not provided; only the hash.
 
 
 For verification and exploration, the code used to process the data and 
 perform different analyses is available for review. It additionally contains
 the specific fingerprinting scripts captured, reverse engineered, and
 modeled for the paper.
 
 
 Download the data
 → 
 Canvas explorer → 
 Analysis code → 
 
 

 Future Research 
 
 
 Far more can be asked of this dataset than we have asked. Some of it
 we chose not to pursue, some of it we simply did not think of, and
 some of it is a better fit for someone who is not us.
 
 
 There is a discussion board for proposing follow-up analyses. Two
 kinds are worth posting:
 
 
 
 Answerable from the published aggregate data. 
 Anyone can run these - the per-operating-system
 distributions are released, and the analysis toolkit is open. Post
 the question anyway, so the work is not duplicated and so the
 result lands somewhere others can find it.
 
 
 Needs the raw data. These we would have to run
 ourselves, since the underlying ping data is not something we can
 ever release. Describe what you want to know and why! To be clear,
 we do not have the raw data anymore but it is possible we
 will perform a re-collection in the future which we could analyze.
 We cannot promise to run everything, and some questions we will
 decline because we do not wish to help build a better fingerprinter.
 
 
 
 Open the discussion
 board
 → 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 This Firefox telemetry collection is opt-out and carries no client
 identifier for this ping. See the paper for the full methodology and
 its limitations.

# Sysinternals Process Explorer for Mac

Sysinternals Process Explorer for Mac is a native macOS implementation of the core Process Explorer experience. It provides a live process tree, lower-pane module/handle/thread inspection, rich per-process properties, system-wide performance graphs, code-signing inspection, and macOS-specific equivalents for Process Explorer workflows.

The app is built with Swift, SwiftUI, and AppKit, with sampling backed by public macOS APIs such as `libproc`, `sysctl`, Mach host statistics, Security.framework, IOKit, Metal, and optional privileged helper support.

![Sysinternals Process Explorer for Mac showing process details and system information](docs/images/process-explorer.png)

## Features

- Live process tree with Process Explorer-style colors for services, own processes, new/deleted processes, suspended processes, sandboxed processes, and packed images.
- Frozen process-name pane with horizontally scrollable metric columns.
- Persisted process-list column widths, ordering, column sets, and selected columns.
- Type-to-select in process and lower-pane lists.
- Immediate tooltips for truncated cells and process path/command-line detail.
- Pause/resume refresh with the spacebar.
- Native menu bar with File, Options, View, Process, Find, Window, and Help commands.
- Toolbar actions for refresh, save, process properties, kill, lower pane, find handle/DLL, target-window picker, and System Information graphs.
- Lower pane modes for DLLs/images, handles/file descriptors, and threads.
- Lower-pane row highlighting for newly appeared and deleted items.
- Per-process Properties window with Image, Performance, Performance Graph, Threads, TCP/IP, Security, Environment, and Strings tabs.
- TCP/IP tab with local address, remote address, async reverse-DNS remote name lookup, TCP state, and column persistence.
- Security/signature detail with signer, publisher, certificate chain, Team ID, notarization status, platform/ad-hoc status, validation reason, SHA-256, and VirusTotal integration.
- Module/image detail windows with metadata, signature verification, VirusTotal, Reveal in Finder, and Search Online.
- Handle/file-descriptor detail windows.
- System Information window with Summary, CPU, Memory, I/O, Network, and GPU pages.
- System Information graphs for CPU, memory, swap, disk I/O, network I/O, GPU, and per-core CPU usage.
- Performance vs. efficiency core labeling and coloring on Apple Silicon.
- Hardware details for CPU topology/cache, memory/page information, storage, network interfaces, GPU device capabilities, and OS/machine data.
- Menu-bar CPU history item.
- Process actions: kill, kill tree, suspend/resume, set priority/nice, restart, bring to front, sample process, Search Online, Check VirusTotal.
- Optional privileged helper architecture for cross-user and privileged operations.
- Release scripts for DMG creation, signing, and notarization.

## Requirements

- macOS 14 or later for the GUI app target.
- Xcode 26.6 or later recommended for the current project configuration.
- Swift 5.9 toolchain or later.
- `xcodegen` for regenerating `ProcexpMac.xcodeproj` from `project.yml`.

Install `xcodegen` if needed:

```sh
brew install xcodegen
```

## Build

Generate the Xcode project and build the Debug app:

```sh
xcodegen generate
xcodebuild -scheme ProcexpMac -configuration Debug build
```

The Debug app is written under Xcode DerivedData. On this machine the path is typically:

```sh
~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/ProcexpMac-czqddcuyalgzfgebjezrhssregtw/Build/Products/Debug/ProcExp\ \(Dev\).app
```

You can also open the generated project in Xcode:

```sh
xcodegen generate
open ProcexpMac.xcodeproj
```

## Run

After a Debug build, launch the app with:

```sh
open "$HOME/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/ProcexpMac-czqddcuyalgzfgebjezrhssregtw/Build/Products/Debug/ProcExp (Dev).app"
```

If your DerivedData suffix differs, locate the product with:

```sh
find ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData -path '*/Build/Products/Debug/ProcExp (Dev).app' -print
```

To relaunch a freshly built app from this workspace:

```sh
app="$HOME/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/ProcexpMac-czqddcuyalgzfgebjezrhssregtw/Build/Products/Debug/ProcExp (Dev).app"
pids=$(pgrep -f "$app/Contents/MacOS/ProcexpMac" || true)
if [[ -n "$pids" ]]; then kill $pids 2>/dev/null || true; fi
open -n "$app"
```

### Bundle identity: development vs. official

Unqualified Xcode and local ad-hoc builds use `ProcExp (Dev).app` with bundle
ID `com.sysinternals.procexpmac.dev`. Its helper uses the separate launchd and
Mach service ID `com.sysinternals.procexpmac.dev.helper`. The development app,
helper approval, preferences, and LaunchServices registration therefore do not
replace an installed official copy.

The official identities are reserved for an explicit Developer ID build or the
Azure release pipeline: `ProcExp.app`, `com.sysinternals.procexpmac`, and
`com.sysinternals.procexpmac.helper`. The build and signing scripts validate the
entire tuple before signing or publishing it.

## Validate

Run the full Swift package test suite:

```sh
swift test
```

Run the live smoke test:

```sh
swift run ProcexpSmoke
```

Run focused test suites:

```sh
swift test --filter ProcexpModelTests
swift test --filter ProcexpNetworkTests
swift test --filter ProcexpSigningTests
```

## TCP/IP Test Fixture

The repository includes a small stateful TCP fixture for testing the TCP/IP tab:

```sh
swift build --product ProcexpTcpFixture
.build/debug/ProcexpTcpFixture --duration 3600 --remote-host github.com --remote-port 22
```

The fixture opens a loopback listener, creates a loopback established connection, and optionally opens a DNS-resolved remote TCP connection. Select the fixture process in Process Explorer and open Properties > TCP/IP to inspect the sockets and remote-name resolution.

## Privileged Helper

The app can use an optional privileged root helper for operations that require
elevated privileges, such as richer cross-user process detail (full process
list, threads, modules, environment) and privileged process control. The helper
is a launchd daemon reached over XPC; the app registers it with `SMAppService`.

macOS gates `SMAppService` daemon registration on the app's code signature and
on an explicit user approval. The app must be signed with a **stable, non-ad-hoc**
identity — a **Developer ID Application** certificate for distribution, or a
self-signed identity for local development — and you approve the daemon once in
**System Settings ▸ General ▸ Login Items & Extensions**. The sections below
cover both the Developer ID install and a local self-signed test.

### Testing with a Developer ID certificate (real install)

This is the same experience end users get.

```sh
DEV_SIGN_IDENTITY="Developer ID Application: NAME (TEAMID)" \
bash Scripts/dev_install_helper.sh
```

This builds a Release app, embeds the helper and its launchd plist at
`Contents/Library/LaunchDaemons/`, signs everything inside-out with the Hardened
Runtime and entitlements, installs `/Applications/ProcExp.app`, and launches
it. Then, in the app, choose **ProcexpMac ▸ Install Privileged Helper…** and
approve the daemon in **System Settings ▸ General ▸ Login Items & Extensions**.
After approval the app adopts the privileged provider and shows all processes.

### Testing without a Developer ID certificate (local self-signed)

For local development you can exercise the same privileged code path with a
throwaway self-signed identity. On first run the script creates the identity in
a dedicated keychain (no login-keychain involvement), builds a signed,
helper-embedded app, installs it to `/Applications`, and launches it:

```sh
bash Scripts/dev_install_helper.sh
```

Then, one time only, choose **ProcexpMac ▸ Install Privileged Helper…** and
approve the daemon in **System Settings ▸ General ▸ Login Items & Extensions**.
After that, every subsequent run of the script rebuilds and relaunches the
signed app with the helper already enabled, so the elevated path is available on
each iteration:

```sh
bash Scripts/dev_install_helper.sh          # Debug (default), fast
CONFIGURATION=Release bash Scripts/dev_install_helper.sh
RESTART_HELPER=1 bash Scripts/dev_install_helper.sh   # after changing helper code
```

Notes:
- The script defaults to a **Debug** build signed with the **"ProcexpMac Dev"**
  self-signed identity. It installs `/Applications/ProcExp (Dev).app` with the
  `.dev` app and helper identifiers. `SMAppService` ties daemon registration to
  the app's signature and location, so reinstalling the same-identity build
  keeps the development helper registered.
- The app changes take effect on relaunch; the root **helper** keeps running its
  already-loaded binary, so pass `RESTART_HELPER=1` (prompts for sudo) when you
  change the helper's own code.
- A corporate-managed Mac can prompt for a keychain password when `codesign`
  touches your login keychain and reject your account password if the login
  keychain drifted out of sync after a rotation. The dedicated keychain the
  script creates avoids that entirely.

### Verifying and cleaning up

Check whether the daemon is registered and running as root:

```sh
launchctl print system/com.sysinternals.procexpmac.dev.helper
```

For an explicit Developer ID install, inspect the official service instead:

```sh
launchctl print system/com.sysinternals.procexpmac.helper
```

If registration succeeded, the process list shows previously hidden cross-user
and system processes. If the daemon is registered but not yet enabled, approve
it in **System Settings ▸ General ▸ Login Items & Extensions** and it becomes
active. Repeated reinstalls can clear a previously remembered approval, in which
case macOS asks you to approve it again. If registration is refused outright
(for example, an ad-hoc signature), the app reports that the helper could not be
registered and continues in unprivileged mode.

Remove the installed app and unregister the helper:

```sh
bash Scripts/dev_uninstall_helper.sh
```

The cleanup script defaults to the development tuple. To remove an explicit
Developer ID test install instead, run:

```sh
PROCEXP_LOCAL_FLAVOR=official bash Scripts/dev_uninstall_helper.sh
```

Remove the throwaway signing keychain when finished:

```sh
security delete-keychain "$HOME/Library/Keychains/procexp-dev.keychain-db"
```

See [Helper/README.md](Helper/README.md) and [docs/RELEASE.md](docs/RELEASE.md)
for the helper architecture and the full Developer ID signing/notarization
pipeline.

## Release Build

Build a release DMG:

```sh
bash Scripts/build_release.sh
```

This local ad-hoc command creates `build/ProcExp-Dev.dmg` containing
`ProcExp (Dev).app`. To prepare the canonical app for Developer ID signing:

```sh
PROCEXP_BUILD_FLAVOR=official PACKAGE_DMG=0 bash Scripts/build_release.sh
```

Sign and notarize a release build after configuring Developer ID credentials:

```sh
bash Scripts/sign_notarize.sh
```

See [docs/RELEASE.md](docs/RELEASE.md) for the full release pipeline.

## Project Layout

- [App](App) - SwiftUI/AppKit GUI application code.
- [Sources/ProcexpModel](Sources/ProcexpModel) - shared model types, providers, formatting, columns, and coloring rules.
- [Sources/ProcexpSampling](Sources/ProcexpSampling) - unprivileged process sampling with `libproc` and `sysctl`.
- [Sources/ProcexpNetwork](Sources/ProcexpNetwork) - socket enumeration and system GPU utilization.
- [Sources/ProcexpSigning](Sources/ProcexpSigning) - code-signing, SHA-256, Keychain, and VirusTotal support.
- [Sources/ProcexpGraphs](Sources/ProcexpGraphs) - AppKit graph views and SwiftUI wrappers.
- [Sources/ProcexpActions](Sources/ProcexpActions) - process actions and confirmation metadata.
- [Sources/ProcexpAutostart](Sources/ProcexpAutostart) - launchd/autostart detection.
- [Sources/ProcexpPrivileged](Sources/ProcexpPrivileged) and [Sources/ProcexpHelper](Sources/ProcexpHelper) - privileged helper client and daemon.
- [Tests](Tests) - Swift package tests.
- [Scripts](Scripts) - build, icon, signing, notarization, and release scripts.
- [docs](docs) - implementation, release, and project notes.

## Notes

macOS does not expose every Process Explorer data source through public APIs. Where macOS denies access or a metric is not available through supported APIs, the UI leaves values blank rather than fabricating data. Some details become available only for same-user processes or when the privileged helper is active.

readme:ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve.text: # DBDelve A fast, native, cross-platform, multi-engine database client. Written in Rust with GPUI, no Electron and no JVM: instant startup, friendly on your memory, and smooth scrolling through large tables where other clients crash or introduce limits. ## Community Ideas and discussion on [Discord](https://discord.gg/7PegWzwqCm). Like DBDelve? [Support its development](https://www.patreon.com/cw/ShayanAbbas1). Support is voluntary and does not provide any additional benefits. ![DBDelve in Gruvbox Dark Glass: a SELECT on the events table in the editor and its result grid below](assets/screenshots/query-dark.png) ![DBDelve in Gruvbox Light Glass: a join in the editor and its result grid below](assets/screenshots/query-light.png) Scrolling a million rows: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6e15d566-a110-46c6-a236-52af7d877d4c Launching, with the last results already there: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9e55da56-8577-43e0-812a-c77eb5d0e701 ## Why I wanted something which is performant, modern and consumes little ram. The existing DB clients are either filled with bloat (Electron and JVM) or paid. This is an alternative to them. No feature is ever going behind a paywall and with time we will have complete parity on features with those too. ## Install **macOS** (Apple Silicon, macOS 12 or later): ```sh brew install --cask ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve/dbdelve xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/DBDelve.app ``` Don't skip the second line: the app isn't notarized, so macOS won't open it until the quarantine flag is cleared. **Linux** (x86_64 or aarch64): `yay -S dbdelve-bin` from the AUR, or the tarball or AppImage from [the latest release][releases]. **Windows** (x86_64): run the installer from [the latest release][releases], or unzip the zip and run `dbdelve.exe`. The installer asks for AppData (just for you) or Program Files (all users). Updating, the `.dmg`, Linux requirements, building from source and where your data lives are all in [docs/install.md](docs/install.md). [releases]: https://github.com/ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve/releases/latest ## Supported databases Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite, Turso, DuckDB, Snowflake, SQL Server, MongoDB, Redis (and Valkey, KeyDB, Dragonfly) and ClickHouse. Any other database with an ODBC driver is reachable through the bundled ODBC bridge, with that driver installed: IBM Db2, Oracle, SAP HANA, SAP ASE (Sybase), Informix, Teradata, Vertica, Exasol, Firebird, Amazon Redshift, Google BigQuery, Databricks, Apache Hive, Trino and Presto, Dremio, InterSystems IRIS, Microsoft Access and more. Grid editing is off, and statements you type run under the connection's mode. See [Connecting through ODBC](docs/odbc.md). ![The welcome screen: paste a connection URL or pick one of the engines, import from DBeaver or TablePlus, or pick a theme](assets/screenshots/welcome.png) ## What it does - **Make it yours.** The app's own themes alongside Catppuccin, Tokyo Night, Gruvbox and Dracula, each in dark, light and glass. Import themes from Zed or VS Code, or [write your own](docs/themes.md). ![The theme picker, with themes imported from Zed and VS Code and the import commands below them](assets/screenshots/themes.png) - **Bring your connections with you.** Import every saved connection, passwords and SSH settings included, from DBeaver, or TablePlus on macOS. - **Organize your connections into projects,** and jump to any of them from the palette, or disconnect back to a home screen that lists them all. ![The palette scoped to connections, grouped into two projects, with the current connection marked](assets/screenshots/projects.png) - **Never mistake prod for staging.** Every connection is isolated and can color the title bar. Run it read-only, read-write or with full access, and DBDelve asks before anything destructive. ![The connection form, grouped into connection, security and behaviour, with a color and a project for the connection](assets/screenshots/connection-form.png) - **Edits you can read first.** Change a cell and DBDelve writes the `UPDATE` for you to check before it runs. - **Keep the columns you need.** Hide or pin columns, and the layout survives a restart. - **Read a row in full** in the row panel, with JSON highlighted, and edit long values there. ![A table open in the grid, with the row panel showing one row's values and its JSON highlighted](assets/screenshots/table-dark.png) - **Import rows** from CSV, TSV or JSON, with every row checked and every statement shown before anything runs. ![Importing events.csv: format options on the left, each file column mapped to a table column, and a preview of the rows](assets/screenshots/import.png) - **Open a data file** by dropping it on the window: a CSV, Excel, Parquet or JSON file opens in DuckDB, held in memory, as a query you can change. A `.sql` file opens in a new query tab on the connection you're on, and runs only when you run it. - **See the query plan** highlighted in its own pane, with bad row estimates called out. ![An Explain Analyze plan for a join: each node with its actual and estimated rows and time, and a ×76 misestimate flagged](assets/screenshots/query-plan.png) - **Completion that knows your schema:** tables, and a table's columns after its name and a dot. ![Completing accounts. to its columns in a join](assets/screenshots/completion.png) - **Keyboard-first.** One palette for commands, tables, saved queries, history and connections, and every shortcut rebindable. - **Your SSH, not a reimplementation.** Tunnels run through your own `ssh`, so your config, agent and hardware keys just work. For Postgres, a Host that is a directory (`/var/run/postgresql`) reaches that Unix socket on the SSH host, optionally as another user (Run as); the server needs `socat`, and passwordless `sudo` for it when Run as is set. TLS modes other than `disable` and `prefer` are refused there. - **Sign in with a short-lived token.** On Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Redis and ClickHouse, a profile's Password command prints the password at every login, so cloud IAM auth keeps working after the token expires. For Amazon RDS: ```sh /opt/homebrew/bin/aws rds generate-db-auth-token --hostname %HOSTNAME% --port %PORT% --username %USERNAME% --region ``` `%HOSTNAME%`, `%PORT%` and `%USERNAME%` are the profile's own. DBDelve quotes them itself, so write them unquoted: one inside quotes stops the command from running. Give the program's full path (`which aws` prints it): an app opened from the Finder or a desktop launcher does not see the PATH your shell sets. Expires after reuses the output for that many seconds, in memory only; blank runs the command at every login. Free and open source, nothing behind a paywall, and no telemetry: the only request DBDelve makes on its own is an update check, which you can turn off. ## Benchmarks DBDelve 0.3.6 against DBeaver 25.3.1 on the same Postgres table, median of 5 runs each (2026-10-11, M1 Pro, 32 GB): | | DBDelve | DBeaver | | ----------------- | ------- | ------- | | Launch | 1.1 s | 5.2 s | | Idle memory | 133 MB | 606 MB | | 1,000-row query | 0.21 s | 1.96 s | | 1M rows, time | 56 s | 208 s | | 1M rows, memory\* | 4.9 GB | 17 GB | \* The whole 1M-row table pulled into memory on purpose, with the row limit off. Method and full results in [BENCHMARKS.md](BENCHMARKS.md). ## Logs and bug reports DBDelve keeps a diagnostic log on your machine and never sends it anywhere. To attach it to an issue, use **Help → Copy Diagnostics** and paste; **Help → Open Logs Folder** shows the files. If the default log doesn't show the problem, turn on **Verbose logging** in Settings and reproduce it. Read a log before you post it and remove anything sensitive. A verbose one can hold hostnames, database names and anything a database driver logs. ## License Copyright (C) 2026 Shayan Abbas and contributors, licensed under the [GPL-3.0](LICENSE). Code contributed before the switch was released under the [MIT License](licenses/MIT-dbdelve.txt), and that notice still applies to it. Third-party font and theme licenses are in [NOTICES.md](NOTICES.md).

Show HN: DBDelve – Open-Source DB Client Made with Rust and GPUI | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Show HN: DBDelve – Open-Source DB Client Made with Rust and GPUI 120 points by shayan_abbas 1 day ago | hide | past | favorite | 48 comments Hi HN, I’m Shayan and a few months ago I started building a DB Client DBDelve with a focus on performance and just making something that feels good to use (in the spirit of Zed, Ghostty, and other tools that just feel pleasant to use). For my workflow I’ve always looked for performance, especially since some time ago I had a really outdated machine and any kind of bloat was really noticeable, I remember using DBeaver and it just crashing on me multiple times, I also had to use postGIS which just made it worse. I migrated all my essential dev tools to use the ones with performance in mind (Zed, Ghostty etc) but the only thing that was missing was DB Client. The main choices everyone has are DBeaver which is a memory hog and an overkill for most of the tasks imo. The other options like Datagrid, Beekeeper, TablePlus are either electron based so bloated and memory hogs or paid and closed-source. DBDelve 0.3.6 against DBeaver 25.3.1 on the same Postgres table, median of 5 runs each (2026-10-11, M1 Pro, 32 GB). Times are from the action to the rows rendered. DBDelve DBeaver
 Launch 1.1 s 5.2 s
 Idle memory 133 MB 606 MB
 1,000-row query 0.21 s 1.96 s
 1M rows, time 56 s 208 s
 1M rows, memory [1] 4.9 GB 17 GB
 
[1] The whole 1M-row, 100-column table pulled into memory on purpose, with the row limit off. Not a normal use case; DBeaver's heap limit had to be raised manually for the benchmark. Scrolling perf with 1 million rows loaded with 100 columns each: https://youtu.be/V2MOhJYFqIE It has most of the features most devs would need for 90% of their workflow plus some more I thought would be a nice touch:
Readonly, read-write and Full Access modes
Glass themes (If you’re into them, I am)
Keyboard focused with every keybinding customizable
Organization of connections into projects Me and some other folks have been daily driving it for more than a month now and most good feedback comes on it having a really simple UI to navigate, very stable for its age and the performance of course. I’m also sharing here because those people tell me this has potential to grow so I’m trying my hand at distributing it. Just want to give a huge shoutout here to the Zed team for GPUI, it's a breeze to work with if you just get through them not updating the crate officially on crates.io but the community has found the solutions for it, you just have to dig deep for it. It performs extremely well and just the HTML-like structure of it, makes it easy to understand for someone from a web dev background and agents are very good at writing it too. GPUI component also solves a lot of problems with having a good component library we can use. I think for anyone starting a GPUI project now, GPUI-kit makes a lot of sense, it just bundles GPUI, GPUI-component together and has some optimizations adding retained mode which is experimental but could provide a lot of benefit, so think all things considered it should be the default way. The major optimization I did was just lowering the memory overhead by using packed rows which reduced the memory usage by 40% on large datasets (8.1GB to 4.9GB on a 4GB table loaded in app), everything else came bundled in with Rust and GPUI mostly or they just made it very easy. Limitations:
It's not signed and notarized, identity verification from apple's side has been a nightmare but it should be signed soon.
Don’t expect feature parity with more mature clients for now, the general direction of this right now is the zed way of adding features in but after making sure the core workflows are done with a high quality. Do give it a try, you can import your connections from dbeaver and tableplus. https://github.com/ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve help
