# MeowDisplay **Mac Everywhere, On Whatever Display** Use MeowDisplay to mirror, extend or view individual Mac windows on your iPhone or iPad. Control your Mac with touch, a trackpad-style pointer, shortcuts and a keyboard. Another Mac can also act as a receiver; Android is available through closed testing. [Website](https://meowdisplay.app) · [Features](https://meowdisplay.app/features.html) · [Setup](https://meowdisplay.app/docs.html) · [Support](https://meowdisplay.app/support.html) · [Privacy](https://meowdisplay.app/privacy.html) · [Support on Ko-fi](https://ko-fi.com/raisecaterror) **[Download MeowDisplay 2.0 for Mac](https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay/releases/download/v2.0.0/MeowDisplay.dmg)** · · Mac 2.0.0 stable, shares and receives (macOS 14+) · [Mac Receiver 2.0.0](https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay/releases/download/v2.0.0/MeowDisplayReceiver.dmg) (macOS 12+) · iPhone/iPad 2.0.0 on the App Store · Android 2.0 in Google Play closed testing, not yet public · [All downloads](https://meowdisplay.app/downloads)

The released Mac app and iPhone Window view, shown in the 2.0 press-kit composition · See the original iPhone screen

## Overview MeowDisplay sends your Mac's display to an iPhone, iPad, Android receiver or another Mac. Choose **Mirror**, **Extend** or **Window view** for each device. Mobile receivers have touch, keyboard, pointer and shortcut controls. Connect over USB (iPhone/iPad), local Wi-Fi or a private network you control. Devices must pair, and sessions are encrypted. You don't need a MeowDisplay account or hosted relay. Mac-to-Mac keyboard and trackpad forwarding is implemented, but physical verification with two Macs is still pending. ## MeowDisplay 2.0 — official release Mac and iPhone/iPad 2.0.0 are released. Android 2.0 remains in Google Play closed testing. ### Platform availability — November 2, 2026 | Platform | Available version | Get it | | --- | --- | --- | | Mac app · macOS 14+ · share or receive | **2.0.0 stable** | [Download MeowDisplay](https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay/releases/download/v2.0.0/MeowDisplay.dmg) · [release notes](https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay/releases/tag/v2.0.0) | | Receiver-only Mac app · macOS 12+ | **2.0.0 stable** | [Download MeowDisplay Receiver](https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay/releases/download/v2.0.0/MeowDisplayReceiver.dmg) | | iPhone / iPad · iOS / iPadOS 16.4+ | **2.0.0 on the App Store** | [App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/meowdisplay/id6817552864) | | Android · Android 10+ | **2.0 Google Play closed testing** (not public) | [Join closed testing](https://meowdisplay.app/android/early-access) | The main Mac app includes both sharing and receiving: share this Mac's display, or use this Mac as another Mac's display. The separate Receiver-only app is also available for Macs running macOS 12 or later. Android 2.0 requires the Mac 2.0 app. Checksums and current installers are listed on the [official downloads page](https://meowdisplay.app/downloads). ## What's new in MeowDisplay 2.0 Version 2.0 adds Window view, Stage Peek and more ways to control a Mac from a phone. The main changes are: - **Window view:** arrange the Mac windows you choose in panes on the receiver. - **Stage Peek:** hold the edge to find and switch windows or show the full desktop. - **Natural Touch:** an optional direct-touch style for tapping, scrolling, dragging and right-clicking. Classic and Trackpad remain available. - **Per-device display modes:** choose Mirror, Extend or Window view independently for each receiver. - **Android receiver:** Android 2.0 is available through Google Play closed testing, not public release. - **Files and clipboard:** Remote Finder and Unified Clipboard on the mobile receivers, with separate permissions granted by the Mac owner. Clipboard sharing starts off on both sides. - **Privacy Shield:** cover the Mac's physical screens during remote use. It is a viewing shield, not a lock; see the [limitations](SECURITY.md#privacy-shield). - **One Mac app, both roles:** the main Mac app shares and receives. A separate Receiver-only app remains available for macOS 12+. - **Mac Receiver input:** control the sending Mac with the receiving Mac's keyboard and trackpad after requesting control. - **Remote Access:** reach a paired Mac over a private network you set up, including supported Tailscale routes. There is no public Internet discovery. The iPhone and iPad apps also provide a Text Bar and Zoom While Typing, which keeps the active line enlarged on the receiver. ### MeowDisplay 2.0 in use

Window view · Stage Peek · Control Tray. These press-kit mockups frame the real 2.0 iPhone screenshots. Select one to inspect the original, unframed interface.

## At a glance | | | |---|---| | **Display** | Mirror an existing Mac display · Extend with a separate virtual workspace · Window view: the Mac windows you pick, side by side · clamshell and headless workflows | | **Control** | Direct Touch (Natural Touch or Classic) · Trackpad · Precise Control in Classic and Trackpad · Smart Touch (Experimental, Classic) · keyboard · Apple Pencil · Mac gestures | | **Devices & permissions** | Active Display · Known Devices · Nearby pairing · connection policies · Allow Input and per-session control requests | | **Picture in Picture** | Keep a View Only window of the live Mac on screen while you use other apps (iPhone and iPad) | | **Shortcuts** | Main Control Tray · Function Tray · Chords and modifier palettes · customizable actions · profiles · Auto-hide | | **Connections** | USB · local Wi-Fi · Remote Access · Auto-Reconnect · Wake & Connect | | **Audio** | Mac system audio on the receiver · Mac keeps playing locally · A/V sync and Resync | | **Security** | Trusted pairing with a matching code · TLS 1.3 · pinned peer identity | | **Receivers** | iPhone and iPad · Android in closed testing · another Mac using the main app's receiver role or Receiver-only app, with keyboard and trackpad control (physical two-Mac input verification outstanding, [#12](https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay/issues/12)) | ## Why MeowDisplay? MeowDisplay is for using your own Mac from a smaller screen, especially an iPhone. The controls are designed for touch, and Window view lets you focus on individual apps instead of shrinking a whole desktop. - **Mirror or Extend.** View an existing display, or create a separate virtual desktop that macOS can arrange alongside other displays. - **Control from a phone.** Use touch styles, a trackpad-style pointer, gestures, shortcut trays and a keyboard. - **Use your own network.** Connect over USB, local Wi-Fi or a private-network route that you configure. No MeowDisplay account or hosted relay is required. - **Personal use first.** This is for accessing your Mac from another screen, not for enterprise fleet management. Comparing it with Sidecar, Duet Display, Luna Display, Astropad or Jump Desktop? These apps handle different devices and workflows. MeowDisplay is free and open source, offers Mirror and Extend, and requires you to set up your own network route for Remote Access. See the [setup FAQ](https://meowdisplay.app/docs#faq) before choosing an option. ## Display: Mirror & Extend

Mac display settings: Mirror (left) and Extend (right). See Extend running on an iPad.

- **Mirror** shows an existing Mac display on the receiver. With multiple physical displays connected, choose which one to share. Mirror needs an active display to copy. - **Extend** creates a separate software virtual display. Move windows onto it and arrange it alongside your other displays in macOS. Where supported, Extend shape controls include **Use Full Display**. Choose the mode on the Mac, or request a switch from the receiver's Settings; the Mac confirms the change. Extend also supports clamshell and headless workflows without a dummy display adapter. Keep a closed MacBook connected to power; headless compatibility is still being tested across Mac models. ## Window mode Choose **Windows** to arrange selected Mac windows in panes on a receiver. Each device has its own display mode, so switching one does not change the others.

Three-pane Window view on an iPad (9th generation) · Open full-resolution screenshot

- **Tiles.** One window is the default. Every receiver supports up to 9 panes, including phones; the available space and minimum pane size decide how many can be shown. - **Choose windows.** Hold three fingers still on the picture, or use Settings → Display → **Show Mac Windows…**. On the Mac Receiver, use **Windows** in the title bar or ⌃⌥W. - **Typing.** One pointer works across the tiles; keys go to the tile you selected, and only while its app is in front on the Mac. Control needs the same session permission as always, and a View Only session can arrange tiles but sends nothing. - **Safe by default.** Removing a tile never closes the Mac window. **Close Window on Mac…** is separate and asks first. A Mac can turn Window mode off under Settings → Displays → Windows. ### Stage Peek Stage Peek is the default Window view switcher. Hold the left or right edge, then slide to find a window or tap to switch. You can search running apps and use **Full Desktop** to return to the complete Mac screen. From there, **Switch to Window view?** offers a way back once per launch. The optional **Rail** switcher is under Settings → Controls → **Window Switcher**. See [WINDOW_MODE.md](WINDOW_MODE.md) for pane and switching behavior. ## Input & gestures Remote control requires **Allow Input** on the Mac, Accessibility permission, and permission for the current session. Pausing the stream also pauses input. Choose an input mode in the receiver's Settings: - **Direct Touch** — a touch maps to the matching position on the Mac screen. Choose a **Touch Style**: **Natural Touch** taps to click, swipes to scroll, presses then moves to drag and touches and holds to right-click; **Classic** keeps the finger as the pointer (tap, then hold and move, to drag) and is where Smart Touch applies. - **Trackpad** — the pointer moves relatively, like a MacBook trackpad. Touching doesn't jump the cursor to that spot. **Trackpad Sensitivity** is adjustable, and multi-finger gestures keep working. Phones initially use Trackpad; iPads and Android tablets initially use Direct Touch. Classic is the default Direct Touch style; Natural Touch is an optional style. Saved choices can differ. ### Allow Input & control requests

Mac Input settings: allowing connections does not grant control.

**Allow Input is the Mac-wide master switch.** Receivers can stay connected and view the Mac while it is off. Every new logical session starts with input off; connecting never grants control. Use **Request Control** in the receiver's Settings. The device's **Input Requests** policy on the Mac decides what happens: - **Ask** prompts on the Mac. - **Always Allow Requests** skips the prompt, but the receiver still has to ask each session. It never bypasses Allow Input. - **Never Allow Requests** rejects requests. Until effective input is allowed, the receiver's control tray is unavailable; the **Settings gear stays reachable**. The Mac can **Revoke Control** in the device's settings, or the receiver can **Turn Off** control. These permissions are separate from permission to connect. A touch that control doesn't allow shows a brief **Request Control** prompt; it never changes a setting on its own. Requests are only sent automatically when you turn on **Request Control Automatically** for that Mac, and the Mac still decides. **Local view navigation is separate from input.** With **Allow Local View Navigation** on (the default), you can pan, zoom, rotate and reset the view on the receiver even while input is off — nothing is sent to the Mac. On iPad, **Move View** lets one finger pan and a pinch zoom without touching the Mac at all. ### Precise Control **Precise Control works in Classic Direct Touch and Trackpad.** Keep one finger down and use another to fine-tune and click at the pointer. There's nothing to turn on. In Natural Touch a second finger during a swipe or drag is ignored. - **In Classic Direct Touch**, the first touch places the pointer at that position. Keep it down for a moment, then add another finger: movement becomes relative for the rest of that touch sequence. Move either finger to fine-tune; the pointer never snaps back under it. Lift every finger and the next Direct Touch starts normally again. - **In Trackpad**, movement is already relative from the first touch. Rest one finger, then use another to click or drag at the existing pointer location. There is no absolute-to-relative transition, and **Trackpad Sensitivity** still scales pointer movement. - **In either mode**, tap the added finger to click, double- or triple-tap for multiple clicks, or tap, then hold and move, to drag. With one finger resting, tap two more fingers together to right-click. See [Precise Control](https://meowdisplay.app/features.html#precise-control) for the full gesture details. ### Smart Touch **Smart Touch (Experimental)** is an optional addition to Classic Direct Touch (Touch Style: Classic), on by default and easy to turn off in the receiver's Settings. It uses the Mac's Accessibility information to recognize supported scrollable areas and window title bars: - Swipe a scrollable area with one finger, with momentum in either axis. - Hold a standard window's title bar or empty toolbar space, then drag to move the window after the confirming haptic. - Hold still before moving in a scrollable area to use ordinary Direct Touch instead. **Smart Touch Haptics** controls the hold feedback. It works best with standard macOS accessibility information and falls back to Direct Touch when it cannot identify the target. It has no effect in Natural Touch or Trackpad mode. Reliability and stability are still being improved; it does not understand every interface. More on [Smart Touch](https://meowdisplay.app/features.html#smart-touch). ### Pointer & viewport gestures The one-finger rows describe Classic and Trackpad. In Natural Touch, a swipe scrolls, press then move drags, and touch and hold right-clicks. | Gesture | On your Mac | |---|---| | Tap | Click | | Double tap | Double-click | | Triple tap | Triple-click | | Tap, then hold and move | Left drag | | Two-finger tap | Right-click | | Two-finger tap, then hold and move | Right-button drag | | Two-finger pan | Scroll, with momentum | | Pinch / spread | **Viewport**, **App**, or **Disabled** | | Two-finger rotate | **Viewport**, **App**, or **Disabled**, with optional **Snap Rotation** | | Two-finger double tap | Reset or restore the viewport zoom and pan | ### Mac system gestures | Gesture | On your Mac | |---|---| | Three-finger swipe up | Mission Control | | Three-finger swipe down | App Exposé | | Three-finger swipe left / right | Next / Previous Space | | Three-finger tap | Spotlight | | Four- or five-finger spread | Show Desktop | | Four- or five-finger pinch | Launchpad | Full details are on the [Features page](https://meowdisplay.app/features.html#pointer). ### Apple Pencil Use Apple Pencil for precise input on supported iPad models: - Pencil strokes reach the Mac as pen-tablet events, separate from finger input - Tilt is passed through with each stroke - Hover moves the pointer before the tip touches, on iPads that support Pencil hover - Strokes are sent at the iPad's full touch sample rate - Fingers resting on the screen are ignored while the Pencil tip is down - Tap and double-tap with the tip to click and double-click Apple Pencil support is still evolving, with additional capabilities and refinements planned for future releases. ### Trackpad mode, without the picture Turn **Video** off and keep using MeowDisplay for pointer and keyboard input. The connection, trays and selected input mode stay active, so the receiver works as a trackpad and keyboard for the Mac. ### Keyboard Tap the tray's Keyboard button for the on-screen keyboard, or connect a hardware keyboard to the iPhone or iPad. In 2.0, the hardware keyboard's **arrow keys**, Escape, Tab and Forward Delete are forwarded to the Mac while remote input is allowed. Latched modifiers from the Control Tray combine with the keys you type. ## Control Trays & Chords ### Main Control Tray The Main Control Tray puts **Command**, **Option**, **Control**, **Shift**, **Escape**, **Tab**, **Dock**, **Keyboard** and **Settings** on the receiver. Reorder or hide buttons and save different profiles. You can also choose haptics, the tray side in landscape, and Avoid Notch. The [iPhone Control Tray screenshot](https://meowdisplay.app/press-kit/Screenshots/iPhone/MeowDisplay-iPhone-Control-Tray.png) shows the actual controls without the device frame. ### Chords Hold or latch a modifier and a palette of matching shortcuts appears beside it. Combine modifiers and the palette changes with the chord — for example **⌘** for Copy, Paste and Undo, **⌘⌥** for Force Quit and Hide Others, **⌘⇧** for Redo and Screenshot. Pick commands without reaching for a physical keyboard, and choose which actions each palette offers. ### Function Tray A separate tray of one-tap actions — **Zoom In**, **Zoom Out**, **Undo** and **Redo** by default. It's customized independently of the Main Control Tray, with its own profiles, and can sit on the same or the opposite side. Add, remove, reorder and rename its actions, and give each one a face — an SF Symbol, text, an emoji, or its keys. Custom actions can be one-tap keyboard shortcuts (including multi-key chords) or short sequences of existing actions, and chord palettes can offer them too. ### iPad controls On iPad, choose how the controls sit around the Mac: - **Strip** — a solid rail on any edge, with the Mac's picture fitted beside it. - **Overlay** — the Mac fills the screen and the controls float over it in compact trays. - **Custom** — up to five layouts of your own, with separate landscape and portrait arrangements, built in a full-screen visual editor with Preview, alignment guides and snapping. Layouts can be shared as a code and imported on another iPad. The Main and Function controls pick their edges independently, **Control Size** scales them, and **Two-Hand Assist** puts helper modifiers on the opposite side. While the on-screen keyboard is up, a keyboard accessory bar with modifiers, Escape and Tab takes the controls' place. iPhone keeps the Control Trays above. ### Auto-hide Auto-hide hides the control trays after a period of inactivity and brings them back when you interact with the receiver. Manual Collapse works separately. You can turn Auto-hide off. ## Devices

Mac Devices settings: manage existing pairings and discover receivers.

Pair a receiver once, then manage it in **Devices** on the Mac: - **Active Display** shows live receiver/display sessions and connection state, with **Pause** and **Disconnect**. - **Known Devices** includes paired receivers that are **Connected**, **Paired · Nearby**, or **Paired · Offline**. When reachable, connect with **Mirror** or **Extend**. Open device settings or **Forget** a pairing. - **Nearby** lists unpaired discoverable receivers ready to pair. **Connection permissions** decide whether a paired device can start sharing. **Automatically Allow Connections** is on by default. Each device can use **Default** (follow that switch), **Always Allow**, or **Block**. Blocking keeps the pairing. These choices never grant remote control. Either side can start a session, and the Mac sender always streams. When connection approval is required, an explicit Connect waits for acceptance; background reconnects never prompt. Receivers include **iPhone**, **iPad**, **Android** (closed testing), and another Mac using the main app's receiver role or the separate **Mac Receiver**. Once the sending Mac allows control, the receiving Mac's own keyboard and trackpad drive it while the video window is in front; press ⌃⌥⎋ to pause. More on [Devices](https://meowdisplay.app/features.html#devices). ## Connections - **USB** — plug in a data-capable cable and trust the Mac. A direct, reliable path with no network setup. - **Local Wi-Fi** — receivers are discovered over Bonjour on your network, including nearby peer-to-peer Wi-Fi. - **Remote Access** — reach a paired Mac through a private network you control, such as Tailscale. The address only routes the connection; pairing still authenticates it. - **Network Transport** — on Wi-Fi and Remote Access, each device can use **Auto** (the default), **QUIC** or **TCP** (Mac Settings → the device). Both use the same pairing and encryption; Auto uses QUIC when both apps support it and uses TCP if QUIC can't get through. USB is unaffected. - **Auto-Reconnect** restores the session whenever the connection becomes available again. - **Wake & Connect** can wake a supported paired Mac on its network and reconnect when it becomes available. It needs Wake for Network Access and compatible hardware, and is designed for a logged-in Mac that has gone to sleep or locked. See [Setup](https://meowdisplay.app/docs.html) for networking limitations. ## Audio Mac system audio can stream to the receiver while the Mac keeps playing locally. Turn it on with the receiver's **Audio** toggle; if sound and picture drift apart, adjust **A/V Sync** or tap **Resync**. ## Picture in Picture On iPhone and iPad, the Mac can stay in view while you do something else. MeowDisplay uses the system's own Picture in Picture window, fed by the same stream the receiver is already showing. - **Automatic or manual.** With **Picture in Picture** on (the default), a live session can enter the system floating window when you leave the app, when supported and available. Receiver Settings also offers **Start Picture in Picture** and **Stop Picture in Picture**. - **For glancing, not controlling.** The window is View Only: it shows what your Mac is doing, but touches in it never reach the Mac. All interaction stays in the full receiver. - **One tap back.** The window's restore button returns you to the full receiver, and opening MeowDisplay again does the same. - **Audio.** If the receiver's **Audio** is on, Mac audio can keep playing while the window is showing. Leaving the app without Picture in Picture still silences the receiver as before. - **Your choice.** Turn Picture in Picture off in the receiver's Settings and leaving the app never starts it. Picture in Picture is new; physical-device validation is not yet complete. ## Security - Devices pair explicitly, confirming a matching verification code (SAS) on both screens. - Every session is encrypted and mutually authenticated with **TLS 1.3** against the **pinned peer identity** you trusted. - There is no plaintext media fallback. More in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) and the [Privacy page](https://meowdisplay.app/privacy.html). ## Requirements | App | Runs on | |---|---| | **MeowDisplay** (the Mac app for sharing and receiving) | macOS 14 or later | | **MeowDisplay Receiver** (a spare Mac as a display) | macOS 12 or later | | **MeowDisplay** for iPhone and iPad | iOS / iPadOS 16.4 or later | | **MeowDisplay** for Android (closed beta) | Android 10 or later; Mac 2.0 sender required. Build requirements: [AndroidReceiver/README.md](AndroidReceiver/README.md); features: [PARITY.md](PARITY.md) | Remote control of the Mac needs Accessibility permission; capturing a display needs Screen Recording. ## Install The links in [Platform availability](#platform-availability--november-2-2026) install stable 2.0. The main Mac app can share and receive; choose the separate Receiver-only app when that is all the Mac needs. **Mac, with Homebrew (optional):** signed and notarized, macOS 14 or later. ```sh brew install --cask raiseCatError/tap/meowdisplay ``` That one command adds the [tap](https://github.com/raiseCatError/homebrew-tap) and installs MeowDisplay into `/Applications`. Update with `brew upgrade --cask meowdisplay`; remove with `brew uninstall --cask meowdisplay` (add `--zap` to also delete preferences and caches). To use a spare Mac (macOS 12 or later) only as a display, install the receiver: `brew install --cask raiseCatError/tap/meowdisplay-receiver`. **Mac, direct download:** get `MeowDisplay.dmg` (or `MeowDisplayReceiver.dmg`) from the [2.0.0 release](https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay/releases/tag/v2.0.0) and drag the app to Applications. **iPhone and iPad:** install MeowDisplay from the [App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/meowdisplay/id6817552864) (iOS or iPadOS 16.4 or later). ## Getting started 1. [Download MeowDisplay 2.0 for Mac](https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay/releases/download/v2.0.0/MeowDisplay.dmg), open the DMG, drag MeowDisplay to Applications and open it. 2. Install [MeowDisplay from the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/meowdisplay/id6817552864) on your iPhone or iPad and open it. Android 2.0 is in [closed testing](https://meowdisplay.app/android/early-access). To receive on another Mac, install the main app or the [Mac Receiver 2.0.0](https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay/releases/download/v2.0.0/MeowDisplayReceiver.dmg) (macOS 12+). 3. Connect over USB or Wi-Fi, and pair the devices by confirming the matching code. 4. Choose **Mirror**, **Extend** or **Window view**. 5. Grant Screen Recording and Local Network permissions as requested. For control, also grant Accessibility, enable **Allow Input** on the Mac, and use **Request Control** in the receiver's Settings. The [Setup guide](https://meowdisplay.app/docs.html) covers permissions, pairing, USB & Wi-Fi, Remote Access and troubleshooting. ## Build from source ```sh git clone https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay.git cd meowdisplay echo "DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=YOURTEAMID" > .env ./generate.sh ``` Open `MeowDisplay.xcodeproj` and run the `OpenSidecarMac` scheme for the Mac app, or `OpenSidecariOS` for the iPhone/iPad receiver. Signing, permissions and troubleshooting are in [SETUP.md](SETUP.md). The release process is in [RELEASE.md](RELEASE.md). ## Documentation - [Features](https://meowdisplay.app/features.html) · [Setup](https://meowdisplay.app/docs.html) · [Support](https://meowdisplay.app/support.html) · [Privacy](https://meowdisplay.app/privacy.html) - [SETUP.md](SETUP.md) — building, signing and local setup - [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) — security model and reporting issues - [PROTOCOL.md](PROTOCOL.md) and [COMPATIBILITY.md](COMPATIBILITY.md) — wire protocol and versioning - [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md) — how the apps fit together and where to start in the code - [WINDOW_MODE.md](WINDOW_MODE.md) — Window mode: tiles, switching, limits - [RECEIVER_CONTROLS.md](RECEIVER_CONTROLS.md) and [PARITY.md](PARITY.md) — what each receiver can do and where its settings live - [AndroidReceiver/README.md](AndroidReceiver/README.md) — Android build and verification - [PRODUCT_SCOPE.md](PRODUCT_SCOPE.md) — product goals, non-goals and idea discussions - [TERMINOLOGY.md](TERMINOLOGY.md) — names and copy rules - [TECHNICAL_NOTES.md](TECHNICAL_NOTES.md) — virtual displays, sleep and wake, and other internals ## Contributing Source, issues and releases live at [github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay](https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay). Bug reports, suggestions, documentation updates and pull requests are welcome, especially testing on different devices, Mac models, external-display setups and networks. Our [contribution guide](CONTRIBUTING.md) has separate forms for bugs, feature requests, exploratory ideas, documentation, and hardware compatibility reports. **Base branches and pull requests on `dev`**, where development happens. `main` holds the latest published release source; only approved release promotions and documentation-only promotions reach it ([BRANCHING.md](BRANCHING.md)). MeowDisplay is **personal-first, not non-commercial**: using it for your own professional or commercial work is welcome. We are **not currently planning an enterprise remote-desktop/IT administration suite** ([discussion #86](https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay/issues/86)). [Windows](https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay/issues/84), [Linux](https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay/issues/85), and [hosted account/relay services](https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay/issues/87) are separate **unplanned ideas**, not roadmap commitments. Discussion does not guarantee consideration or implementation. See [PRODUCT_SCOPE.md](PRODUCT_SCOPE.md), [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Report security vulnerabilities privately as described in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md), never in a public issue. **Want to translate MeowDisplay?** Community translations are welcome. Human-written translations only, please — no AI or machine-generated localization. See [Translations in CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md#translations) for how to get started. ## Support development MeowDisplay stays free and open source. If it helps you, supporting its continued development is appreciated, but entirely optional: [Ko-fi](https://ko-fi.com/raisecaterror) · [GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors/raiseCatError). Bug reports, translations and help with testing are useful too. ♥️ ## Built on OpenDisplay MeowDisplay started as a fork of [OpenDisplay](https://github.com/peetzweg/opendisplay) by Philip Poloczek. OpenDisplay provided the original foundation for Mac screen capture, virtual displays, video encoding and an iPhone/iPad receiver. Thanks to Philip Poloczek and the OpenDisplay contributors for that work. Most of MeowDisplay's own work since then has gone into what happens on top of that foundation: Direct Touch, Trackpad and gestures, Smart Touch, Precise Control, the control trays, Remote Access, pairing and security, the session lifecycle, clamshell and headless use, audio, Picture in Picture, and a lot of polish. If you only need the core second-display experience, or compatibility that the OpenDisplay project serves better, OpenDisplay is well worth a look. MeowDisplay is developed and released independently of it ([BRANCHING.md](BRANCHING.md), [REFERENCE.md](REFERENCE.md)). ## Responsible use MeowDisplay is intended for devices you own or are authorized to use. Don't use it to watch, access or control someone else's device without their permission. ## License & credits MeowDisplay is licensed under [GPL-3.0](LICENSE). It began as a fork of [OpenDisplay](https://github.com/peetzweg/opendisplay) by Philip Poloczek, which provided the original display, capture, encoding and receiver foundation.  Choose which devices can control your Mac.

 Precise Control 
 Fine-tune the pointer with a second finger. 
 A fingertip covers exactly what you’re aiming at. In Direct Touch or Trackpad, keep one finger down and use a second: the pointer moves from where it already is, and a tap clicks right where it points. 
 
 Place it, then refine it. In Direct Touch, your first finger puts the pointer where you touch. Add a second finger and the pointer stops jumping. Move either finger to nudge it onto small targets. 
 Tap to click at the pointer. Tap the second finger to click. Tap twice to double-click, or tap, then hold and move, to drag from that exact spot. 
 Trackpad works the same way. The pointer is already relative there. Rest one finger, then tap another to click or drag right where the pointer is. 
 Lift to finish. Lift every finger and your next touch starts fresh.

 Smart Touch Experimental 
 Scroll and move windows with one finger. 
 With Direct Touch, Smart Touch checks what’s under your finger before it acts. Scrollable areas scroll with one finger, and title bars move their window. 
 
 Up, down, sideways and diagonally. Lists, documents, web pages and spreadsheets follow your finger. Straight swipes stay on course; diagonal ones move both ways. 
 Hold a title bar to move the window. Hold for a moment, then drag. A haptic tells you when the window is ready. 
 Hold anywhere else for Direct Touch. Holding still turns that touch into plain Direct Touch.

 Scratchpad

The Function Tray keeps Zoom, Undo, Redo and Return one tap away, on either side of the screen. Made yours. Choose the shortcuts in each palette, reorder or hide controls, and keep separate profiles. 
 Automatically hide the Control Tray. Auto-hide hides the Control Tray after a short period of inactivity. It stays visible while you use it and reappears when you reach for it. Prefer it always visible? Turn Auto-hide off. Show, Hide and Collapse still work the way they always have. Explore the trays › 
 
 Android closed testing Try MeowDisplay on Android. Use an Android phone or tablet as a receiver over Wi-Fi or a private network. Mirror, Extend, Window view and Natural Touch are available to closed testers. Android connects over the network; USB isn’t supported. JOIN CLOSED TESTING ON Google Play Closed test · Android 10 or later · Needs the Mac 2.0 unified app · How to join › 
 
 Connections Connect by USB, Wi-Fi or a private network. Connect over USB on iPhone/iPad, local Wi-Fi, or a private network such as Tailscale. Android uses network connections, not USB. There’s no MeowDisplay account or hosted streaming relay. Find your connection › 
 
 01 USB on iPhone and iPad Connect a data cable, unlock your iPhone or iPad, and tap Trust. No extra USB tunnel tool is required. 
 02 Local Wi-Fi On the same network, your Mac finds your device on its own. Nearby devices can also connect directly over peer-to-peer Wi-Fi. 
 03 Private-network connections Use a private network you already trust, such as Tailscale, to reach a paired Mac from elsewhere. Pairing still verifies every connection. 
 
 
 
 Remote Access Reach your Mac over a private network. Connect through a private network such as Tailscale. Paired devices can exchange their own Tailscale addresses; automatic dialing is enabled only on verified Android–Mac IPv4 routes. You can also enter an address yourself. Set up Remote Access › 
 Wake and reconnect to your Mac. Wake & Connect sends a Wake-on-LAN request to your paired Mac, then reconnects. It needs Wake for Network Access, supported hardware, and a way for the wake request to reach the Mac’s local network. Auto-Reconnect restores the session when the connection returns. A sleeping Mac can’t pass along its own wake request over Tailscale. From farther away, another device or router on the Mac’s network has to send it. Designed for an existing logged-in Mac session that sleeps or locks. Cold boot and the fully logged-out login screen are outside the current supported workflow. 
 
 
 
 Built for your devices Native apps for Mac, iOS and Android. Native Mac and iPhone/iPad apps are built with Swift, and the Android receiver is built in Kotlin. Capture, decoding and input use platform-native frameworks. A Mac remains the sender. 
 Swift 6 SwiftUI ScreenCaptureKit VideoToolbox Network.framework Metal Kotlin Jetpack Compose MediaCodec 
 
 
 Pairing & privacy Pair your devices with a matching code. Confirm the matching code on both devices. Future connections authenticate against the device identity you trusted. MeowDisplay uses mutually authenticated TLS 1.3 and pins each paired device’s public key. A saved network address helps find your Mac; it doesn’t replace that trust. Identity & trust Stored in your Keychain MeowDisplay account None required MeowDisplay-hosted relay None Read about privacy › 
 Support independent development Support MeowDisplay MeowDisplay stays free and open source. If it helps you, a contribution supports its development. Thank you ♥ Support on Ko-fi ↗ GitHub Sponsors ↗ Built in the open. MeowDisplay is open-source software under GPL-3.0. Read the code, follow development, or contribute. Explore on GitHub ↗ 
 
 A few good questions Before you connect. 
 Is MeowDisplay free? Yes. The Mac, iPhone and iPad apps are free, and Android is in free closed testing. There are no subscriptions, ads or MeowDisplay accounts. The source is open under GPL-3.0. Donations are optional and greatly appreciated. 
 Where can I download MeowDisplay? The latest public Mac installer is the stable v2.0.0 release. Android 2.0 testers also need Mac 2.0 . Get the iPhone/iPad app on the App Store . Android 2.0 is available through Google Play closed testing . 
 Which devices are supported? The sender runs on macOS 14+. Receivers include iPhone/iPad (iOS/iPadOS 16.4+), Android (10+, closed beta), and another Mac (standalone receiver from macOS 12, or integrated receiving in 2.0). Mac-to-Mac input is implemented but physical two-Mac verification is pending. Compare platforms › 
 Do I need a monitor or a dummy display adapter? No dummy adapter is needed. Extend creates a virtual display in software, so your iPhone or iPad can be the Mac’s screen, including with the lid closed. MeowDisplay is designed to work with no monitor attached; headless setups are still being tested on more Macs. Mirror copies a physical display, so it needs one to be active. Clamshell and headless use . 
 Is MeowDisplay a remote desktop app? MeowDisplay lets you use your own Mac from another device, including for professional work. It is not an enterprise remote-support or fleet-management service. Feature availability depends on the receiving platform and release version. 
 Do I need Tailscale? No. USB and local Wi-Fi work without it. Remote Access needs a reachable network; Tailscale is one option. Third-party networking services have their own terms. 
 Can I wake my Mac from another network? Local Wake & Connect depends on Mac hardware and settings. Waking an unreachable Mac from another network requires something on its own LAN to send a wake packet. MeowDisplay does not provide a hosted wake relay. 
 
 
 Get started Get MeowDisplay for your devices. Free on Mac, iPhone and iPad today. Android 2.0 is in closed beta. Mac 2.0 companion JOIN CLOSED TESTING ON Google Play All downloads › Setup guide › Find help › The unified Mac 2.0 app shares and receives displays on macOS 14 or later. Older Mac? The receiver-only Mac Receiver runs on macOS 12 or later.

# STE80 Humanizer

[![skills.sh installs](https://skills.sh/b/Dodaios/ste80-humanizer)](https://skills.sh/Dodaios/ste80-humanizer) [![validate](https://github.com/Dodaios/ste80-humanizer/actions/workflows/validate.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Dodaios/ste80-humanizer/actions/workflows/validate.yml) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)

STE80 Humanizer makes AI-written text read like a careful person wrote it, without changing what it says. It combines two methods:

1. **The humanizer method.** Remove the 26 tells from Wikipedia's [Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing), in the catalog of [blader/humanizer](https://github.com/blader/humanizer).
2. **Karpathy's STE80 method.** Rebuild the sentences "80% of the way to ASD-STE100", the controlled English of aircraft maintenance manuals.

**Before:**
> Great question! Kubernetes liveness probes are a powerful mechanism that enables the kubelet to determine whether a container is healthy — and it's not just a health check, it's your first line of defense. When a probe fails, the container will be automatically restarted by the kubelet, ensuring that your application remains available. However, it's important to note that misconfigured probes could potentially cause cascading restarts, so parameters like `initialDelaySeconds` and `failureThreshold` should be carefully tuned.
>
> Get this right, and your cluster heals itself.

**After:**
> A liveness probe tells the kubelet if a container is healthy. If the probe fails, the kubelet restarts the container. This keeps the application available.
>
> A bad probe can also cause many restarts. For example, a timeout that is too short makes healthy containers fail the probe. To prevent this, set `initialDelaySeconds` and `failureThreshold` to values that fit your application.

The goal is text that people read easily. Getting past AI detectors is not a goal.

## Why two passes

Most humanizers only remove phrases. The text loses "Great question!" and "seamless", but it keeps long sentences that carry three ideas, hide the actor and stack hedges. It still reads like AI. You can see it in the worked example in [SKILL.md](SKILL.md):

| Step | What is left |
|---|---|
| Original | Chatbot opener, dash, "not just X", "-ing" rider, "however", "could potentially", dramatic closer |
| After Pass 1 (tells) | "...the container will be automatically restarted by the kubelet, which keeps your application available. Misconfigured probes can cause cascading restarts, so parameters ... should be carefully tuned." Clean words, but heavy sentences. |
| After Pass 2 (STE80) | Short sentences, one idea each, active voice, the instruction apart from the description. |

## The method: what Karpathy said

On 2 October 2026, [Andrej Karpathy posted](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2105819303471976479) tips for one problem: as LLMs do more of the work, people spend more time reading and understanding what the models produce. His first tip:

> Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent.

The post then goes up a ladder: diagrams, then HTML pages, then explainer videos. His conclusion is that our work moves "up the abstractions into oversight and understanding". Clear output is the bottleneck, and writing is the first step.

[![Simplified Technical English: overview. Document structure, anatomy of STE sentences, verb forms, dictionary entries, writing rule limits and history.](assets/ste100-overview.png)](assets/ste100-overview.png)

*The STE overview graphic from [Karpathy's post](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2105819303471976479). Click to enlarge. Note: a later fact check found errors in the dictionary panel (D). In ASD-STE100 Issue 9, "approximately" is approved, "TEST" is approved only as a noun (not as a verb), and there is no entry for "in order to". This skill follows Issue 9.*

**ASD-STE100** (Simplified Technical English) is from the 1980s aerospace industry. It was made for mechanics whose first language is not English, because a misread step on an aircraft can kill. Its rules:

- 20 words per instruction and 25 per description
- one instruction per sentence
- active voice and simple tenses
- one meaning per word, with about 900 approved words
- one topic per paragraph, and six sentences at most

**Why "80%"?** At 100%, "check" and "test" are nouns only, "may" and "should" are banned and many common words are not allowed. Normal prose sounds stiff. At 80%, you keep the full structure and only as much vocabulary as still sounds natural:

| STE rule | 100% (Strict mode) | 80% (default) |
|---|---|---|
| Sentence length 20 / 25 | Hard limit | A few words over is fine |
| One idea per sentence | Always | Always |
| Active voice, simple tenses | Always | Always |
| Approved dictionary only | Yes | No, use the plain common word |
| "check", "test" as verbs | No | Yes |
| "may", "should" | No | Yes, for real uncertainty |
| Contractions | No | Yes, in casual text |
| Semicolons | No | No |

Karpathy's tip is about readability. It does not remove chatbot phrases, so Pass 1 does that first.

## How to read the skill

[SKILL.md](SKILL.md) has two numbered lists:

- **§1 to §26:** the AI tells (Pass 1).
- **S1 to S15:** the STE80 structure rules (Pass 2).

Both lists are compact tables with a short example. Pass 2 says what changes between **80%** and **Strict**. The full entries, with **Watch for**, **Problem**, **Before** and **After**, are in [references/ai-tells.md](references/ai-tells.md) and [references/ste80-rules.md](references/ste80-rules.md). *Weak alone* means: act only if other tells are near. The skill reports its edits by number, for example "§1, §8, S2", so you can look each one up.

## Installation

Once installed, the skill answers to `/ste80-humanizer`. It also starts by itself when you ask to humanize, simplify or de-AI a text, or ask for STE.

### Any agent (skills.sh)

```bash
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer
```

Global install for one agent, or for all of them:

```bash
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent claude-code
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent codex
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent cursor
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent '*'
```

Without `--global`, the skill goes into the current project only. The [skills CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills) from Vercel works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and many more agents.

### Claude Code plugin

```
/plugin marketplace add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer
/plugin install ste80-humanizer@ste80-humanizer
```

### Claude.ai and Claude Desktop

Download this repo as a ZIP (Code → Download ZIP). Upload it in Settings → Capabilities → Skills.

## Usage

```
/ste80-humanizer
<paste text>
```

Or just ask:

```
This sounds like ChatGPT wrote it. Make it sound like a person.
Rewrite this README 80% of the way to ASD-STE100.
Explain how TLS handshakes work in STE.
Light touch: just remove the AI stuff from docs/intro.md.
Convert docs/runbook.md to strict STE.
Does this email sound like AI? Just tell me, don't rewrite it.
```

| Mode | When | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Humanize (default)** | Normal requests | Pass 1 fully, Pass 2 at 80%. Keeps your voice. |
| **Light** | "light touch", "just remove the AI stuff" | Pass 1, plus only the worst sentences from Pass 2. |
| **Strict STE** | "strict", "full STE", procedures, safety notes | Pass 1 and all of Pass 2 at 100%. |

**Match your voice.** Add a sample of your own writing. The skill then matches your sentence length, words and punctuation.

**Fidelity first.** The skill keeps every fact, keeps "may" as "may", keeps "40+" as "40+", adds nothing and flags contradictions in the source. In our tests, this was the clearest difference from a plain prompt (see Tests).

## Pass 1: the 26 AI tells

| # | Tell | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Staging instead of stating** ||||
| 1 | **Not X but Y** | It's not just a faster build tool, it's a new way to think. | The build tool caches each step. |
| 2 | **One-line closers** | ...No cold starts. No excuses. That's the power of the edge. | Latency dropped to 40 ms. |

## Pass 2: the 15 STE80 rules

| # | Rule | 80% vs Strict |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | One idea per sentence | 80% allows two linked facts with "and" or "because" |
| S2 | Short sentences: 20 words (instructions), 25 (descriptions) | 80% allows a small overrun |
| S3 | Condition first: "If X, do Y." | Same |
| S4 | Do not drop words ("the", "a", "that") | 80% allows fragments in tables and headings |
| S5 | Lists for steps and complex content | Same |
| S6 | Active voice | Same |
| S7 | Simple tenses only | Same |
| S8 | Verbs, not nouns, no "-ing" chains | Strict: "check" and "test" are nouns |
| S9 | Honest modals: can, must, will | 80% keeps "may" and "should" for real doubt |
| S10 | Plain words, one meaning each, no phrasal verbs | 80% keeps natural words |
| S11 | One term per thing | Same |
| S12 | No noun stacks over three words | Same |
| S13 | One topic per paragraph, six sentences at most | Same |
| S14 | Procedure apart from description, warnings first | Same |
| S15 | Simple punctuation, no semicolons | Strict: also no contractions |

More examples: [references/ste80-rules.md](references/ste80-rules.md). Full strict rules and a checklist: [references/strict-mode.md](references/strict-mode.md). More than 100 plain-word swaps: [references/word-swaps.md](references/word-swaps.md).

## Checker

`scripts/ste_check.py` is a small Python linter with no dependencies. It flags many Pass 1 tells, such as not-X-but-Y, chatbot phrases, run-ups, fake depth, stacked hedges, vague authority and association, "-ing" riders, inflated claims, AI words, hyphen pairs and curly quotes. It also flags the measurable Pass 2 rules: sentence and paragraph length, semicolons, dashes, passive voice, perfect and progressive tenses, "-ing" forms and phrasal verbs.

```bash
python scripts/ste_check.py README.md
python scripts/ste_check.py --strict docs/runbook.md
cat draft.txt | python scripts/ste_check.py -
```

It is a heuristic, not an AI detector and not a compliance checker.

## Tests

`evals/` has four cases in the `claude plugin eval` format: a README rewrite, an explanation from scratch, a strict runbook and a casual LinkedIn post that does not mention STE. Run them with `claude plugin eval . --allow-tools Write,Edit,Bash`.

What we saw: when the prompt names ASD-STE100, the base model already gets the style mostly right. The skill made the difference in fidelity. In the LinkedIn rewrite, the run without the skill invented a quote and changed "40+ customers" to "40-odd". The run with the skill kept every fact. In the README rewrite, it kept "you may need to" and flagged a contradiction in the source. These are small tests, so treat them as a hint, not proof.

## Limits

- **STE is for clear explanatory text.** For fiction, speeches and brand copy, the skill does Pass 1 only.
- **STE is an English standard.** For other languages, the skill applies the tells and the structure rules, but not the English word lists.
- **"STE style" is not "STE compliant."** Compliance needs the official dictionary, trained writers and review.

## Sources and credits

- Andrej Karpathy on X, 2 October 2026: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2105819303471976479
- ASD-STE100 Issue 9 (2025): https://www.asd-ste100.org
- Wikipedia, [Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing) (WikiProject AI Cleanup)
- [blader/humanizer](https://github.com/blader/humanizer) by Siqi Chen (MIT). Pass 1 follows its 26-pattern catalog and order, with new examples. Its license notice is in [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).
- Hacker News discussion of STE skills (July 2026): https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49114639

## Disclaimer

This skill does not contain the ASD-STE100 specification or its dictionary. The STE rules are paraphrased and simplified. ASD-STE100 and Simplified Technical English are trademarks of ASD (AeroSpace, Security and Defence Industries Association of Europe). This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by ASD.

 Twelve nodes. Two registers per node. Fifteen lines of code. In TIS-100 , even multiplying two numbers is a small engineering project, and players have spent a decade optimizing these programs on a public community leaderboard . We gave 16 LLMs the game and its manual, withheld the leaderboard, and told them to keep improving. 
 133 new frontier points 18 / 55 puzzles with new frontier points 3 outright cycle records 
 Within days, players picked up the models’ programs and improved on most of them. 
 
 
 
 
 
 Watch the launch video. 
 
 
 
 
 Each node is a tiny processor, and neighboring nodes have to wait for one another to exchange values. The game scores a working solution on cycles, nodes, and instructions , and you start wondering whether one more instruction could disappear. Lower is better, but improving one score can make another worse, so each puzzle has a frontier of tradeoffs instead of one best answer. 
 Discovering the tricks is much of the fun, and this article spoils them. If this sounds cool, play it first: Buy on Steam Buy on GOG DRM-free 
 
 
 
 Leaderboard 
 We ran 16 LLMs, covering leading frontier and open-weight models. Every model attempted all 47 puzzles in the game, plus eight community tournament puzzles , in one scored attempt each (pass@1), with 10 to 45 minutes per puzzle, depending on difficulty, to find a working program and keep improving it. 
 New frontier point A solution that no community solution ties or beats on all three scores at once. It can use more code to run faster, for example. We froze the community leaderboard on October 15, 2026, before submitting anything, and count a point only if it also passes 100,000 tests.

 How it works: harness design 
 Every result here is a program we can run and test on fresh inputs, which makes a programming game a useful benchmark. Models get what a player can inspect, through text tools instead of a mouse and screenshots: the manual, visible test inputs, registers, and game feedback. They don’t get community code or exact records, only the game’s coarse score histograms. 
 
 Read, edit, run Models read the puzzle and language reference, edit programs, and run them in the real game. 
 Diagnostics Wrong outputs and deadlocks return mismatches, registers, and blocked ports, so the next edit can respond to evidence. 
 Saved progress Every passing program joins the model’s own frontier and can be recovered with get_best , so a risky edit can’t lose an earlier result. 
 Reminders If a model ends its turn early, a reminder asks it to keep testing, so quitting early doesn’t decide the score. Reminders contain no solution hints. 
 A visible clock Models see time used against a 10-, 30-, or 45-minute limit. Setup doesn’t count; thinking and game calls do. Models can’t end an episode early. 
 Run limits Game execution stops after roughly 1 second without state changes, 5 seconds without output, or 60 seconds overall, and returns diagnostics. 
 
 Why test 100,000 inputs? The game checks a small set of cases per run. Our headline count requires a fresh-game replay and 100,000 passing tests on the independent TIS-100-CXX simulator , providing stronger evidence that a program generalizes to new inputs. 
 
 
 One record up close 
 Undecimal Twin Rounder SPEC44149538 , one of the eight tournament puzzles, rounds an input to the nearest multiple of N on one output and of 11−N on the other. When we froze the leaderboard, the best community program took 2,694 cycles . Opus 5.5 passed its first program after 6.5 minutes, at 5,669 cycles. It went under the record 16 minutes in and finished at 1,918 , which is 29% faster . That speed cost one more node and 28 more instructions than the old record. 
 The core of the program is a two-speed search. Instead of subtracting N one step at a time, nodes 5 and 6 subtract 4N until they overshoot, then add N back until the value turns positive. Each drives a small coprocessor, node 2 or node 7, by sending it jump offsets through a port, so the coprocessor works as a lookup table for 4N and N.

 What the models built 
 We grouped all 55 puzzles by their main demand, then read the programs. Fifteen of the sixteen models solved all five routing puzzles, and none found a new frontier point there. The examples below show how different designs spend the same resources.

 Multiplication: spend code to save cycles 
 Signal Multiplier 43786 has no MUL . Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-6 Astra use JRO , a relative jump, to enter a block of repeated instructions at the right position. The jump selects how many copies of a value to send and add, saving the counter updates and branches of a multiplication loop. Gemini 4 Argon ’s fastest program uses two paths to multiply in parallel and a final node to interleave their outputs. It takes 436 cycles against GPT-6 Astra ’s 523, about 17% faster , at a cost of two more nodes and 33 more instructions. 
 The cost of a faster multiplier Cycles per run · lower is better Gemini 4 Argon 436 cycles 7 nodes · 64 instructions GPT-6 Astra 523 cycles 5 nodes · 31 instructions Gemini 4 Argon 436c · 7n · 64i GPT-6 Astra 523c · 5n · 31i 
 
 Window sums: distribute the history 
 Signal Window Filter 60099 outputs the sums of the last three and last five inputs, so a solution has to remember history as well as add. Gemini 4 Argon ’s four-node program uses SWP to rotate stored values and ADD / SUB to update running state. GPT-6.1 Sol spreads that delay and aggregation across seven nodes, passing intermediate values between them. GPT-6.1 Sol ’s program runs in 318 cycles with 26 instructions; Gemini 4 Argon ’s takes 428 cycles with only 17 . The difference is how much of the work runs in parallel, and how much communication and code that costs.

 Indexed access from stacks 
 T31 Node Emulator NEXUS.23.727.9 needs eight addressable storage slots, but the available memory nodes are stacks. These programs move values between stacks to reach the requested slot, then read or replace it. MiMo-V2.6-Pro uses counted transfer loops; Opus 5.5 uses JRO to pick among unrolled transfers, spending extra instructions to save cycles. Memory isn’t one skill: MiMo-V2.6-Pro solves this emulator but fails Sequence Mode Calculator NEXUS.09.904.9 and Signal Window Filter 60099 .

 Each row is that model’s fastest saved program for the puzzle, picked for illustration. Not all are new frontier points. 
 
 
 God mode: what if the model could see the target? 
 The main benchmark hides the community’s scores. In a separate study on six puzzles, five models got: 
 
 The target: exact community scores, showing which tradeoffs remain unbeaten. 
 Diagnostics: cycle-by-cycle traces and profiles of where each node stalls. 
 Edge cases: a fast simulator that runs 10,000 random tests and returns failures. 
 More time: 30 minutes, plus extensions for progress, up to 60. 
 
 Every model improved: GPT-6 Astra from 82.8 to 91.8, GPT-6.1 Sol from 82.9 to 90.6, Opus 5.5 from 81.4 to 89.1, Grok 4.7 from 67.5 to 75.1, and Gemini 4 Argon from 83.5 to 87.9 in mean record proximity. Scores rose in 28 of the 30 model–puzzle pairs. 
 Score quality with a richer setup Mean record proximity · same six puzzles per model · higher is better Standard episode God mode 
 The diagnostics changed what models did next. On Signal Multiplexer 22280 , GPT-6.1 Sol ’s first passing program took 294 cycles . Its profile showed node 2 working 86% of the time while nodes 1 and 3 spent 84% blocked waiting to write to it. GPT-6.1 Sol moved the branching out of node 2 and into those two neighbors. The next run took 204 cycles , 31% faster , at a cost of two more nodes and five more instructions. 
 The extra time behind those scores Mean elapsed minutes per puzzle · same episodes Standard episode God mode 
 Information, tools, and time all changed together, so this study can’t say which addition helped most. These runs are outside the main leaderboard and the headline count. 
 Puzzles: Signal Multiplexer, Sequence Generator, Signal Edge Detector, Interrupt Handler, Sequence Peak Detector, and Signal Error Corrector. 
 
 
 Co-discovery 
 
 We submitted selected programs to the leaderboard, and the community improved on them almost immediately. On Undecimal Twin Rounder SPEC44149538 , @LongingForRest took Opus 5.5 ’s 1,918-cycle program and cut it to 1,744 by the next day. The record is now credited to both: LongingForRest/opus-5-5 . 
 Neither got there alone. The models found new tradeoffs quickly, and players read those programs, worked out why they worked, and took them further. 
 Mathematics is seeing the same shift. Terence Tao and colleagues used LLM-guided search across 67 problems and improved on the best known results in several. In “After Math,” Silvia De Toffoli and Eamon Duede argue that a result only becomes a solution once mathematicians can understand it, and that AI fits better as an assistant than a competitor. TIS-100 is a small, measurable version of that future: a model finds a better program, and people turn it into something they understand.

 Methods Expand 
 
 Suite. All 22 campaign puzzles, all 25 TIS-NET puzzles, and eight tournament puzzles from 2018: 19 easy (10 minutes), 17 medium (30), and 19 hard (45). Every model has one scored episode per puzzle. Time limits differ by difficulty, so difficulty and search time can’t be separated. 
 Scoring. Each model–puzzle pair contributes one selected attempt, with no best-of-attempts scoring, so solve rates are pass@1: a puzzle counts as solved when that one episode saved a program that replays in a fresh game. Unsolved puzzles stay in every average and score zero. 
 New frontier points. The reference is the community leaderboard as of October 15, 2026. Ties don’t count. Models found 154 candidate points on 23 puzzles. Our count pools and deduplicates them across models and keeps the 133 on 18 puzzles with fresh-game replay and 100,000 passing tests. Testing is strong evidence of correctness, not proof. 
 Record proximity. The community record divided by the model’s best score, averaged across the three scores and all puzzles, ×100. Each score can come from a different program. 
 Limits. One episode per pair compares the configurations as tested and doesn’t measure repeated-run variability. Spread between puzzles is variation across tasks. Public puzzles may overlap with training data. Mechanic groups are our own labels. 
 Programs. Every model Pareto point’s program is public under the MIT License, in TIS-100 save format and named like the community leaderboard’s files ( <puzzle>.<cycles>-<nodes>-<instructions>.txt ). They are mirrored as one file per program on GitHub and as a table on Hugging Face . Two points replay in the game but fail some random tests; they are included and never count as new frontier points. 
 Resources. Costs are estimated from recorded October 2026 API list prices, including cache discounts. Tokens accumulate across responses, so repeated input counts again, and tokenizers differ. Game calls count individual dispatched tools, including errors, and exclude the automatic final submission.

A sandboxed scripting tool for game calls was available in 46–54 of each model’s 55 episodes. A note about the game’s random test reached 841 of 880 episodes. 6 Opus 5.5 episodes and 5 Sonnet 5.5 episodes ran in a different agent client at the same effort. 
 
 
 Related work 
 ISA-Bench studies reasoning with constrained instruction sets, including TIS-100. Opus Magnum Bench tests agents’ ability to build and optimize machines in another Zachtronics game. We focus on optimization across all TIS-100 puzzles and eight community puzzles, keeping tradeoffs across cycles, nodes, and instructions. The tasks and protocols differ, so scores aren’t directly comparable.

 Title: Learning Heterogeneous Tactile Representation for General Dexterous Manipulation 
 Authors: Bing Han , Yichuan Peng , Haoyu Dong , Yuanmeng Hu , Yongyi Jia , Fangjing Wang , Kecheng Zheng , Yiming Zhang , Yanhong Zeng , Xiaoqing Zhang , Chen Song , Rundong Zou , Anqi Dong , Yuan Guan , Ka Leong Cheng , Xing Zhu , Yujun Shen , Nan Xue , Wei Ning View a PDF of the paper titled Learning Heterogeneous Tactile Representation for General Dexterous Manipulation, by Bing Han and 18 other authors 
 View PDF 



 
 Abstract: Tactile sensing is an indispensable modality for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, a capability that hints at the ultimate frontiers of embodied intelligence. However, commercially available tactile sensors are still at a relatively early stage of development, with each type of sensor offering irreplaceable strengths alongside its own drawbacks. A key challenge is thus to free tactile understanding from sensor-specific physics, so that embodied models can effectively leverage heterogeneous tactile data. To this end, we develop LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model characterized by the following properties. (i) Our model yields a unified representation across different tactile sensors (i.e., piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors), and is easily extensible to new sensor types. (ii) The resulting tactile tokens are plug-and-play: they can be seamlessly integrated into policy models across paradigms, from diffusion policy to vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $\pi_{0.5}$ and LingBot-VLA, consistently enhancing manipulation dexterity. (iii) Extensive experiments, spanning simulation and real-robot deployments across multiple hardware platforms, demonstrate that our tactile representation substantially benefits complex manipulation tasks while maintaining strong computational efficiency. We believe the findings in this work demonstrate the potential of leveraging cross-sensor data to scale tactile learning, and offer encouraging insights for the design of future hardware and embodied models.
